title: Quantum Sensing Analyzer
summary: The “Quantum Sensing Analyzer” project aims to address critical limitations in existing electromagnetic measurement technologies by developing a novel quantum-based sensing capability utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors.
description:
The “Quantum Sensing Analyzer” project aims to address critical limitations in existing electromagnetic measurement technologies by developing a novel quantum-based sensing capability utilizing Rydberg atomic sensors. These sensors, leveraging quantum properties, exhibit extraordinary sensitivity and accuracy over a widespread frequency spectrum ranging from DC to 1 THz, with potential scalability to even broader ranges. This initiative is designed to modernize and standardize test and evaluation processes within the Department of Defense (DoD), particularly benefiting the Benefield Anechoic Facility (BAF) and its mission to support advanced electromagnetic system testing.

Problem Statement and Opportunity:
Current electromagnetic measurement techniques rely on diverse and complex instruments, which introduce inefficiencies, inconsistencies, and increased costs for the acquisition, testing, and integration of modern radar systems, electronic warfare platforms, communication systems, and antennas. These existing systems also face challenges in maintaining accuracy and repeatability, particularly when evaluating performance across a wide range of radio frequencies or within controlled environments like anechoic chambers.
The introduction of Rydberg sensor technology represents a disruptive opportunity to establish a universal, high-precision, SI-traceable standard for electromagnetic measurements. By adopting a single, compact, and adaptable sensor for diverse measurement tasks—including spectrum analysis, field strength monitoring, and chamber characterization—this capability promises to significantly reduce infrastructure requirements, simplify operational workflows, and enhance confidence in test data accuracy.

Project Objectives:

Develop and validate a proof-of-concept Rydberg-based quantum sensing system capable of performing highly accurate and repeatable electromagnetic measurements across 1.5 MHz to 40 GHz.
Demonstrate the ability of the sensor to serve as a universal measurement standard for radar, electronic warfare, communication systems, and antenna evaluation.
Establish enhanced chamber characterization capabilities, including electromagnetic leakage detection, direction finding, near-field measurement, reflection mitigation, and quiet zone mapping, to improve the testing environment quality.
Progress the technology readiness level (TRL) from TRL 2 at project initiation to TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II.

Required Efforts and Phase Activities:
Phase I:

Perform a comprehensive feasibility study to assess the applicability of Rydberg atomic sensors as a universal electromagnetic measurement standard.
Evaluate the sensors’ technical attributes, including sensitivity (targeting sub-microvolt/meter thresholds), dynamic range, and bandwidth.
Identify potential integration challenges with existing test facilities and systems, particularly those used in the BAF.
Deliverables: Feasibility study report detailing technical analyses, identified challenges, and potential solutions; preliminary system design for a prototype quantum sensing analyzer.

Phase II:

Develop, fabricate, and demonstrate a functional prototype of the Rydberg-based quantum sensing system, incorporating key findings from Phase I.
Conduct extensive testing and validation of the prototype in operationally relevant environments, including the BAF, with emphasis on precision, SI-traceability, and repeatability of electromagnetic measurements.
Integrate the system into existing DoD testing workflows, showcasing improvements in efficiency, reduced equipment requirements, and testing performance.
Deliverables: Fully operational prototype, detailed test and evaluation report, system integration plan, and transition strategy for scaling and deployment within the DoD.

Desired Outcome:
The successful development of a Quantum Sensing Analyzer will revolutionize the DoD’s electromagnetic measurement and testing capabilities by delivering a single, universal, quantum-enabled sensing standard. This solution will eliminate the need for multiple specialized instruments, streamline developmental and operational testing, and significantly enhance test accuracy and repeatability. Furthermore, the technology will address critical modernization priorities, such as advancing quantum science and enabling operationally focused Advanced Battle Management Systems (ABMS). This effort aligns with the Air Force’s strategic goals to improve mission readiness, accelerate technology deployment to the warfighter, and invest in cutting-edge testing capabilities that sustain innovation and technical superiority in defense systems.

title: Solid Propellent Environmental Effects Digital Twin
summary: Solid Rocket Motors (SRMs) provide propulsion for many critical defense applications including surface launched, air launched, ballistic, and space vehicles.
description: Solid Rocket Motors (SRMs) provide propulsion for many critical defense applications including surface launched, air launched, ballistic, and space vehicles. The propellant that creates acceleration through these SRMs is a complex active material that can be sensitive to environmental effects from thermal loads, exposure to air or humidity, chemical changes, pressure, or vibration loads due to time or ingredient changes. Both mechanical response characteristics and ballistic properties can be affected. This topic requests projects that will combine computational modeling and design capability from several sources to simulate aging responses due to environmental effects. The framework must follow Modular Open Systems Approach standards mandated in 10 U.S.C. § 4401 for compatibility with several commercially available computational tools such as ANSYS, ABAQUS, Python, MatLab, SysML, and others.

title: Low - Cost Neuromorphic Edge Intelligence for Persistent Autonomous Change Detection and Machine Situational Memory
summary: Traditional airborne ISR architectures frequently collect and transmit large quantities of data even when little or nothing within the observed environment has changed. This creates substantial burdens on: Communications bandwidth. Processing. Storage. Power. Analysts. Command-and-control systems.
description:
Traditional airborne ISR architectures frequently collect and transmit large quantities of data even when little or nothing within the observed environment has changed. This creates substantial burdens on: Communications bandwidth. Processing. Storage. Power. Analysts. Command-and-control systems. Neuromorphic and event-driven sensors offer a fundamentally different sensing architecture in which the system responds primarily to changes within the observed environment.
The desired capability should combine event-driven sensing with onboard edge intelligence and temporal machine memory. Fundamental engineering considerations include: Event-driven/neuromorphic sensor characterization. Low-latency onboard processing. Low power consumption. Detection of operationally relevant changes. Rejection of irrelevant changes caused by lighting, weather, vegetation, shadows, sensor motion, or environmental clutter. Temporal comparison across repeated observations. Persistent representation of previous environmental state. Confidence scoring for detected changes. Autonomous prioritization of significant changes. Ability to cue additional onboard sensors. Generation of compact change products instead of continuous raw-data transmission. Multi-UAS sharing of relevant environmental changes. Open interfaces for integration with aircraft mission systems. Desired change classes may include movement, addition, removal, modification, displacement, construction, damage, altered activity patterns, or other Government-defined changes.

title: High-Efficiency Expeditionary Group 2 and Group 3 VTOL UAS for Long-Range Distributed ISR/SOF Operations
summary: Runway independence provides substantial operational flexibility for ISR/SOF missions but creates significant technical penalties in aircraft weight, propulsion complexity, energy consumption, endurance, payload, reliability, and cost.
description:
Runway independence provides substantial operational flexibility for ISR/SOF missions but creates significant technical penalties in aircraft weight, propulsion complexity, energy consumption, endurance, payload, reliability, and cost. The research challenge is to minimize these penalties while enabling a persistent, expeditionary autonomous aircraft capable of operating from austere and distributed locations. The Government seeks emerging VTOL technologies combining reliable vertical operations with efficient forward flight, extended endurance, useful payload capacity, resilient communications, and autonomous mission execution. Solutions may employ tilt-wing, tilt-rotor, lift-plus-cruise, tailsitter, distributed propulsion, hybrid propulsion, or other technically viable architectures. Companies should specifically highlight demonstrated capabilities, current maturity, projected performance, and remaining technical risks in the following areas:
VTOL Endurance: Capability to achieve 12-15 hours of flight time is critical. Offerors should identify payload, speed, altitude, loiter profile, environmental assumptions, and propulsion configuration associated with demonstrated or projected endurance. Propulsion: Gas-powered propulsion is of particular interest for meeting extended sortie-duration requirements. Fully electric, hybrid-electric, or alternative propulsion solutions are acceptable if they can meet the required sortie duration and mission-performance objectives. In-Flight Recharge: Technologies enabling in-flight energy replenishment or recharge are of interest, including architectures supporting a six B.A. battery configuration, where applicable. Payload: Adjustable and modular payload capacity with a minimum desired capability greater than 60 pounds while maintaining an 12-15-hour loiter/endurance profile. Offerors should additionally characterize performance and design tradeoffs associated with payload growth toward 75 pounds.
Network Node / Layered Effects / Force Packaging: Ability to operate as an airborne network node and participate in distributed, layered effects and multi-platform force packages. BLOS: Resilient beyond-line-of-sight communications and autonomous mission execution without reliance upon continuous line-of-sight C2. Vigilant Spirit: Existing integration, interoperability, or a clearly defined integration pathway with Vigilant Spirit. Dynamic Targeting: Ability to receive mission updates and dynamically retask, revisit/retest areas or objects of interest, reassess previous observations or effects, and conduct authorized subsequent mission actions. NKE / ESM: Ability to host, support, and employ modular non-kinetic effects and Electronic Support Measures payloads. Extended Autonomy: Architecture capable of supporting autonomous missions approaching 15 hours, including reliable operation for representative periods of at least 5 minutes without human intervention. Companies should characterize autonomy reliability, intervention rate, failure modes, contingency behavior, recovery, and lost-link performance. VTOL Efficiency Demonstrate autonomous vertical takeoff and recovery. Quantify hover and VTOL fuel/energy consumption. Demonstrate efficient transition between vertical and forward flight. Quantify VTOL energy penalty relative to total mission energy. Range and Endurance Demonstrate or substantiate a credible path to8 hours of flight endurance with representative payload. Characterize mission radius, maximum range, endurance, and loiter time. Quantify payload/range/endurance trade space. Characterize forward-flight propulsion efficiency. Identify fuel or energy requirements associated with representative ISR/SOF mission profiles. For fully electric systems, demonstrate the ability to achieve required sortie duration. Where proposed, characterize in-flight recharge or energy replenishment. Payload and Mission Systems Support an adjustable/modular payload of at least 25 pounds at the desired 8-hour profile. Characterize growth potential toward60 pounds. Characterize payload mass, volume, power, data, thermal, RF, and mechanical interfaces. Support Government or third-party payload integration. Support NKE and ESM payloads. Support airborne network-node functionality. Provide documented interfaces supporting integration with Vigilant Spirit and other Government mission systems. Expeditionary Operations
Minimize launch/recovery footprint. Minimize personnel and ground-support equipment. Minimize arrival-to-launch and recovery-to-relaunch timelines. Minimize assembly, disassembly, maintenance, and site-preparation requirements. Support distributed ISR/SOF employment from austere locations. Autonomy and Dynamic Mission Execution Autonomous takeoff and landing. Autonomous transition. Autonomous navigation, loiter, mission execution, return, and precision recovery. Dynamic inflight mission retasking. Support dynamic targeting and authorized retest/revisit and reattack/re-engagement sequences. Deterministic contingency and lost-link behavior. Architecture capable of missions approaching12 hours of autonomous operation. Demonstrate representative mission periods of at least5 minutes without human intervention. Characterize autonomy reliability, intervention frequency, mission-completion rate, fault tolerance, failure modes, and recovery behavior. Resilient Communications and Operations
Maintain useful navigation and mission capability during GNSS degradation or loss. Support BLOS communications and mission operations. Maintain autonomous mission capability during intermittent, degraded, or lost C2. Demonstrate deterministic lost-link behavior. Support network-node functionality within distributed force packages. Exchange mission, sensor, platform-status, and targeting information with Government systems. Affordability and Producibility Quantify projected recurring unit cost. Identify major cost drivers. Demonstrate production-relevant manufacturing. Quantify manufacturing labor, lead time, supply-chain constraints, and scalable production rate. The Government seeks existing aircraft and enabling technologies requiring engineering maturation and integration. Clean-sheet aircraft without demonstrated underlying flight technology are not the target of this effort.

title: Collaborative Autonomous UAS for Distributed Non-Kinetic Effects
summary: Traditional non-kinetic capabilities can be constrained by platform availability, cost, survivability, operator workload, communications requirements, and centralized mission architectures.
description:
Traditional non-kinetic capabilities can be constrained by platform availability, cost, survivability, operator workload, communications requirements, and centralized mission architectures.
Distributed autonomous UAS create the opportunity to separate the mission effect from a single exquisite platform and distribute sensing, decision-making, communications, and payload employment across multiple lower-cost aircraft.
The Government seeks modular technologies enabling Group 2/3 UAS and similarly expendable autonomous aircraft to collaboratively carry and employ Government-approved non-kinetic payloads while operating under a human-on-the-loop command architecture.
Potential mission functions may include lawful and authorized:
Electronic support. Communications relay. Spectrum sensing. Deception and decoy functions. Distributed RF effects. Cooperative sensing. Network extension. Authorized cyber-physical mission effects. Signature generation. Mission-support effects. Other non-destructive effects.
This topic is focused on enabling technologies, payload integration, distributed autonomy, mission coordination, and command-and-control architecture, not development of offensive cyber capabilities.
Fundamental engineering considerations include:
Modular Mission Systems
Modular payload integration. Open mechanical, electrical, power, data, RF, and software interfaces. Integration of Government or third-party payloads without fundamental aircraft redesign. Support for multiple payload types and aircraft architectures. Low-SWaP-C implementation suitable for expendable UAS.
Collaborative Autonomy
Autonomous task allocation. Collaborative mission planning and execution. Distributed decision-making. Dynamic reassignment of tasks following aircraft or payload loss. Cooperative sensing and information sharing. Graceful degradation as individual aircraft become unavailable. Quantifiable collaborative mission performance.
Human-on-the-Loop Control
Human-on-the-loop mission command and authorization. Positive control over initiation and termination of mission effects. Operator ability to modify objectives, constraints, or mission priorities. Deterministic responses to loss of communications. Abort and safe-state functionality. Appropriate human authorization for mission functions requiring Government approval.
Communications and Distributed Operations
Operation with intermittent, degraded, or unavailable communications. Distributed decision-making without persistent centralized control. Low-bandwidth coordination methods. Time and spatial synchronization. Network extension and relay capability. Resilient interfaces with Government mission and C2 systems.
Mission Assurance
Geographical, temporal, frequency, target-set, or mission-based constraints as applicable. Prevention of unintended or unauthorized effects. Defined operating boundaries. Fault detection and graceful degradation. Quantifiable reliability and mission-effect performance.

title: Long-Range, Expendable Autonomous Air Vehicle for Distributed Effects in Contested Environments
summary: Future contested operations may require the ability to generate large numbers of distributed airborne effects at ranges beyond those achievable by many existing Group 2/3 UAS.The desired system should combine sufficient aerodynamic efficiency, propulsion performance, autonomous mission execution, modular payload integration, resilient navigation, and low-cost manufacturing to enable operations…
description: Future contested operations may require the ability to generate large numbers of distributed airborne effects at ranges beyond those achievable by many existing Group 2/3 UAS.The desired system should combine sufficient aerodynamic efficiency, propulsion performance, autonomous mission execution, modular payload integration, resilient navigation, and low-cost manufacturing to enable operations at ranges between approximately 400 and 1,200 NM. Solutions should emphasize a modular vehicle architecture allowing Government or third-party payloads, autonomy, navigation, and communications components to be integrated without redesigning the entire aircraft. Range and Mission Performance ≥400 NM threshold to 1,200 NM with demonstrable varying ranges under a clearly defined mission profile.Document payload/range/endurance trade space.Characterize representative payload, launch conditions, altitude, speed, propulsion configuration, and mission profile.Demonstrate sufficient aerodynamic and propulsion efficiency to achieve long-range operation at acceptable recurring cost. Autonomous Mission ExecutionAutonomous launch and transition to mission flight.Autonomous navigation and mission execution.Autonomous terminal mission functions appropriate to the proposed concept.Continued mission execution during intermittent or extended loss of command-and-control connectivity.Deterministic and configurable lost-link behavior.Mission-planning interfaces that minimize operator workload.Architecture capable of incorporating Government-provided autonomy.Resilient NavigationMaintain useful navigation during representative GNSS degradation, denial, interference, or loss. Characterize navigation performance, accumulated error, availability, and recovery. Support integration of complementary navigation sources. Collaborative navigation approaches are of interest where sufficiently mature for Phase II integration and flight demonstration. Navigation technologies should be mature enough to support the overall D2P2 schedule; maturation of 5-6 TRL fundamental navigation concepts is not the primary intent of this effort..Modular Mission ArchitectureModular mechanical, electrical, power, data, and software interfaces.Integration of Government or third-party payloads without fundamental air-vehicle redesign.Architecture capable of accepting Government-provided autonomy, navigation, communications, and payload components.Document Government-accessible interfaces necessary for transition.PropulsionCharacterize propulsion performance.Quantify fuel/energy consumption across representative mission profiles.Identify propulsion reliability and remaining maturation risks.Characterize range, payload, and propulsion trade space.Environmental and Structural PerformanceDemonstrate environmental and structural suitability for representative operational employment.Characterize launch loads, flight loads, environmental limitations, and relevant storage/transport constraints.Affordability and Scalable ManufacturingTreat recurring unit cost as a primary system-level design consideration.Identify major unit-cost drivers.Demonstrate production-relevant manufacturing approaches.Reduce dependence on scarce materials, specialized tooling, and labor-intensive production where technically feasible.Quantify production scalability, lead time, labor content, and supply-chain risks.Consider rapid, distributed, or high-rate manufacturing approaches.The Government is interested in existing technologies requiring integration and maturation, not clean-sheet conceptual aircraft requiring extended basic research.

title: Rapidly Reconfigurable Pod-Based System Survivability Suite for Air Operations in Contested Environments
summary: Modern multi-domain operational environments present increasingly agile, multi-spectral threat emitters spanning radio frequency (RF), infrared (IR), and electro-optical (EO) regimes. Conventional aircraft survivability equipment (ASE) suffers from hardwired, federated implementations, tightly coupled mechanical and electrical host dependencies, and high-latency upgrade cycles.
description:
Modern multi-domain operational environments present increasingly agile, multi-spectral threat emitters spanning radio frequency (RF), infrared (IR), and electro-optical (EO) regimes. Conventional aircraft survivability equipment (ASE) suffers from hardwired, federated implementations, tightly coupled mechanical and electrical host dependencies, and high-latency upgrade cycles. Overcoming these barriers requires foundational research into containerized, hardware-agnostic modular payloads, high-efficiency edge processing architectures, and adaptive aperture configurations that can operate autonomously while remaining fully interoperable with joint command-and-control networks.
This topic solicits applied research and experimental development into an externally carried, modular open-system survivability architecture. While leveraging mature sensing and countermeasure components where appropriate, the primary technical investigation focuses on heterogeneous compute abstraction and advanced processing architectures. This entails researching novel architectural patterns that abstract diverse federated signal processing, countermeasure arbitration, threat correlation, and cross-platform networking into a unified, modular, software-defined compute environment. Key research activities include evaluating containerization paradigms, real-time deterministic virtualization, and Open Mission Systems / Universal Command and Control Interface (OMS/UCI) standard execution under strict size, weight, power, and thermal (SWaP-C) limitations.
Simultaneously, the effort must resolve multi-physics boundary constraints and sensor obscuration challenges. This requires developing high-fidelity analytical, computational fluid dynamic (CFD), and electro-optical/electromagnetic models to characterize and mitigate aircraft-induced obscuration and aero-optical distortion across diverse carriage regimes. Research will further focus on distributed aperture hand-off algorithms and multi-pod sensor correlation to synthesize complete, gapless spherical coverage (steradian field-of-regard) across heterogeneous, dynamic flight profiles.
Finally, the investigation addresses dynamic interoperability and low-latency autonomous response mechanisms. Investigation is needed into machine-to-machine autonomy algorithms capable of conducting real-time threat detection, localized track clustering, and immediate self-protection countermeasure dispense and pointing without operator-in-the-loop dependencies, while concurrently synthesizing threat telemetry for dissemination across communications links. Underpinning this entire capability is the design of open, non-proprietary physical and logical interface syntax aligned with Modular Open Systems Approach (MOSA) guidelines to enable zero-rework substitution of future experimental payloads.

title: Multi-Function Processor, Rapid Architecture, Miniaturized (MFP-RAM)
summary: Tactical communications systems must operate in RF-dense and contested environments while adapting to changing mission requirements. Current tightly coupled, proprietary, single-purpose hardware limits rapid technology insertion and the coexistence of multiple security domains.
description: Tactical communications systems must operate in RF-dense and contested environments while adapting to changing mission requirements. Current tightly coupled, proprietary, single-purpose hardware limits rapid technology insertion and the coexistence of multiple security domains. The Government seeks a COTS-first, modular, reconfigurable hybrid communications Line Replaceable Unit that integrates multi-band Software Defined Radios, modular open-system interfaces, secure RED/BLACK separation, and a containerized software environment. The capability must support integration into representative air platforms while reducing host-aircraft modification burden and enabling future waveform or payload changes with minimal redesign.Proposals must address the remaining system-level research and development required to integrate, validate, qualify, and flight-demonstrate the hybrid communications capability. Proposals do not have to result in a production-ready capability, but must be sufficient to facilitate a minimum viable product (MVP) which can be used in a surrogate flight demonstration.

title: A unified model for specification and simulation to design, acquire, and sustain a hybrid- or multi-cloud large scale data analytics system that balances cost, performance, modularity, and security.
summary: Modern software-centric data systems across the Department of War operate in highly dynamic, shared cloud and hybrid infrastructure environments. Within complex weapon system sustainment platforms, such as the RSO CBM+ enterprise, accurately predicting and managing lifecycle resource consumption, computing performance, and ongoing operational costs presents a substantial operational challenge.
description:
Modern software-centric data systems across the Department of War operate in highly dynamic, shared cloud and hybrid infrastructure environments. Within complex weapon system sustainment platforms, such as the RSO CBM+ enterprise, accurately predicting and managing lifecycle resource consumption, computing performance, and ongoing operational costs presents a substantial operational challenge. Cloud and hybrid hosting costs fluctuate due to stochastic workload behaviors, data egress, and dynamic compute allocation. Across commercial and defense sectors, approximately 49% of organizations lack dedicated FinOps capabilities, resulting in frequent budget variances exceeding 18% and inefficient allocation of critical resources.
Traditional MBSE methodologies and legacy toolchains (e.g., static Cameo models, detached MATLAB scripts, disconnected spreadsheets) lack the capability to execute high-fidelity, time-dependent simulations directly within the primary system specification model. This fragmentation creates significant lag between architectural planning, empirical software telemetry, and financial governance, severely limiting rapid system analysis and trade-space optimization.
To address this capability gap, this project seeks innovative solutions that bridge DevOps, FinOps, and MBSE into a unified, executable environment. The proposed solution must demonstrate how system design specifications and executable simulation software can coexist within a cohesive architecture, such as an extensible, layered Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) utilizing Systems Modeling Language (SysML) or equivalent open modeling frameworks. Offerors should propose methods to capture continuous empirical data from operational and developmental environments, allowing the model to dynamically update, calibrate, and predict both Capital Expenditures and Operational Expenditures. The solution must support hybrid operational constraints, verifying that on-premise components sustain secure, disconnected operations while remaining optimized alongside cloud assets.
The entry Technology Readiness Level (TRL) for this D2P2 effort is expected to be TRL 4, progressing to TRL 6 by the conclusion of Phase II, culminating in a fully integrated, operationally viable prototype model and software suite demonstrated under representative operational conditions.

title: Mobile Expeditionary 3D Concrete Printer (MX3DCP)
summary: Problem: The U.S. Air Force faces an urgent and growing gap in its ability to rapidly harden, repair, and reconstitute expeditionary airbase infrastructure during combat operations.
description: Problem: The U.S. Air Force faces an urgent and growing gap in its ability to rapidly harden, repair, and reconstitute expeditionary airbase infrastructure during combat operations. Recent attacks against airbase infrastructure in the Middle East have reinforced a reality already evident in planning for the Indo-Pacific and other contested theaters: U.S. forces must be able to operate from bases that are vulnerable to missiles, rockets, artillery, one-way unmanned aircraft, and fragmentation-producing weapons. Current expeditionary infrastructure is often too slow to construct, too logistics-intensive to transport, or too lightly protected to provide meaningful survivability under modern attack conditions. Put bluntly, the Air Force has spent decades building exquisite kill chains while too often housing the Airmen who sustain them in tents, trailers, and flat-walled structures that were never designed for the threat environment now arriving overhead.Opportunity: 3D concrete printing offers a potential step-change in expeditionary construction by enabling military engineers to rapidly print protective structures using automated or semi-automated construction workflows, reduced skilled labor, and locally available cementitious materials where feasible. Prior work has demonstrated that cementitious materials can be printed, that full-scale structures can be produced with mobile 3DCP systems, and that limited blast testing can be performed on printed wall assemblies. However, the existing state of the art has not yet fully addressed the combined problem that matters most for combat survivability: printable expeditionary materials, field-executable operator workflows, and structure geometry deliberately optimized to mitigate blast-wave behavior and fragmentation effects.This Direct-to-Phase II effort will improve the current DoD technological state by integrating three related areas of technical development: advanced cementitious materials suitable for expeditionary printing; mobile, field-operable 3D concrete printing systems and workflows; and printable protective geometries designed to mitigate blast and fragmentation effects. First, the project will evaluate advanced cementitious materials, including Air Force Civil Engineer Center-developed materials and other candidate mixes, for printability, strength gain, curing behavior, environmental tolerance, pumpability, layer adhesion, and compatibility with native or in situ material sourcing. Second, the effort will develop and evaluate novel printable geometries that improve survivability beyond conventional flat-wall construction, including shapes intended to reduce blast reflection, limit pressure amplification, interrupt fragmentation paths, and improve internal occupant protection. Third, the project will validate these material and geometry combinations through representative printing, structural evaluation, and controlled blast/fragmentation testing.The initial technology readiness level is estimated at TRL 5, with discrete material, printer, and structure demonstrations approaching TRL 6. The current manufacturing readiness level is estimated at MRL 4 to 5, because the underlying processes exist but require maturation for repeatable production in austere conditions by lightly trained military personnel. The target at the end of Phase II is TRL 6 to 7 and MRL 5 to 6, supported by relevant-environment demonstrations, printed test articles, validated print parameters, documented material performance, and blast-response data suitable for transition planning.The required Phase II effort will include material screening and characterization; evaluation of locally sourced or partially substituted cementitious feedstocks; printability testing under relevant environmental conditions; development of candidate protective geometries; computational modeling of blast interaction and fragmentation exposure; printing of representative components and structure sections; controlled structural, blast, and fragmentation testing; operator workflow development; logistics and deployment analysis; and documentation of design rules, print parameters, safety considerations, and transition recommendations.Minimum deliverables will include a material characterization report; a printability and expeditionary logistics assessment; a geometry design and modeling report; representative printed test articles; blast and fragmentation test results; validated print parameters for selected material/geometry combinations; operator-ready draft technical procedures; and a final transition package identifying recommended use cases, limitations, equipment requirements, training requirements, and follow-on test needs.The desired outcome is a validated technical foundation for rapidly printed protective infrastructure that can be employed by Air Force civil engineers in expeditionary and combat environments. A successful effort will not replace all conventional construction, but it may give commanders a faster and more survivable option when the choice is currently between slow construction, vulnerable temporary shelters, or telling Airmen to make do with whatever was shipped before the shooting started.

title: Wide Pass Bandwidth, High Selectivity, Continuously Tunable Notch Filters
summary: The objective of this topic is to develop miniature, low power, and high selectivity tunable notch filters capable of protecting wideband receivers from large interferers. The effort will target the largest interferers which are in L, S, C, and X bands with tunable notch filters, while allowing pass bandwidths spanning L through Ku bands.
description:
The objective of this topic is to develop miniature, low power, and high selectivity tunable notch filters capable of protecting wideband receivers from large interferers. The effort will target the largest interferers which are in L, S, C, and X bands with tunable notch filters, while allowing pass bandwidths spanning L through Ku bands. Each notch filter must be continuously tunable across a minimum of 3 of the 4 targeted bands (L, S, C, and X) while having a notch depth > 20 dB and a notch bandwidth < 1 % across all tuned frequencies. With a narrow notch bandwidth, each notch filter must be programmable and maintained with an accuracy of 50% of the notch bandwidth and should maintain this accuracy over temperature. The notch filters must be able to reject large interfering signals and therefore should be able to notch receive interference levels greater than 5 dBm. In the bandpass each filter must cover L-Ku band (1-18 GHz) while maintaining a low insertion loss and noise figure of less than 1.5 dB and low passband distortion with an IIP3 > +50 dBm. Each notch filter must be small, less than 3 cc, and should be connectable in series without interfering with one another to notch multiple frequencies in the same receive chain. Finally, the power consumption, including any tuning electronics, of each notch filter should be less than 100 mW. The required metrics are:
Passband frequency range (GHz)1 – 18
Maximum passband insertion loss or noise figure (dB) ≤ 1.5
Passband IIP3 (dBm)≥ 50
Notch band tunable frequency range (GHz)1 – 12
Number of bands covered by a single, continuously tunable notch≥ 3
Minimum notch depth across all tuned notch states (dB)≥ 20
Maximum notch fractional bandwidth (%)≤ 1Size (cc)≤ 3
Power consumption (mW)≤ 100

title: Domestic Liquid Phase Epitaxy of Yttrium Iron Garnet Films for Resilient Microwave Filter Supply Chains
summary: This topics seeks proposals to design, procure, and commission a fully domestic LPE growth facility capable of producing device-grade YIG films on gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrates across the 10–150 µm thickness range. Efforts shall demonstrate system integration, process optimization, and material qualification sufficient for insertion into operational microwave filter architectures.
description: This topics seeks proposals to design, procure, and commission a fully domestic LPE growth facility capable of producing device-grade YIG films on gadolinium gallium garnet (GGG) substrates across the 10–150 µm thickness range. Efforts shall demonstrate system integration, process optimization, and material qualification sufficient for insertion into operational microwave filter architectures. Required technical performance thresholds include film thickness uniformity of ±5% across 1-inch wafers, surface roughness below 5 nm RMS, and saturation magnetization (4πMs) values within ±50 Gauss of specification. Offerors shall employ a systematic process characterization approach — such as design-of-experiments (DOE) methodology — to establish repeatable, production-ready growth processes governing flux composition, growth temperature, rotation rate, and cooling profile.Proposed solutions shall include a structured material qualification program incorporating X-ray diffraction (XRD), profilometry, vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM), and FMR spectroscopy. Qualified films shall be suitable for delivery to government-designated filter manufacturers and laboratories for device-level insertion and performance verification.Successful Phase II performance shall result in a domestic LPE production capability with documented process controls, material qualification data packages, and a clear transition roadmap to Phase III commercialization and direct supply to DoW prime contractors. This topic directly supports the AFRL strategic priority of eliminating foreign single-source dependencies for critical electronic materials and establishing a sovereign U.S. industrial base for high-performance garnet magnetic films.

title: Hyperdimensional Neurosymbolic Cyber Course-of-Action Planning and Replanning under Deception
summary: Future cyber operations will be conducted in contested environments in which observations are incomplete, timing is compressed, adversaries actively manipulate defender beliefs, and the state of the mission cannot be fully observed from any single node or operator position.

title: Autonomous Metacognitive Collection Orchestration for Multi-Domain Intelligence
summary: Modern intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) enterprises ingest multi-source indicator streams whose native tempos span four or more orders of magnitude.
description:
Modern intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) enterprises ingest multi-source indicator streams whose native tempos span four or more orders of magnitude. Overhead imagery (EO/IR, SAR, MSI, HSI) arrives at revisit cadences of minutes to hours; RF and SIGINT detections resolve in seconds to minutes; maritime AIS and acoustic returns update continuously at sub-second tempos; and open-source, supply-chain, and pattern-of-life indicators mature over hours to weeks. A single decision of operational consequence, such as whether a vessel of interest is a combatant or a civilian fisher, or whether an observed buildup presages a near-term operation or reflects routine activity, typically turns on whether causally related evidence drawn from several of these phenomenologies can be assembled, reasoned about, and surfaced fast enough and cheaply enough to matter.

Classical early- and late-fusion pipelines assume temporally aligned inputs and emit single snapshot outputs, useful when cadences match and brittle when they differ by orders of magnitude or when a depended-on sensor is denied. Reinforcement- and active-learning policies can select next observations but treat operational constraints as reward-shaped scalars the optimizer can trade away, and require retraining cycles measured in weeks when priority intelligence requirements or adversary tactics shift in hours. Neuro-symbolic and causal methods contribute structure and interpretability, yet in practice operate over hand-authored graphs and synchronous data, with post-hoc explanations rather than forward-looking traces. Agentic large-language-model orchestrators produce narrative rationalizations whose internal state cannot be audited, and whose plans cannot be inspected for constraint feasibility before execution. What is missing across all of these approaches is a structured, auditable, constraint-feasible substrate whose rationale for each recommendation is transparent, reproducible, and directly inspectable from internal state.

This topic seeks novel approaches to artificial metacognition: an orchestration substrate that reasons about its own reasoning while reasoning about the world. A metacognitive substrate maintains a structured model of evidence-to-outcome relationships across heterogeneous modalities and tempos; tracks its own uncertainty, prediction error, and representational coherence; computes expected information gain for candidate collection actions under hard operational constraints; returns option-sets rather than single collapsed policies; and, when denial, deception, or distribution shift is detected, locally refines its internal model rather than triggering a full retraining cycle. The resulting capability is the computational backbone of a human-machine formation: the autonomous system acts at machine speed inside a bounded operating envelope, while the human commander sets objectives, constraints, and rules of engagement before the mission and reviews the auditable decision record after.

Candidate substrate families for the metacognitive layer include hyperdimensional computing and vector-symbolic architectures; neuro-symbolic architectures that couple learned encoders with symbolic or probabilistic inference; and graph-based reasoning over typed knowledge graphs, causal graphs, and structured inference engines. Hybrids across these approaches are encouraged. This topic is deliberately substrate-agnostic within that class. Offerors are expected to justify their choice on quantitative grounds. Any viable substrate shall provide:
• Compositional, inspectable operators (algebraic, logical, graph-based, or probabilistic) that support real-time assembly and decomposition of multi-source evidence structures, rather than end-to-end learned embeddings whose compositional semantics cannot be examined.
• Bounded degradation under partial, corrupted, delayed, or adversarially manipulated input, quantified against a mainstream deep-learning baseline.
• Transparent, reproducible reasoning operations that yield auditable explanations directly from internal system state, rather than post-hoc narrative produced by a prompted language model.
• Efficient operation under sparse and few-shot regimes, with measurable performance at small label budgets on novel scenario classes.
• A credible path to tactical-edge deployment on Size-Weight-and-Power-constrained platforms.

Recent work across these areas has independently demonstrated subsets of these properties, including graph-structured anomaly reasoning, compositional multi-modal scene understanding, and interpretable edge AI with online adaptation.

Converging them into a single autonomous metacognitive orchestration substrate is the objective of this topic. Approaches that rely on monolithic end-to-end deep networks without compositional or causal structure, or on narrative-only explanations produced by prompted language models, fall outside the scope of this topic.

The program seeks novel approaches to key technical challenges, including:
• Representing and reasoning over time-lagged causal dependencies across multi-modal sensor streams whose native tempos span four or more orders of magnitude, under missing, late, corrupted, and adversarially manipulated inputs.
• Computing expected information gain over candidate collection actions while treating operational constraints (emissions, bandwidth, power, time-to-decision, access) as hard-binding semantic variables rather than reward-shaped scalars, and producing Pareto-optimal option-sets rather than single collapsed policies.
• Self-monitoring the system’s own confidence, prediction error, and representational coherence; detecting adversarial denial, deception, and distribution shift as learning signals; and triggering targeted local refinement of the internal model without offline retraining.
• Generating forward-looking “why / why-not” traces, reproducible from internal system state, that link each recommendation to its supporting evidence chain, the constraints it satisfies, the alternatives it dominated, and the expected futures it forecasts, supporting downstream review by a subject-matter expert (SME) or within a human-machine formation.
• Probabilistic root-cause analysis of observed outcomes, tracing back through the internal representation to identify contributing evidence across domains and timescales, with ranked alternative hypotheses and quantified confidence.

title: Human Universal Remote
summary: Surface electromyography (sEMG) is a proven technique for detecting biomedical voltage measurements from the skin generated by the electrical current of muscle fibers during skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation. These signals, which reflect neuromuscular activity, typically range in amplitude from 0 to 10 millivolts and operate at frequencies between 20 and 450 Hz.
description:
Surface electromyography (sEMG) is a proven technique for detecting biomedical voltage measurements from the skin generated by the electrical current of muscle fibers during skeletal muscle contraction and relaxation. These signals, which reflect neuromuscular activity, typically range in amplitude from 0 to 10 millivolts and operate at frequencies between 20 and 450 Hz. While historically used to restore hand function for transradial amputees via non-invasive fiber membrane potential measurement, this topic proposes leveraging state-of-the-art sEMG in concert with other non-invasive muscle sensing modalities to significantly enhance the operational capability of the warfighter. For example, ultrasound is a high-resolution non-invasive sensing modality capable of probing deep muscle tissues and providing complementary information to electromyographic signals. This topic is divided into two distinct, parallel Technical Areas (TAs) that must be addressed concurrently. Proposers must deliver an integrated solution spanning both domains:

Technical Area 1 (TA1): Microphone
Signal capture will focus on the non-invasive detection and extraction of EMG signals and/or electrical, acoustic deep muscle sensing signals from the user. The approach should include the utilization of signals for arm control as both a command and as biological sensors to understand where muscle activity is occurring and to function as an active indicator of warfighter stress. Hardware systems developed under this Technical Area must reliably detect, isolate, and extract these microvolt-to-millivolt level biopotential signals directly from the warfighter’s skin without invasive techniques. Proposers should address the following TA1 criteria:
{INSERT TA1 CRITERIA CHART HERE}

Technical Area 2 (TA2): Speaker
This Technical Area focuses on translating decoded physiological intent into standardized, platform-agnostic output modalities. The system must reliably differentiate between passive muscle strain and active, intentional micro- and macro-gestures to generate high-confidence external commands. The approach should include command output that translates the processed signals into an actionable trigger via standard communications channels designed for easy integration into Team Awareness Kit (TAK). To prevent over-engineering to a singular use case or platform, the generated signaling protocol should be standardizable for use across multiple external systems. At a minimum, the platform should be built with at least one communications channel using radiofrequency (RF). Example platforms include enabling users to task robotic systems, low-level ISR drones, comms drones, trigger communications, and generate visual indicators directly on a TAK display.
