title: UAS-based Precision Aim for Device Render Safe in CBRN Environments
summary: DTRA is in need of technical innovations associated with warfighting units performing very long range WMD device render-safe missions from a safe distance, outside of potentially CBRN contaminated environments.
description:
DTRA is in need of technical innovations associated with warfighting units performing very long range WMD device render-safe missions from a safe distance, outside of potentially CBRN contaminated environments. Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD) definitions and terms are commonly used by many nations and exist on the public internet including steps involving EOD detection, identification, field evaluation, render safe, recovery and disposal. Successfully performing stand-off EOD missions with personal positioned away from the contaminated environment requires a payload capable of remotely and accurately aiming via employment of currently fielded EOD disruptors against the explosive ordnance threat with a high degree of precision.
Payload capabilities of the proposed solution should ideally be sized to be compatible with currently fielded Department of War UAS systems. The desired end state is a system weight that is designed for small-unit operations UAS.
DTRA conducts counter WMD science and technology research and testing efforts for Joint Services EOD missions. Ground robotic platforms currently provide the only fielded remote-employment method for EOD disruptors, but these lack terrain-independent access and approach-angle flexibility that an aerial platform would provide. Small unit operations UAS platforms with sufficient flight endurance and payload capacity to carry current EOD-relevant payloads into contested or austere environments. This topic seeks novel approaches to providing precision remote-aiming payloads delivered and emplaced by remote UAS with subsequent operational render safe execution orchestrated from remotely. The capability should be able to be remotely recovered and re-charged to enable system re-use at another location after the render safe mission is completed
STATE OF TECHNOLOGY:
• Significant technical challenges exist in achieving operational standoff. Standoff is defined as the ability to gather information about, or employ tools against, an explosive ordnance threat at a meaningful physical distance, without the EOD technician or the EOD tool itself needing to be placed directly against or immediately adjacent to the threat.
• The Stand Off objective is a novel precision-aiming render safe capability that can be delivered to a meaningful distance from the threat and still deliver accurate, useful results without requiring direct contact or close-in emplacement against the device itself. In some cases, physically touching or bringing a metal object too close to the device may trigger it’s detonation.
• The Remote Objective is defined as the ability to employ Joint Service EOD tools using robotic platforms, hook-and-line techniques, or a combination of tools and techniques without the EOD technician being physically present at the threat site. For example, employing a disruptor via a ground robot so that the technician never approaches the device directly. In an existing CBRNE environment or if the unexploded ordinance is associated with a CBRN warhead, is critical to conduct the mission from a remote location.
• Current EOD disruptor technology is capable of engaging a threat at a distance once it is properly aimed and fired, but current aiming and emplacement methods require the disruptor to be physically positioned and adjusted by hand, meaning an EOD technician must be directly at the tool to set it up correctly. As a result, even though the disruptor’s terminal effect has standoff, the technician does not retain standoff during the aiming and emplacement process itself. Existing remote delivery methods can get a disruptor near a threat, but it remains difficult to finely position and aim it once it arrives.
• Current ground robotic platforms are limited by terrain and access. A threat located on a rooftop, upper floor, or otherwise inaccessible position is simply unreachable by a ground platform, regardless of any aiming capability it might have. Novel aerial delivery capabilities are emerging that could resolve this access constraint by providing rapid ingress and egress over obstacles, terrain, rubble, and structures common to austere and urban environments, along with the ability to approach threat devices from angles and approach paths unavailable to ground robots.

title: Remote UAS-based X-Ray for Device Assessment in CBRNE Environments
summary: DTRA is in need of technical innovations associated with Warfighters performing long range WMD device assessment and characterization from a safe distance outside of potentially CBRN contaminated environments.
description:
DTRA is in need of technical innovations associated with Warfighters performing long range WMD device assessment and characterization from a safe distance outside of potentially CBRN contaminated environments. Explosive Ordinance Disposal (EOD) definitions and terms are commonly used by many nations and exist on the public internet including steps involving EOD detection, assessment, identification, field evaluation, render safe, recovery and disposal. Current device assessment is manual, requiring personnel to approach closely and manually move x-ray transmitters and x-ray receivers around an unknown device to perform the required assessment mission. Current stand-off capabilities are typically ground robots manually driven a short distance which may be safe for some unexploded ordinance (UXO), but are not safe for suspected WMD warheads. Recent UAS innovations associated with coaxial form factor systems that can perch or land as part of their mission flight profile appear to offer a novel approach to conducting bi-static x-ray image collection.
STATE OF TECHNOLOGY.
• Current Portable digital radiography systems that depend on hand- or robot-emplacement of a source and flat-panel detector near the device are limited in a CBRN environment. There is no current technology solution that can generate diagnostically useful transmission images (sufficient penetration of ordnance casings plus resolution of fine fuse features such as wires, switches, or delay elements) without any ground contact or personnel entry into the contaminated zone.
• Mobile x-ray transmitters and various options for exposing images, and stitching multiple images together to create a 3-D assessment of an unknown device exist, but they are generally hand-carried and emplaced. Complex mathematics and algorithms for capturing and rendering X-ray results from multiple simultaneously moving transmitters and receivers each with potential uncertainties in position and angle are limited.
• Tactical UAS systems are generally small, carry lighter payloads, do not have open architectures for payloads, and payload options are generally difficult and limited to the bottom side to integrate without adversely affecting flight profiles.
• Robotic x-rays exist but are typically fixed, large and devices are brought to them and put on a turntable. This topic is for x-rays done in the field, at 5km distances, without moving the threat device.
• No UAS-based x-ray capability currently exists.

title: Dynamic Sensor-Tasking and Routing System for Subsurface Hazard Detection
summary: Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards.
description:
Current field-deployable capabilities for WMD device and component defeat, route reconnaissance, and sensitive site exploitation have made significant strides in rapid surface-level mapping and visual threat triage using unmanned aerial and ground platforms. However, these operational systems encounter a critical bottleneck when confronting subsurface hazards. Visual, optical, and topographic sensors are fundamentally blind to threats that are partially buried, completely subsurface, or obscured beneath soil, blast debris, or disturbed earth. When subsurface geophysical instruments are integrated onto these unmanned platforms to address this blind spot, current field architecture suffers from a severe "collect everything" bottleneck. Lacking localized intelligence, platforms typically execute static, pre-programmed survey scripts which force sensors to operate continuously and indiscriminately across an entire area. This floods constrained tactical communication networks with massive volumes of raw sensor data, overwhelms field computing devices, drastically slows operational tempo, and results in sensor operational blindness when local soil physics degrade or invalidate specific sensor modalities. When conducting standoff reconnaissance of suspected hazard areas—which may contain buried chemical or biological munitions, radiological dispersal device (RDD) components, bulk precursor storage vessels, or associated explosive triggers and conventional ordnance—these bottlenecks force operators into dangerous, prolonged exposure on target. Furthermore, relying on rigid, static classical logic to manage these complex sensor suites in real time introduces a critical limitation, as traditional rule-based programs cannot adapt to highly dynamic, uncharacterized environments where the boundary conditions are not known beforehand.
A proactive system is required to answer:
"Given this specific environment and mission profile, which sensor should be deployed first, what detection threshold triggers the next modality, and which sensors may be inhibited due to the environment or other physical boundary conditions?"
This topic seeks an adaptive, machine-learning-driven sensor-tasking and routing decision engine capable of scheduling sensor deployment and routing platform payloads in real time using probabilistic, data-driven optimization methods. The primary need is an intelligent edge capability that continuously monitors changing site conditions and dynamically queues, activates, or inhibits physical sensor payloads on an autonomous platform. Rather than streaming raw data or running all sensors simultaneously, the system must govern sensor execution through learned decision policies (utilizing techniques such as reinforcement learning, contextual bandits, or partially observable Markov decision processes) that optimize performance based on sensor-inferred environmental physics (such as electrical conductivity and dielectric permittivity), immediate mission constraints (such as required advance speed, standoff distance requirements, and target priority), and real-time sensor performance signatures. When an initial screening modality detects an anomaly, the engine must evaluate the environmental context to dynamically determine if a secondary, higher-fidelity sensor is required to verify and classify the threat, or if the platform should continue its route. By automating this sensor-queuing and routing logic at the edge through explainable and efficient AI, the system will overcome the subsurface bottlenecks of current field suites, eliminate tactical network saturation, minimize time on target, and ensure reliable detection and defeat of subsurface WMD devices and associated hazards across diverse, uncharacterized operational environments.
State of Technology: Currently deployed military and commercial technologies have reached a high level of maturity in distinct, stove-piped domains, but they do not integrate these capabilities into a single, closed-loop, in-stride subsurface decision engine. The current technical landscape is characterized by the following:
• Standoff Aerial and Surface Visual Mapping Systems: Existing fielded systems utilize unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and ground platforms to perform rapid photogrammetric, optical (EO/IR), and LiDAR mapping of surface terrains. These systems feature mature edge-computing architectures that run real-time automated target recognition (ATR) to classify surface munitions, craters, and obstacles on tactical hand-held tablets in under 30 minutes. However, these systems lack subsurface sensing capability, limiting their ability to detect and characterize hazards that are partially buried, covered by debris, or below the ground surface.
• Geophysical Post-Processing Classification Suites: For subsurface detection, advanced electromagnetic induction (EMI) and ground-penetrating radar (GPR) systems are highly mature and accredited for DoD munitions response. These systems utilize sophisticated physics-based inversion models to extract target polarizability tensors and classify anomalies against standard munitions libraries. However, these software suites are strictly designed for post-processing desktop environments. They are not integrated into real-time, in-stride robotic platforms, and they cannot make autonomous decisions in the field regarding active sensor scheduling.
• Uncoordinated "Collect-Everything" Sensor Payloads: Current multi-sensor ground platforms operate in a fixed, concurrent acquisition mode where all integrated sensors (such as magnetometers, GPR, and EMI) run continuously regardless of whether the local terrain and environment is physically compatible with the sensor. For example, when a platform transitions into wet, highly conductive clay, a ground-penetrating radar (GPR) antenna suffers from severe signal attenuation, rendering the collected data ineffective for its intended detection purpose. Current systems lack the real-time feedback loops to recognize these environmental changes and limitations then automatically adjust, disable, or redirect sensor payloads. This lack of dynamic management creates a major operational inefficiency, resulting in the collection of highly degraded data that requires excessive post-processing, while unnecessarily consuming onboard battery power, communication bandwidth, and valuable mission time.
• Static Autonomous Path Planning: Existing autonomous ground and aerial navigation algorithms plan paths based on surface traversability, geometric obstacle avoidance, and pre-mapped terrain features. They do not ingest real-time subsurface hazard maps or dynamically adjust their routing, payload dwell times, or sensor modalities based on changing subsurface soil electromagnetic properties or detected anomalies.
• Adaptive AI/ML for Sequential Decision-Making and Path Planning: In adjacent fields such as autonomous warehouse robotics, dynamic network routing, and space domain awareness, machine learning is highly mature for solving complex, real-time sensor scheduling and path-planning challenges. State-of-the-art approaches utilize Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and Contextual Multi-Armed Bandits to train autonomous agents that make optimal sequential decisions under extreme uncertainty. These AI models observe dynamic environmental contexts (e.g., localized obstacle density or changing wireless signal-to-noise ratios), weigh the trade-offs between exploring unknown areas and exploiting known paths, and automatically adjust sensor power cycles or update the platform’s route on-the-fly. However, these advanced decision-making frameworks have not yet been integrated with or trained on subsurface geophysical physics, leaving a critical gap where current autonomous AI agents remain incapable of managing multi-modal subsurface sensor suites.

title: Validation and Verification of Computational Modeling of Human Blast Injury on Battlefield
summary: Blast events accounted for over 70% of casualties among service members engaged in ground combat events. The energy generated by an explosion can cause devastating physical trauma, affect multiple body systems and result in severe injuries or even fatalities (1.2).
description:
Blast events accounted for over 70% of casualties among service members engaged in ground combat events. The energy generated by an explosion can cause devastating physical trauma, affect multiple body systems and result in severe injuries or even fatalities (1.2). Although there has been extensive research into injury mechanisms of blast trauma, including primary overpressure effects, secondary fragmentation wounds, tertiary blunt trauma, and quaternary thermal or chemical injuries, there are no modeling & simulation (M&S) tools currently available which can provide a comprehensive view of the types and severity of injuries in the context of the uncertainties and complexities of realistic battlefield scenarios.
Existing injury modeling tools, such as Operational Requirements-based Casualty Assessment model (ORCA) developed by US Army DEVCOM, the INJURY code developed by the Medical Research and Development Command, and the AUDITORY model developed by the Joint Intermediate Force Capabilities Office (JIFCO), each model individual injuries occurring to a single person in the absence of PPE. They are not designed to address multiple, multi-modal injuries that may occur in ground combat, and they model wounds from the “skin in,” rather than accounting for the effects of clothing or PPE. These tools can only be used for research purposes and are not designed to support battlefield operation.
In contrast, the Human Injury Prediction (HIP) tool, developed by Defense Science and Technology Laboratory (DSTL) of United Kingdom, predicts injuries to multiple people from a terrorist attack. Unfortunately, this tool is limited to modeling the effects of only a single blast event caused by a terrorist weapon detonated in an urban environment. And, again, HIP models isolated injuries and cannot address multiple, multi-modal injuries.
Finally, a major challenge of leveraging these tools in DTRA Technical Reachback mission is that injuries are predicted based upon biomechanical effects, and do not address human physiology. This shortcoming becomes particularly critical with multiple injuries, where the human body response to injuries is intact and synergetic among organs/tissues.
Apart from the specific challenges of modeling injuries and the associated changes in physiology, a comprehensive battlefield blast injury M&S tool is a multidisciplinary endeavor, requiring expertise in diverse domains, to include medicine, military operations, weaponeering, synthetic population modeling, epidemiology, structures, machine learning, computational modeling, and PPE.
ASME V&V 40 serves as the gold standard for computational model credibility in biomedical applications, and DoD Instruction 5000.61 (Modeling and Simulation Verification, Validation, and Accreditation) requires human injury models to be validated before moving to support military operation (3,4,5). The modeling effort should align with the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office (BIRCO) and the Blast Injury Prevention Standards Recommendation (BIPSR) process. The access to sensitive battle databases must be tightly controlled and limited to need-to-know personnel (6). Based on the regulation and scientific merit, the current request for proposal (RFP) will focus on validation of the on-going approach by using independent groups.

title: Domestic Fabrication Of High-Purity Precursor Materials For Advanced Radiation Detection Scintillator Crystals
summary: High-purity precursor materials are the foundational input for all high-performance inorganic scintillator crystals used in the DoW radiation detection and nuclear forensics missions. Current supply chains for key halides (e.g., LaCl₃, LaBr₃, YCl₃, LiCl, CsCl, CeCl3 etc.) and rare earth oxides (e.g., Gd2O3, CeO2, etc.) are heavily dependent on foreign sources.
description:
High-purity precursor materials are the foundational input for all high-performance inorganic scintillator crystals used in the DoW radiation detection and nuclear forensics missions. Current supply chains for key halides (e.g., LaCl₃, LaBr₃, YCl₃, LiCl, CsCl, CeCl3 etc.) and rare earth oxides (e.g., Gd2O3, CeO2, etc.) are heavily dependent on foreign sources. Several of the materials used for inorganic scintillator crystal growth are included in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 2025 List of Critical Minerals. This need is further reinforced by Executive Order 14415, "Securing America's Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials" (July 20, 2026), which directs the DoW to prioritize domestic sources for critical materials, restrict routine waivers for adversarial foreign suppliers effective January 1, 2027, and require supply chain mapping and mitigation plans from contractors and subcontractors.
Scaling crystal growth of these scintillators and maintaining consistent performance requires precursor materials with stringent control of purity, stoichiometry, moisture, and trace radioactive contaminants. Poor quality precursor materials often introduce variability that degrades crystal quality, light yield, energy resolution, and PSD figure-of-merit.
Desired materials typically have the following attributes, confirmed by analytical means and demonstrated by crystal growth results:
• High Chemical Purity: At least ≥4N (99.99%) anhydrous metal halides or pre-reacted mixes; sub-ppm levels of contaminants that interfere with the selected scintillator’s performance, such as transition metals (e.g., Fe, Cr, Ni, Cu) and alkali contaminants (e.g., K, Rb).
• Low Moisture / Oxygen Content: < 50 ppm (minimum) for hygroscopic materials.
• Precise Stoichiometry Control (for pre-reacted elpasolites): Precise control of multi-cation ratios to enable growth of phase-pure crystals with minimal secondary phases or compositional gradients
• Radioactive Impurity Control: Minimized 40K, 87Rb, 138La, 176Lu, and U/Th series contaminants to levels supporting low-background detector applications

This topic specifically targets the development of domestic synthesis, purification and quality-assurance processes capable of producing scintillator-grade precursor materials at laboratory, pilot, and eventually production scales. The goal is to reduce or eliminate reliance on foreign sources while enabling the next generation of compact, high-performance, ruggedized detectors for WMD detection and nuclear security applications.
The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:
• Analytical Characterization: Comprehensive analytical characterization confirming chemical purity, low moisture/oxygen content (if applicable) and stochiometric control. Appropriate methods should be used for trace-metal purity or trace moisture measurement.
• Domestic Feedstock Utilization: Primary use of U.S. or allied-nation sourced precursor materials (e.g. carbonates, oxides, chlorides) and any specialized equipment with documented traceability.
• Validation Method: Rapid feasibility screening of material performance, which may include small-scale crystal growth and measurements such as powder radioluminescence or optical transmittance.
• Production Scale: Reliable and reproducible laboratory-scale batches (e.g., 50-100 g) in Phase I; pilot-scale (e.g., 1–5 kg) in Phase II with batch-to-batch consistency. Ultimately, the focus is on material quality and potential for process scale up.
• Open market commercialization: Process development must lead to high-purity precursor materials made commercially available to the broader U.S. industrial base, rather than exclusive licenses, proprietary arrangements, or other restrictions.
Objective specifications (desired but not required for basic consideration):
• Advanced Validation Method: Produced batches must be validated through single crystal growth and complete radiation detection performance benchmarking against commercially available crystals, to include absolute light yield (photons/MeV), energy resolution at 662 keV, and PSD where applicable.
• Production Scale: Demonstration of multi-kilogram batch yields achieving or with a roadmap to achieve cost competitiveness with foreign-sourced material.
• Radiopurity: Identification of means to mitigate or minimize naturally occurring radioactive isotopes that impact detector background.
• Extensibility: Tailoring materials to be directly compatible with transparent ceramic scintillator fabrication processes (e.g. desirable particle size distribution and particle morphology).
This effort shall develop reliable domestic manufacturing processes for high-purity scintillator precursor materials while meeting the performance parameters above. Proposed work must include validation. The developed processes and materials will also be tested and validated in Phase II by delivery to DTRA or a designated partner for independent evaluation.

title: Domestic Scalable Growth Of Large-Format Pixelated CZT Crystals For Advanced Radiation Detection
summary: Compact, high-resolution, room-temperature gamma imaging and spectroscopy systems are critical for a number of government agency applications (DoW, DTRA, DOE/NNSA, IAEA, DHS), in addition to a number of commercial applications (nuclear power, medical community).
description:
Compact, high-resolution, room-temperature gamma imaging and spectroscopy systems are critical for a number of government agency applications (DoW, DTRA, DOE/NNSA, IAEA, DHS), in addition to a number of commercial applications (nuclear power, medical community). CZT-based 3D position-sensitive detectors provide these capabilities without cryogenic cooling, leveraging the small-pixel effect and depth-of-interaction (DOI) sensing via pixelated anodes and timing readout.
Current advanced systems rely on high-quality pixelated CZT, but most commercial modules use smaller crystals (~20–22 mm lateral dimensions). Furthermore, finished crystals with a thickness of around 5 mm are readily available for medical imaging; however, thicker crystals are often available from manufacturers by long-lead, custom order. Scaling to monolithic 44 × 44 × 15 mm crystals would significantly increase intrinsic efficiency (particularly for higher-energy gamma rays), reduce the number of crystals and interfaces per imager, improve geometrical coverage, simplify module assembly, and lower overall system complexity while maintaining or exceeding energy resolution targets of <1% FWHM at 662 keV.
High-performance spectrometer-grade CZT at this scale is currently supplied primarily by a limited number of foreign or foreign-owned sources, creating recognized supply-chain vulnerabilities for critical national security radiation detection hardware. Tellurium feedstock is heavily concentrated overseas, and domestic high-end crystal growth capacity remains limited. Zinc and Tellurium are identified in the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) 2025 List of Critical Minerals. Additionally, Executive Order 14415 "Securing America's Defense Supply Chains and Ensuring Domestic Acquisition of Critical Materials" (July 20, 2026), and related DoW supply chain initiatives, emphasize the need to strengthen domestic reliance on critical materials and components.
This topic directly addresses that gap by focusing on domestic crystal growth and machining innovation—including process improvements to the Traveling Heater Method (THM), Accelerated Crucible Rotation Technique (ACRT)-enhanced methods, alternative or hybrid growth techniques, in-situ monitoring, and stoichiometry/defect control—capable of delivering the required size, uniformity, and spectroscopic performance at scalable yield and cost. Successful development will strengthen U.S. supply chain resilience while accelerating technology transition to operational systems. A successful development under this topic should result in CZT material freely available on the commercial market rather than for exclusive or limited use by license or other restrictions. Furthermore, it is not the intent of this topic to develop detector systems utilizing CZT.
The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:
• Crystal Form Factor: Monolithic single-crystal CZT, nominal dimensions up to 44 × 44 × 15 mm (or equivalent large-format), suitable for pixelation with approximately 22 × 22 pixel anode contact matrix at ~2 mm pitch, a single cathode contact, and a guard ring contact around the edge of each.
• Material Quality: High spatial uniformity of carrier transport properties (electron μτ and adequate hole properties) across the full crystal volume; low defect density (e.g., Tellurium inclusions, grain boundaries, twins, etc.) sufficient to support high-performance spectroscopic operation; and low current leakage.
• Performance Target: Demonstrated or projected capability to achieve < 1% FWHM energy resolution at 662 keV when configured with pixelated readout and DOI sensing in a representative detector geometry.
• Domestic Production: U.S.-based growth process with clear, documented path to scalable yield, lot-to-lot reproducibility, and cost reduction; primary use of U.S. or allied-nation sourced raw materials with traceability.
• Validation: Precursor and crystal lots must be validated through non-destructive characterization (e.g., IR transmission, X-ray topography, μτ mapping) and, where feasible, proxy electrode testing or delivery to a qualified detector fabricator for performance assessment.
• Cost: Demonstrate that under high volume production cost per crystal volume is competitive with CZT commercially available from other commercial vendors.
Objective specifications (desired but not required for basic consideration):
• Larger or thicker monolithic crystals (e.g., approaching 50 × 50 × 20 mm) with maintained uniformity.
• Demonstrated full pixelated detector performance meeting or exceeding < 0.8% FWHM at 662 keV in 3D configuration.
• Production-scale batches (multiple crystals per run) with ≥ 70% single-crystal yield meeting all quality metrics.
• Cost-competitive pathway versus current foreign-sourced material at equivalent performance.
• Extensibility to related materials or detector architectures (e.g., array tiling, alternative electrode designs).

title: Real-World Applications for Prototype ISAC Demonstrations (RAPID) Small Business
summary: The Department of War (DoW) seeks to accelerate U.S. leadership in Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC), a 5G-Advanced feasibility-study area and a key technology for 3GPP 6G specifications.
description:
The Department of War (DoW) seeks to accelerate U.S. leadership in Integrated Sensing and Communications (ISAC), a 5G-Advanced feasibility-study area and a key technology for 3GPP 6G specifications. This project addresses the challenge of adding sensing capabilities to communication networks without degrading the primary communication link across diverse missions and environments, from established bases to remote and contested areas. The goal is to develop innovative, dual-use ISAC prototypes that leverage existing cellular infrastructure including 5G, emerging Open RAN interfaces, and SI-native networking. These solutions should offer a smaller, more cost-effective footprint than separate radar and communication systems. The effort will focus on three pathways: ISAC on fixed infrastructure, ISAC on mobile platforms, and joint SI optimization of radio resources. Success of this project will reduce barriers to market entry, enable new ISAC and SI applications, and strengthen U.S. industrial competitiveness in a field receiving substantial investment from adversaries.
The following documents are incorporated as part of this topic.

1. Appendix A - ISAC KPI Framework for RAPID
2. RAPID Statement of Objectives (SOO)

title: Resilient Tactical Edge Networks
summary: The realistic near-to-mid-term serviceable addressable market for private 5G in U.S. agriculture is the subset with real mobility, coverage, reliability, or data-volume pain: row-crop operations running GPS-guided and autonomous equipment, specialty-crop growers using machine vision and agricultural robotics, dairies and feedlots with dense livestock-monitoring deployments, irrigated operations…
description:
The realistic near-to-mid-term serviceable addressable market for private 5G in U.S. agriculture is the subset with real mobility, coverage, reliability, or data-volume pain: row-crop operations running GPS-guided and autonomous equipment, specialty-crop growers using machine vision and agricultural robotics, dairies and feedlots with dense livestock-monitoring deployments, irrigated operations with distributed pump and center-pivot control, and large ranches requiring wide-area coverage for animal and asset tracking. The scale of the opportunity is well documented. USDA Economic Research Service data show about 1.88 million farms in 2024 (roughly 39% of all U.S. land). Only 79% of farms reported internet access of any kind, leaving roughly one in five farms without even basic connectivity. There is also documented evidence that productivity of farms with connectivity is significantly higher than the ones without any connectivity. Furthermore, FCC data show that 39% of rural Americans lack access to minimum fixed broadband speeds, compared with 4% of urban Americans, and coverage on cropland and rangeland specifically is worse still. Public carrier networks will not close this gap on their own; carrier tower economics favor population density, and most agricultural land has almost none.

This segment buys on measurable operational outcomes (machine uptime, yield per acre, input cost per acre, water use, herd health, labor hours saved), not on global platform standardization, and its stated barriers to adoption are consistent and compounding: ROI ambiguity, high capex against tight and cyclical farm margins, no in-house RF/cellular or IT staff, harsh outdoor operating environments, a fragmented device ecosystem spanning tractors, drones, sensors, and wearables, and coverage requirements measured in thousands of acres rather than thousands of square feet. A proprietary private 5G platform from a tier-one vendor addresses almost none of these barriers directly; it is priced and supported for industrial campuses and multi-site enterprise accounts, not a single farm with a handful of mission-critical connectivity problems to solve.

An all-open-source stack removes the structural cost and lock-in that makes proprietary platforms a poor fit for this segment. Because OCUDU's O-CU/O-DU communicate with the rest of the network over open, standardized interfaces (especially the O-RAN 7.2x split to the O-RU), the network can be assembled from whichever RU vendor best fits a given operation's coverage geometry and budget, including high-power CBRS Category B radios and high-gain sector antennas mounted on existing farm infrastructure (grain legs, silos, center-pivot towers, farmstead masts) to maximize covered acres per radio. Together, OCUDU, SD-Core, SD-RAN, and OSC form one integrated, fully open-source 5G stack that a regional systems integrator, agricultural equipment dealer, rural wireless ISP, or electric/telephone cooperative can deploy, support, and price as a right-sized, as-a-service offer for a single operation, instead of selling a broad, vendor-locked platform. That directly answers this market's stated preference for outcome-first, economically flexible offers, and it supports a coexistence posture (private 5G for mobility, coverage, and uplink-intensive problems; existing farmstead Wi-Fi and LPWAN sensors where they already work) rather than a rip-and-replace sale.

The trade-off of an all-open-source stack is that the burden of proving interoperability, stability, and security shifts from a single vendor's warranty to the integrator and the open-source community itself. Agricultural buyers, who by their own account lack in-house cellular and cybersecurity expertise, have little tolerance for integration failures discovered mid-season, when planting, spraying, irrigation, and harvest windows cannot be rescheduled. This is exactly the gap the on-going OCUDU Testing & Validation Plan, and its Radio Access Network (RAN) Testing and Evaluation Center (RTEC)-centered extensions, are designed to close: independently witnessed, multi-vendor testing of device diversity, RU diversity, long-range outdoor RF performance, Core/RIC/SMO integration, and security. The proposal should leverage the current, on-going testing and evaluation activities in RTECs and associated results on this front.

Although this topic is anchored in a specific vertical to ensure a concrete deployment environment, real users, and a defensible commercialization path, proposers should recognize and are required to present the technical work in terms of the generic network performance classes it advances. Improvements made to the OCUDU O-CU/O-DU under this effort (scheduler behavior, mobility management, uplink capacity, stability under sustained load, security features) are expected to generalize across verticals and to benefit the broader community of RAN developers building on OCUDU. The Technical Volume shall include a mapping of each selected use case, and its associated Section 3.0 KPMs, to the performance class or classes it exercises, and shall identify which anticipated OCUDU code or feature enhancements correspond to each class.

For this topic, the dominant performance classes are massive scale and wide-area coverage: maximizing covered acres per radio using high-power CBRS Category B configurations, supporting large, sparse populations of low-rate sensor devices alongside high-uplink mobile equipment, and maintaining session continuity across long-range outdoor propagation conditions, with an evolution path to NTN integration.
Research and development for this effort should address, at minimum, the following questions:

• All-Open-Source Economics: What is the fully loaded cost (integration, support, spectrum, hardware, mounting infrastructure, and backhaul) of an OCUDU + SD-Core + SD-RAN + OSC deployment at farm scale relative to carrier coverage extensions and proprietary private-network platforms, and how should that be packaged as a CBRS-based, as-a-service offer within the price point agricultural buyers require ($75,000-$200,000 for a reference deployment covering approximately 2,000 acres)?

• Last-Acre Coverage Economics: What combination of high-power CBRS Category B radios, high-gain sector antennas, existing vertical assets (grain legs, silos, pivot towers), and backhaul options (fiber where available, fixed wireless, or satellite/NTN) maximizes reliably covered acres per dollar, and how does the open RU ecosystem enabled by the O-RAN 7.2x split change that optimization relative to a single bundled radio line?

• Use-Case-First Automation: Which of the use cases defined below deliver the fastest, most measurable ROI on the open-source stack, and what RTEC-executed interoperability tests (Device, RU, Core, RIC/SMO, and Infrastructure dimensions) are needed to validate each one end-to-end under realistic seasonal, weather, and terrain conditions?

• Trust in Open Source: How does RTEC-executed testing of the full open-source stack (not just OCUDU) reduce the integration risk and skills-shortage barrier that agricultural buyers most often cite, and what evidence package best converts community-maintained, no-license-fee software into a procurement-ready proof point for a buyer with no in-house cellular expertise?

Solutions leveraging super intelligence (SI) and machine learning (ML) for variable-rate input optimization, crop and livestock analytics, predictive equipment maintenance, network optimization, or automated fault resolution are encouraged but not required. DoW will consider any novel concept that increases the reliability, economics, and trustworthiness of an all-open-source private 5G/FutureG platform for the resilient tactical edge networks. Dual-use opportunities are expected across commercial agricultural operations, DoW installation land- and range-management, perimeter and agricultural-buffer operations on DoW installations, expeditionary logistics over large unimproved areas, and food-supply-chain resilience as a national-security concern.

Proposers should address at least two of the following four use cases in their Phase II Statement of Work, and must identify which use case(s) their reference architecture and pilot deployment are designed to validate. Each use case below is defined in terms of the operational scenario it supports, the connectivity requirement it places on the platform, and the corresponding KPM table in Section 3.0. Because agricultural traffic spans extremes (from low-throughput, high-device-count telemetry such as soil sensors, livestock wearables, and irrigation command-and-control, to high-throughput, latency-sensitive streams such as UAS (unmanned Aircraft System) imagery backhaul, machine vision, and equipment teleoperation video) proposers are strongly encouraged to employ 5G network slicing to serve these disparate service classes simultaneously on the same physical network. Proposals that demonstrate slice-based traffic isolation and per-slice quality-of-service enforcement, with at least one low-throughput and one high-throughput use case operating concurrently on separate slices of a single deployment, will be viewed favorably. Device-Class Diversity and 5G RedCap. Each use-case set spans device classes from full-capability UEs (equipment modems, cameras, broadcast and production units) to reduced-capability IoT endpoints (sensors, wearables, tags, and trackers). Proposers shall address how the platform serves reduced-capability device classes, including 3GPP Release 17 Reduced Capability (RedCap) and Release 18 eRedCap UEs, and shall identify any OCUDU scheduler or feature enhancements required to support RedCap operation; such enhancements are strongly encouraged as upstream contributions under the common OCUDU benchmarking and enhancement work package. Where RedCap-certified devices are not commercially available for a given endpoint type at demonstration time, proposers may demonstrate with available device classes (or emulated RedCap UE profiles) and shall document the RedCap migration path.Use Case 1: Autonomous & Semi-Autonomous Field Equipment Connectivity
GPS-guided and autonomous tractors, sprayers, harvesters, and field robots move continuously across fields, along farm roads between fields, and in and out of farmstead staging areas, requiring an uninterrupted control-plane, telemetry, and remote-supervision connection as they roam. Fully autonomous equipment cannot legally or safely operate without a live, low-latency link for remote monitoring and emergency stops, and farms without high-speed coverage cannot use it at all. So, this use case requires the platform to sustain low-latency, high-reliability connectivity and seamless handover as equipment moves between cells across the full field footprint, including possible road transit between non-contiguous parcels.
Use Case 2: Aerial & Fixed Crop Intelligence Backhaul
Drones/UAS performing scouting, mapping, and spot-spraying missions, machine-vision cameras on harvesters and sorting lines, and dense fields of soil-moisture, weather, and plant-health sensors generate continuous, uplink-heavy data streams that must reach an on-farm edge analytics system or agronomy platform with low delay to support same-pass and same-day decisions on irrigation, fertility, and pest control. This use case requires the platform to sustain high uplink throughput with low jitter for multiple simultaneous UAS and camera streams while concurrently aggregating telemetry from thousands of low-rate sensors per cell.
Use Case 3: Livestock Monitoring & Ranch Operations
Cattle, dairy, and other livestock operations increasingly rely on connected ear tags, collars, rumen boluses, and virtual-fencing systems that must reliably reach a monitoring platform to detect health events (calving, lameness, illness), enforce virtual fence boundaries, and locate animals across grazing land that public carrier networks do not cover. This use case requires the platform to sustain consistent, wide-area, low-rate coverage for high device counts across pasture and confinement areas, with low-latency alerting for time-critical animal-health and containment events.
Use Case 4: Connected Farmstead, Irrigation & Grain Operations
The equipment that keeps a farm running is scattered across the farmstead and the fields around it: center-pivot irrigation systems, pump stations, grain dryers and grain-handling equipment, security cameras, and safety devices such as lone-worker monitors and confined-space alarms for grain bins. The cost of a lost connection is high: a stalled pivot or failed pump during peak heat can cost yield within days, an unmonitored grain dryer is a fire risk, and a missed confined-space alarm at a grain bin can cost a life. Yet most of this equipment sits beyond the reach of farmstead Wi-Fi, leaving operators dependent on unlicensed, best-effort wireless links that were never designed for critical operations. This use case requires the platform to close that gap by extending secure, private coverage from the farmstead to all surrounding equipment on the same OCUDU-based network, delivering (1) reliable, low-data-rate command-and-control for irrigation and grain equipment, and (2) continuous uplink capacity for security video and worker-safety alerts.

title: Low Cost Infrared Seeker
summary: Develop a cost-effective IR interceptor seeker through methods such as novel material development, advanced manufacturing and/or scalability, novel commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) integration, or other innovations that could reduce costs and maintain acceptable seeker performance.
description: Develop a cost-effective IR interceptor seeker through methods such as novel material development, advanced manufacturing and/or scalability, novel commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) integration, or other innovations that could reduce costs and maintain acceptable seeker performance. Both full seeker solutions and novel seeker components (focal plane array, readout integrated circuit, cooling system, telescope optics, etc.) are acceptable so long as cost savings are explicitly quantified in the proposal. A "full seeker" solution should include: Cover (if applicable), telescope assembly/ optical system (lenses, mirrors, filters, etc.), the IR sensor (filter, Focal Plane Arrays (FPAs) Readout Integrated Circuit, cooling systems (if applicable, etc.), gimbal system (as applicable), signal processing electronics, and the Final seeker production cost should be less than $150,000 for objective cost or less than $250,000 for threshold. Proposed solutions should be amenable to repeatable high throughput production processes. Proposal should include a plan for demonstration of seeker performance in a ground test facility. Additionally, proposers should identify the threat type(s) (ballistic, hypersonic, cruise missile, etc.) that are relevant to the proposed technology, and any assumptions made concerning the technology or its integration into the missile defense system should be explicitly referenced.

title: Rapidly Deployable Aerial Interdiction Cluster
summary: The Missile Defense Agency seeks novel solutions for a rapidly deployable aerial interdiction cluster for close-in defense against evolving threats to national security assets, including counter-air; counter-drone; electronic warfare; and force protection.
description: The Missile Defense Agency seeks novel solutions for a rapidly deployable aerial interdiction cluster for close-in defense against evolving threats to national security assets, including counter-air; counter-drone; electronic warfare; and force protection. The proposed cluster should be capable of transitioning from a standby state to a deployed state and be capable of autonomous, sustained operations. Cluster should contain a number of continuously cycling elements capable of multiple modes of operation (i.e., surveillance, discrimination, electronic warfare, attack). The cluster should contain a high volume of elements that are low size, weight, power, and cost (SWaP-C). The assets should be capable of maneuvering and loitering. Assets should be able to host various sensors and/or effectors capable of interdicting various threats (i.e., hypersonic vehicles, glide vehicles, drones, low-flying aerial objects). Modular cargo bays capable of carrying payloads are desired. System should employ a resilient mesh-node architecture and utilize multiple communication pathways.

title: High Speed Low Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) Radio Frequency (RF) Communications Systems for Space-to-Space and Space-to-Terrestrial Applications
summary: Specific to this topic, to support the Missile Defense Agency (MDA) mission of developing and deploying a layered Missile Defense System to defend the United States, its deployed forces, and friends from missile attacks in all phases of flight, the MDA seeks improved defensive communication capabilities by increasing bandwidth of new low size, weight, and power, radios and antennas to gigabyte…
description: Specific to this topic, to support the Missile Defense Agency (MDA) mission of developing and deploying a layered Missile Defense System to defend the United States, its deployed forces, and friends from missile attacks in all phases of flight, the MDA seeks improved defensive communication capabilities by increasing bandwidth of new low size, weight, and power, radios and antennas to gigabyte speeds. Small form-factor (.1L) or less volume and low power (<10 W) RF radio utilizing Ku bands or higher (due to National Telecommunication and Information Administration (NTIA) restrictions) capable of transmitting data at speeds of 1.5Gbps or greater in a natural space environment is desired. Technology should also be capable of burst transmission of data through the atmosphere to flight vehicles at speeds of 1 Gbps or greater. Communications system capable of meshed (self-forming, self-healing network, high probability of delivery network) High Assurance Internet Protocol Encryptors (HAIPE) interactions for inclusion into "Zero Trust" platforms and networks. Solutions should consider frequency diversity, antenna diversification, and advanced modulation and coding schemas for security and jamming prevention. At the end of the Phase II, two flight radio payloads would be the deliverables.

title: Modeling UV/VIS/near-IR Observables of Dim Hypersonic Configurations
summary: To address dim hypersonic threats in missile defense scenarios, the government desires to enhance current physical modeling tools with the ability to simultaneously predict at-source observable properties in the ultraviolet (UV), visible (VIS), and near-infrared (near-IR) spectral regimes that are founded and built upon Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Direct Simulation Monte…
description: To address dim hypersonic threats in missile defense scenarios, the government desires to enhance current physical modeling tools with the ability to simultaneously predict at-source observable properties in the ultraviolet (UV), visible (VIS), and near-infrared (near-IR) spectral regimes that are founded and built upon Navier-Stokes Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) techniques and which accounts for, but is not limited to, vehicle surface heating and ablation, Arrhenius and collisional chemically reacting flows, non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (NLTE) effects, boost and divert jet exhaust interactions with the hypersonic body flowfield, and electro-optical radiative transfer physics-based models. The modeling suite provided by the Joint Army-Navy-NASA Air Force (JANNAF) Exhaust Plume and Signatures Subcommittee (EPSS) [1-4] computes RF and certain IR observables. It is founded on CFD and DSMC flowfield codes, hardbody heating models, and radiative transfer / radar propagation techniques. However, the suite does not model all the underlying chemical and physical mechanisms needed to account for radiative emissions in the identified parts of the electromagnetic spectrum. Phenomenologies that must be enhanced within or added to the suite include, but are not limited to: characterization of thermal protection system response, development of material degradation models, detailed Arrhenius and collisional chemical kinetics models that consistently apply across the continuum and rarefied regimes, and generation of molecular band models for UV, Visible, and near-IR radiative emission. The developed models should be compatible with the JANNAF suite infrastructure. And the resulting assemblage should be able to model realistic hypersonic configurations (such as boost-glide, divert jet, and cruise missiles) under steady, unsteady, and maneuvering flight conditions lasting tens of minutes with high Mach within the atmosphere over a wide range of continuum and rarefied altitudes. The resulting capability is expected to facilitate the acquisition and tracking of dim hypersonic threats in modeling and simulation venues, such as MDA’s existing agency framework, and operational scenarios.

title: Mobile Sea-Based Launch Platform
summary: The Missile Defense Agency (MDA) Directorate for Test and Targets (DT) Directorate designs, develops and provides missile targets to test US missile defenses. The Department of War is pushing towards the deployment of sea-based launch capabilities for a variety of applications to enhance range and survivability of hypersonic technologies [1].
description: The Missile Defense Agency (MDA) Directorate for Test and Targets (DT) Directorate designs, develops and provides missile targets to test US missile defenses. The Department of War is pushing towards the deployment of sea-based launch capabilities for a variety of applications to enhance range and survivability of hypersonic technologies [1]. A commercially-owned and operated mobile sea-based platform capable of launching a variety of commercially-procured target vehicles from any point on the ocean will enable MDA to more accurately and cost-effectively replicate adversary threats while increasing equatorial launch access and enabling more responsive launch coordination [2].

title: Performance Enhancement of Solid Rocket Motors Applied to Existing Systems
summary: The Missile Defense Agency designs, develops, and delivers advanced missile defense capabilities to protect the United States, its allies, and deployed forces from missile attacks in all phases of flight. Traditional SRM propellant formulations and motor designs are mostly optimized, creating some limitations in regards to capability when form factor is constrained [1].
description: The Missile Defense Agency designs, develops, and delivers advanced missile defense capabilities to protect the United States, its allies, and deployed forces from missile attacks in all phases of flight. Traditional SRM propellant formulations and motor designs are mostly optimized, creating some limitations in regards to capability when form factor is constrained [1]. Methods to enhance and optimize the performance of SRM technology at reasonable cost have been researched for decades, incorporating a variety of potential solution paths such as burn-rate enhancement, particle size modifications, propellant composition optimization, and more [2]. Performance enhancements of SRMs in existing missile systems are desired to provide increased capability to both defensive systems and target systems used to validate defensive capabilities.

title: Low Cost / Rapidly Producible Booster Insulation Methods
summary: Solid propellant rockets use insulation to protect motor cases from the high temperature combustion gases and, in the case of composite cases, prevent egress of gases. Heritage methods for insulating motor cases utilize filled polymers with low thermal conductivities which absorb heat as they decompose.
description: Solid propellant rockets use insulation to protect motor cases from the high temperature combustion gases and, in the case of composite cases, prevent egress of gases. Heritage methods for insulating motor cases utilize filled polymers with low thermal conductivities which absorb heat as they decompose. The insulation layer is typically applied through time consuming processes on custom mandrels which require significant manual labor. The Government seeks novel insulation material/processing technologies which reduce insulation processing time and/or cost compared to legacy processes for a variety of motor case geometries and sizes. The primary motor case materials of interest for this solicitation are polymer matrix composites, though applicability to metallic cases is also desirable. Proposals developing reusable or low-cost consumable mandrels which can be easily and quickly removed after insulation lay-up and winding are also of interest. The proposed insulation solution must consider stress limitations in the propellant with variations in temperature during storage and operation. The proposed insulation technology should also meet or exceed the insulating ability of the current state of the art with equal or lower inert mass with an increased production rate and/or lower per unit price.

title: Configurable Operator Decision Models for Constructive Test and Evaluation Simulations
summary: Government problem: Missile defense test and evaluation rely on constructive simulations to examine large numbers of scenarios, explore operational concepts, evaluate system-of-systems interactions, and reduce risk before live flight events.
description:
Government problem: Missile defense test and evaluation rely on constructive simulations to examine large numbers of scenarios, explore operational concepts, evaluate system-of-systems interactions, and reduce risk before live flight events. These simulations can represent physical platforms, sensors, weapons, communications, terrain, and threat laydowns, but operator decision effects are often represented by fixed scripts, simplified timing rules, or manually coded behaviors. This can cause analysis results to overstate or understate operational performance because human choices influence detection, classification, engagement, prioritization, communication, and response timing across the kill chain.

Capability gap: The Government lacks a reusable and validated way to generate, configure, execute, and assess operator decision representations across many scenario variations and proficiency levels. Current approaches can require extensive custom programming for each model, scenario, or operator role; may not provide traceable rationale for actions taken during simulation; and may be difficult to compare across test events, analysis teams, or simulation environments. The gap affects the Government’s ability to understand sensitivity to operator behavior, evaluate alternate tactics, and support VV&A with documented evidence of intended use, assumptions, limitations, data pedigree, and risk.

Why innovative solutions are likely available: The Government believes innovative small businesses can apply advances from artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled simulation, human behavior representation, synthetic data generation, reinforcement learning, design of experiments, digital engineering, development, security, and operations, and modular simulation integration to address this problem. Related industry capabilities already demonstrate AI-assisted constructive simulation, synthetic data generation, intelligent agents, and integration of commercial simulation toolchains with Government simulation environments. This topic seeks to mature those types of innovations into a Government-purpose capability suitable for missile defense test and evaluation workflows.

Government interest: The Government is not seeking a vendor white paper, a visualization-only training game, or a single hard-coded operator model. The Government is seeking a Direct-to-Phase-II prototype capability that can be adapted to multiple missile defense analysis contexts; that can use Government-provided scenarios, models, data, and subject matter expert (SME) input; that can be evaluated against explicit measures of performance and effectiveness; and that can produce artifacts needed for future transition, reuse, and accreditation.

Desired characteristics:
•Open, modular interfaces for integration with constructive simulations and analysis workflows.
•Configurable operator roles and behavior profiles that can be reviewed and adjusted by authorized Government analysts or SMEs.
•Support for scenario ensembles, design of experiments, and repeatable Monte Carlo-style analysis.
•Decision traceability, data provenance, uncertainty characterization, and explainable outputs suitable for analyst review.

Responsible AI, cyber, data-management, and VV&A considerations incorporated from the beginning of Phase II.

title: Multi-Fidelity Transfer Learning for Defense Applications
summary: Rapid Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into the MDS is required for the United States to properly defend itself against its adversaries.
description: Rapid Artificial Intelligence (AI) integration into the MDS is required for the United States to properly defend itself against its adversaries. The development of robust Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) agents for complex missile defense and aerospace applications is often constrained by the computational cost, limited availability, and security restrictions of high-fidelity simulation environments. Transfer learning provides a critical pathway to overcoming these barriers. By initially training agents on low-fidelity models or unclassified representations—where data is abundant and computational demands are reduced—core behaviors, strategies, and decision-making frameworks could be efficiently developed and refined. These pretrained models could then be adapted and optimized in high-fidelity and/or environments at higher classification levels, allowing the agent to leverage its foundational knowledge while rapidly acquiring the nuanced performance required for operational deployment. This staged approach significantly reduces training time, minimizes resource expenditure, and mitigates the risk of overfitting to scarce high-fidelity/classified data. Moreover, it enables iterative development cycles where low-fidelity environments serve as agile testbeds for innovation, and high-fidelity environments refine and validate for mission-readiness. Leveraging transfer learning in this manner not only accelerates capability delivery but also ensures that AI/ML systems achieve the precision, resilience, and adaptability necessary for real-world mission success.

title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Frequency-Based Persistent Artificial Intelligence Tracking and Surveillance Capability
summary: The Navy faces acute operational challenges in intercepting and characterizing covert, highly agile adversarial emissions across dense electromagnetic operational environments.
description:
The Navy faces acute operational challenges in intercepting and characterizing covert, highly agile adversarial emissions across dense electromagnetic operational environments. Modern threat systems increasingly utilize Low Probability of Intercept and Low Probability of Detection (LPI/LPD) techniques—such as Direct-Sequence Spread Spectrum (DSSS), ultra-fast frequency hopping (UFLH), wideband Linear Frequency Modulation (LFM), Costas frequency coding, and polyphase pulse compression (e.g., Frank, P1–P4 codes)—deliberately depressing emission power densities below the thermal noise floor [Refs 1, 2]. Consequently, conventional Electronic Support Measures (ESM) and wideband radiometer/energy-detection receivers exhibit severe performance degradation, failing to detect stealth radar transmissions, covert datalinks, and distributed sensor relays. This visibility shortfall undermines the tactical sensor-to-shooter timelines foundational to Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control (CJADC2) and Distributed Maritime Operations (DMO).

To counter advanced stealth emitters, an AI-driven signal processing framework can draw upon several modular algorithmic pathways and candidate techniques, such as:

Sub-Noise-Floor Cyclostationary Analysis: For instance, computing the spectral correlation density (SCD) or cyclic autocorrelation can expose covert signal periodicities (e.g., symbol rates, chipping sequences, and carrier modulation artifacts), isolating structured LPI/LPD waveforms from stationary thermal background noise and Gaussian interference [Refs 3, 4].

Time-Frequency Deep Learning Architectures: As an example for intra-pulse modulation recognition, raw wideband In-phase/Quadrature (I/Q) samples can be transformed into high-resolution time-frequency representations—such as Wigner-Ville Distributions (WVD) or Continuous Wavelet Transforms (CWT)—and processed by deep convolutional or recurrent neural networks (CNN/RNN) to classify polyphase or frequency-coded pulses without requiring prior waveform templates [Refs 5, 6].

Adaptive Multi-Channel De-interleaving: For high-density pulse environments, candidate approaches include reinforcement-learning-guided spectral search or adaptive filter banks to isolate agile hopping channels and separate co-channel, overlapping LPI signals across wide instantaneous bandwidths [Ref 7].

Calibrated Operator Decision Metrics: To support tactical watchstanders, Bayesian neural networks or conformal prediction methods can be applied to generate uncertainty bounds alongside extracted parameters (e.g., pulse repetition intervals, modulation bandwidths, chirp rates), providing validated, interpretable indicators of stealth emitter activity.

SWaP-Constrained Edge Optimization: Potential implementation paths for tactical platforms include neural network quantization, weight pruning, and tensor acceleration to facilitate low-latency inference on Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP)-constrained naval edge computing hardware.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and NAVWAR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Ultra-Low Latency Technology for Radio Applications 5G
summary: Modern C3 operations increasingly depend on commercial 5G and IP-based network infrastructures, which are vulnerable to latency, jitter, packet loss, and adversarial interference.
description:
Modern C3 operations increasingly depend on commercial 5G and IP-based network infrastructures, which are vulnerable to latency, jitter, packet loss, and adversarial interference. As highlighted in recent industry consensus on how 5G technology is going to transform the Department of War (DoW) [Ref 2], in contested and congested environments, these challenges jeopardize mission-critical data flows, particularly time-sensitive audio communications essential for tactical decision-making. While the Multifunctional Information Distribution System (MIDS) Joint Tactical Radio System (JTRS) is the current standard for secure, jam-resistant tactical data links, it must be modernized to interoperate with these evolving network environments.

To maintain a strategic advantage in alignment with the National Defense Strategy (NDS), the Department of Defense Private 5G Deployment Strategy [Ref 1], and Joint All-Domain Command and Control (JADC2) initiatives, the Navy seeks to design, develop, and prototype a software-only solution for ultra-low latency audio data obscuration. This technology must be tailored for IP-based communications operating across 5G and Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) environments and be seamlessly integrable into existing MIDS JTRS platforms.

These software-only innovations will strengthen C3 links in real-time operational scenarios, drawing technical parallels from critical commercial capabilities such as ultra-reliable low-latency 5G for industrial automation [Ref 3] to support high-precision activities including cooperative motion control, video-guided remote operations, and node-to-node tactical communications. By integrating these technologies into existing communication infrastructures, the DoW aims to ensure robust, secure, and resilient communication channels, even in congested spectrum environments or under adversarial jamming and electronic interference.

The proposed solution should:

Achieve Ultra-Low Latency Audio Transmission: Develop software-based obscuration methods capable of delivering secure, intelligible audio over IP-based 5G networks. The threshold goal is an end-to-end latency of under 20 milliseconds, with an objective goal of 1 millisecond to meet JADC2 and NDS real-time operational requirements.

Enhance Resilience in Contested Environments: Ensure audio data integrity and communication continuity in environments affected by spectrum congestion, electromagnetic interference, or intentional jamming, using robust data hiding and spread-spectrum techniques. To satisfy PMO requirements, system resilience and audio intelligibility must be demonstrated and verified against the following representative operational profiles:
• 1. Network Packet Loss Resilience: The software-based recovery and reconstruction algorithms must maintain communication continuity under severe channel degradation:
• Threshold Target: Maintain continuous link and zero audio stream dropouts under a continuous random packet loss profile of up to 10%.
• Objective Target: Maintain link alignment and intelligibility under burst/consecutive packet loss profiles of up to 30%.
• 2. Spectrum Congestion Performance: Under simulated high-traffic 5G slice congestion (congested multi-user IP environments):
• Threshold Target: End-to-end processing and transmission latency must remain under 20 milliseconds.
• Objective Target: End-to-end processing and transmission latency must remain under 1 millisecond.
• 3. Jamming and Interference Immunity: The spread-spectrum and data-hiding layers must resist intentional electromagnetic interference:
• Threshold Target: Maintain link stability and synchronization under narrow-band and barrage jamming up to a Jamming-to-Signal (J/S) ratio of 15 dB.
• Objective Target: Maintain link stability under dynamic tracking jamming up to a J/S ratio of 30 dB.
• 4. Audio Intelligibility Standards: Restored and unobscured audio streams must meet standard military voice intelligibility baselines:
• Threshold Target: Achieve a Perceptual Evaluation of Speech Quality (PESQ) score of 3.0 or higher (providing fully intelligible, clear voice communication).
• Objective Target: Achieve a PESQ score of 4.0 or higher (delivering excellent, high-fidelity voice reproduction).

Enable Scalable Integration with Existing DoW Systems: Design modular, software-defined solutions for seamless integration into platforms such as the MIDS JTRS SDR, supporting the modernization of tactical communication networks under the MIDS Program Office.

Support Seamless Transition to Operational Systems: Ensure the final solution supports a seamless transition to operational systems, including full integration into the MIDS JTRS platform.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and NAVWAR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Advanced Multi-User Signal Separation for Tactical Waveforms
summary: The Program Office championing this effort is PMW/A 101 that manages and delivers advanced, secure tactical communication systems for naval platforms.
description:
The Program Office championing this effort is PMW/A 101 that manages and delivers advanced, secure tactical communication systems for naval platforms. A core mandate of this office is to continuously integrate next-generation capabilities that enhance waveform resilience, increase spectral efficiency, and ensure robust connectivity for warfighters operating in highly congested and contested electromagnetic environments. The technology developed under this SBIR Direct to Phase II topic is intended to transition directly into the PMW 101 portfolio of tactical radio systems.

In modern tactical networks, the proliferation of friendly assets creates a dense signal environment where simultaneous transmissions on the same frequency cause multi-user collisions and limit operational effectiveness. This problem is exacerbated in contested domains where very low Signal-to-Noise Ratios (SNRs) are common. Current baseline receiver systems typically treat these overlapping friendly signals as insurmountable noise. Because legacy systems lack the ability to untangle these collisions, they simply drop the packets or fail to decode them entirely, which severely limits network throughput and the real-time data exchange required for mission-critical operations.

To overcome these limitations and maintain a critical operational advantage, this SBIR Direct to Phase II topic seeks the development of an advanced signal processing core capable of robust multi-user signal separation for tactical waveforms. By enabling non-orthogonal multiple access-like schemes, this capability will significantly increase network capacity and user count without requiring additional spectrum.

The goal is to deliver high-quality soft signal likelihoods recovered from simultaneous-user collisions to downstream soft-decision decoding algorithms. To achieve close-to-optimal performance in two-user collisions, proposed approaches must operate effectively at very low SNRs and mitigate intermittent interference by dynamically detecting burst collisions and nullifying compromised likelihood data. While advanced joint demodulation represents one viable pathway, proposers are highly encouraged to suggest any innovative framework that targets an approximate 3dB improvement over current baselines. The targeted improvement will be measured against the current baseline receiver under comparable two-user collision conditions and will reflect improvement in multi-user separation and downstream decoding performance rather than overall receiver sensitivity. This 3dB gain will translate directly to longer communication ranges, higher data rates, and increased resilience against jamming.

This effort requires the performer to:

Develop an advanced algorithm for multi-user separation that is effective in low SNR and interference-prone environments.

Generate high-quality Log-Likelihood Ratios (LLRs) for modern soft-decision forward error correction (FEC) decoders, utilizing novel, proposer-defined technical approaches.

Implement a mechanism to detect burst collisions and erase or correct corrupted likelihood data to prevent decoder failure.

Design, implement, and test the algorithm within a modular Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) core based on open-systems principles.

The successful transition of this capability will fundamentally improve the resilience of tactical networks. By delivering a modular FPGA core built on open-systems principles, the solution could be seamlessly integrated into a wide range of current and future Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) radio platforms, which could significantly reduce the life-cycle costs associated with developing entirely new systems to achieve these capabilities. This Direct to Phase II effort seeks proposers who can rapidly demonstrate these advanced receiver techniques with a clear transition path into operational military hardware.
