title: DIRECT TO PHASE II: Modular Software Reference Implementation for Waveforms
summary: The Multifunctional Information Distribution System (MIDS) Program Office (PMA/PMW-101) is driving a critical architectural pivot in tactical data link (TDL) communications. Historically, the defense sector has relied heavily on FPGAs to host complex tactical waveforms due to strict RF timing constraints.
description:
The Multifunctional Information Distribution System (MIDS) Program Office (PMA/PMW-101) is driving a critical architectural pivot in tactical data link (TDL) communications. Historically, the defense sector has relied heavily on FPGAs to host complex tactical waveforms due to strict RF timing constraints. However, as noted in recent software-defined radio (SDR) surveys, this hardware-centric approach suffers from severe developmental friction [Ref 1]. Programming FPGAs via Hardware Description Languages (HDL) requires lengthy synthesis, complex place-and-route cycles, and difficult timing closures. Because software compilation bypasses these physical routing and synthesis barriers, transitioning from HDL to high-order software languages (C/C++) on general-purpose architectures typically reduces development timelines by 50% to 80%—compressing multi-year hardware upgrade cycles into a matter of months.

To overcome legacy constraints, this initiative mandates a transition toward a modular open systems architecture (MOSA). By decoupling the physical layer (PHY) from the underlying hardware, containerized Software-Defined Waveforms (SDWs) can be deployed across modern processing. Because standard Central Processing Units (CPUs) often lack the deterministic throughput required for heavy RF pipelines, modern SDR frameworks dynamically offload computationally intensive PHY tasks to coprocessors like GPUs, Neural Processing Units (NPUs), or adaptive System-on-Chips (SoCs).

This heterogeneous approach enables the execution of highly parallel mathematical pipelines via software Application Programming Interfaces (APIs), including:

Vectorized Signal Processing on GPUs or NPU cores:
• Executing Fast Fourier Transforms (FFTs)
• High-throughput Forward Error Correction (FEC)
• Matrix Multiplications

AI-Driven Cognitive Radio: As demonstrated by O'Shea and Hoydis [Ref 2], traditional heuristic PHY blocks can be replaced by "neural receivers" and deep learning autoencoders. By reusing embedded AI inference blocks, radios can perform real-time channel estimation, signal classification, and non-linear error correction at the tactical edge.

By migrating to this software-first model, the Navy ensures rapid portability across joint-force platforms to provide highly scalable parallelism, allowing waveforms and AI-enhanced microservices to execute, reconfigure, and recover dynamically, ensuring maximum resiliency in contested electronic warfare environments.

title: Mobile Vehicle Forensics
summary: Operational Need & Gap: During tactical site exploitation (TSE), Marine Corps and Joint operators require immediate, field-deployable hardware and software to recognize, preserve, and collect materials of forensic value. While multi-purpose forensic kits exist to process traditional materials, a critical intelligence gap remains regarding vehicle-derived data.
description:
Operational Need & Gap: During tactical site exploitation (TSE), Marine Corps and Joint operators require immediate, field-deployable hardware and software to recognize, preserve, and collect materials of forensic value. While multi-purpose forensic kits exist to process traditional materials, a critical intelligence gap remains regarding vehicle-derived data. Modern vehicles function as mobile data hubs featuring advanced navigation, localized track logs, and cached external device connections. Exploiting this telematics and informatics data is vital for generating actionable intelligence, mapping networks, and establishing identity dominance.

The Problem (Technological Fragmentation): The primary barrier to tactical vehicle exploitation is severe technological fragmentation. Current vehicle forensic solutions are often designed for controlled laboratory environments. Because In-Vehicle Infotainment (IVI) systems and Electronic Control Units (ECUs) rely on proprietary software architectures and inconsistent file structures, existing tools are often restricted to narrow manufacturer subsets. Consequently, field operators may be forced to perform invasive, time-consuming physical disassembly of the vehicle dashboard—a method that is untenable in many field environments.

Scope of Effort: This SBIR topic seeks innovative proposals to develop a low-SWaP (Size, Weight, and Power), ruggedized, all-in-one device that automates the forensic exploitation of vehicle data systems. The system must interface via standard external access points (e.g., On-Board Diagnostic [OBD-II] ports or Universal Serial Bus [USB]); automatically profile the vehicle’s make, model, year, and digital architecture; and execute an automated script to extract and structure data. Crucially, these features must be achieved through a non-invasive approach requiring no component disassembly, while maintaining strict forensic data integrity and verifiable accuracy.

The system must seamlessly interface with a broad registry of modern commercial and civilian vehicles across diverse model years, makes, and international manufacturers. Specifically, the device must extract and normalize data from disparate telematics systems (e.g., embedded GPS, localized track logs) and informatics modules (e.g., infotainment systems, paired Bluetooth logs, Wi-Fi cache, and cellular device pairings) without requiring laboratory-grade component disassembly.

Performance Goals:
• Threshold (Minimum): Demonstrate compatibility with representative samples of common vehicles; extract high-priority telematics (i.e., GPS, route history) and informatics (paired device logs) in under 15 minutes with verifiable accuracy (i.e., comparison with test data collected separately); packaged in a portable, field-ruggedized kit.
• Objective (Ideal): A pocket-sized, plug-and-play device that requires minimal operator training; demonstrates a modular path to broad vehicle compatibility; and extracts a comprehensive forensic data set in under 5 minutes via an intuitive, automated interface.

title: Lightweight, Energy-Efficient Portable Nitrogen Generator for Expeditionary Operations
summary: The United States Marine Corps (USMC) requires high-pressure nitrogen gas at forward operating locations to perform essential maintenance tasks, including aircraft and ground vehicle tire servicing, recoil mechanism servicing, recharging of gas suspension and accumulator components, and filling gas cylinders.
description:
The United States Marine Corps (USMC) requires high-pressure nitrogen gas at forward operating locations to perform essential maintenance tasks, including aircraft and ground vehicle tire servicing, recoil mechanism servicing, recharging of gas suspension and accumulator components, and filling gas cylinders. Historically, the military relies on pre-filled, heavy steel gas cylinders resupplied through a vulnerable logistics chain. This process creates a severe logistical burden and hazardous material handling risk. Generating nitrogen at the point of need is essential to sustaining mission readiness in distributed, austere, and expeditionary environments consistent with USMC Force Design 2030 and Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations (EABO) concepts. The final product will be employed by USMC maintainers operating from forward tactical enclosures, specifically integrating with the JLTV Electronic Maintenance Shelter (JEMS). The system will provide point-of-need, high-purity nitrogen to service tactical vehicle and aircraft tires, hydraulic accumulators, recoil mechanisms, and suspension struts in support of distributed expeditionary operations.

While the USMC currently utilizes a legacy portable nitrogen generation system, it presents severe technical limitations that hinder expeditionary operations. First, the legacy system weighs 450 pounds, severely limiting mobility and requiring a four-person lift. Second, it requires 240-volt single-phase electrical power drawing 25 Amps. This exceeds the standard 120-volt, 25-Amp electrical limits of forward tactical enclosures, such as the Joint Expeditionary Maintenance Shelter (JEMS). Third, the current system only achieves 99.0% nitrogen purity (falling short of the required 99.5% for sensitive aviation and vehicle struts) and suffers from extremely slow flow rates, taking up to 6 hours to fill a standard 244-cubic-foot cylinder.

Commercial industry has introduced 120-volt single-phase configurations that achieve high purity. However, these state-of-the-art commercial units fall short of expeditionary physical requirements: they weigh in excess of 650 pounds, require separate external air compressors to operate, and maximize output at only 3,000 pounds per square inch (PSI). No known existing solution simultaneously achieves man-portable weight limits, 120-volt/25-Amp operation, self-contained air compression, high purity (Develop and demonstrate a man-portable, self-contained nitrogen generator capable of producing high-purity (equal to or less than 99.5%) nitrogen at 1,800 to 3,500 pounds per square inch (PSI), operating strictly within a 120-volt, 25-Amp single-phase electrical limit to support United States Marine Corps (USMC) expeditionary maintenance operations.

This SBIR topic seeks innovative small business proposals to design, develop, demonstrate, and deliver a prototype device for a man-portable, energy-efficient, self-contained nitrogen generator that overcomes the stated limitations. Proposed approaches may include advanced membrane separation, pressure swing adsorption (PSA) with novel sorbent materials, hybrid separation architectures, lightweight composite enclosures, advanced electric motor/compressor technologies, intelligent power management, or other innovative approaches that meaningfully advance the state of the art. The prototype device must address extreme environmental challenges, specifically maintaining gas separation efficiency in high heat and high humidity, and must physically fit within tactical maintenance shelters.

The prototype device shall target the following performance parameters to bound the scope of effort, while remaining open to innovative approaches that may refine specific parameters:

Performance Parameter Phase II Threshold (T = Minimum Acceptable) Phase II Objective (O = Desired)
Output Pressure (Selectable/Continuous): No less than 3,500 PSI (T); Greater than 3500 PSI (O)
Nitrogen Purity: =/- 99.5% (T); =/- 99.99% (O)
Continuous Output Flow Rate: =/- 60 Standard Cubic Feet per Hour (SCFH) (T); =/- 120 SCFH (O)
System Weight & Transportability: =/+ 250 lbs total. Must include two-wheeled cart configuration. System can break down into modular components where no single module exceeds the two-person lift limits defined in MIL-STD-1472 (T); =/+ 150 lbs total. System can break down into modular components where no single module exceeds the two-person lift limits defined in MIL-STD-1472 (O)
Form Factor/Size Limits: Must physically clear a 51.5 in (W) x 64.5 in (H) shelter door Modular, compact footprint (e.g., =/+ 30 in x 30 in base) (T = O)
Electrical Power Input: =/+ 3.4 kW, 120 VAC (single-phase, 50-60 Hz, max 25-Amp draw) (T): =/+ 3 kW, 120 VAC (single-phase) AND/OR 28V DC (Tactical Vehicle Integration) (O)
Operational Temperature: 40°F to +90°F (-32°C to +49°C) (T); -40°F to +140°F (-40°C to +60°C) (O)
Operational Humidity: Operable in 0% to 95% Relative Humidity (RH) (T); Operable in up to 100% RH (condensing) (O)

Proposals shall clearly identify the selected nitrogen generation approach, provide a credible technical basis for meeting the target performance parameters (particularly regarding thermal/moisture management and weight reduction), demonstrate awareness of the state of the art, and demonstrate that the effort is achievable within SBIR Phase I and Phase II timelines.

title: Integrated Multi-Spectral Periscope for the Amphibious Combat Vehicle (ACV)
summary: Current periscopic vision systems on Marine Corps combat vehicles are limited to daylight optical performance, over a limited Field of View (FoV), and lack the ability to integrate modern digital imaging, thermal, and night vision technologies.
description:
Current periscopic vision systems on Marine Corps combat vehicles are limited to daylight optical performance, over a limited Field of View (FoV), and lack the ability to integrate modern digital imaging, thermal, and night vision technologies. The new system shall provide daylight, low-light/night vision, and thermal (IR) imaging capabilities through a single, compact, and modular unit; and enhance situational awareness, target detection, and crew safety for Marines during water, transition, and land operating environments.

This SBIR topic seeks to develop an integrated camera-based periscope module that:
• Provides visible (Electro-Optical [EO]), night vision (Near-Infrared Low-Level Laser (or Light) [NIR/LLL]), and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imaging in a compact unit.
• Is retrofit-compatible with existing periscope housings used in the USMC ACV FOV, or is capable of replacing optical viewports with an electronic display module.
• Includes onboard image fusion and low-latency video output for vehicle displays and augmented-reality systems.
• Meets ruggedization standards (MIL-STD-810H, MIL-STD-461D, and EC Standard 60529, rating IP66) for temperature, shock, vibration, EMI, dust and water resistance.
• Provides hardware resistance to seawater corrosion, as tested in accordance with GMW 14872, “Exterior, Exposure D” as stated in Table A3.
• Does not result in significant weight increase over that of the standard periscope.
• Supports integration with vehicle electronics architectures, including Vehicular Integration for C4ISR/EW Interoperability (VICTORY) and NATO STANAG 4609 standards.

Novel design approaches may include:
• Digital overlay in periscope eyepieces, merging optical and sensor imagery for seamless situational awareness.
• Edge processing and AI-assisted fusion of EO/NIR/LWIR feeds to highlight threats or movement.
• Wireless or wired integration with crew display systems such as:
o Integrated Visual Augmentation System (IVAS)
o Enhanced Night Vision Goggle – Binocular (ENVG-B)
o Joint Mounted Display System (JMDS)

title: Distributed Multispectral Event-Driven Integrated Sensing and Communications
summary: The Navy Aegis Program Office is interested in expanding battlespace awareness to support cross-domain operations through the integration of remote passive sensors.
description:
The Navy Aegis Program Office is interested in expanding battlespace awareness to support cross-domain operations through the integration of remote passive sensors. Currently, these sensors rely on real-time frame-based processing that generates large volumes of data, requiring significant processing power and energy and creating constraints for resource-limited hardware platforms with finite battery life, processing capabilities, and memory. In addition, transmitting large volumes of data over dynamic communication links can introduce delays and encounter bandwidth limitations that cannot meet time-critical operational needs. The complexity of the battlespace and electromagnetic environment further presents challenges for robust detection, classification, and identification. Advanced remote passive-sensor technologies that enable efficient and distributed sensing and processing will support multidomain operations by providing timely and resilient battlespace awareness. Successful technologies will be transitioned to the Aegis Combat System (ACS) to enhance distributed sensing, accelerate decision-making, and enable cross-domain operations.

The Navy is seeking to develop Multispectral Integrated Neuromorphic Sensing and Communications (MINSC) technology to support endurant remote sensing capability. MINSC is an event-driven sensor featuring low-probability-of-intercept (LPI) data transmission that can timely identify a wide range of objects and transmit the information to remote platforms to integrate into the existing decision-making process. Neuromorphic computing can provide energy efficient, parallel processing, and low-latency framework for passive sensing, edge computing, and remote inference.

Neuromorphic sensors deliver high temporal resolution, asynchronous, energy and bandwidth efficient data inspired by biological vision. The Navy seeks to build an Event-Driven Energy-Efficient Ecosystem to support Endurant Long-Range Sensing and Communications capability. Solutions can be software, neuromorphic hardware, and/or end-to-end neuromorphic system that can deliver robust information and fuse with existing sensors to provide improved tracking, detection, classification, and identification. The Navy is open to innovative ideas of novel system design that can make decisions locally and communicate sparingly or timely send out the event-driven information for remote inference. The intended capability is an integrated remote passive-sensing capability that performs event-driven local sensing and processing, communicating only the information necessary to enhance remote awareness, and fuses with existing sensors to improve tracking, detection, classification and identification.

Distributed MINSC will provide advantages in dynamic environment and resilience to noise and debris associated with military applications. Incorporating event-based multispectral remote sensors with onboard sensors will expand operational battlespace, contribute to robust Common Operational Picture (COP) and enhance situational awareness. It will integrate with the Aegis and permit realistic testing of all threat types and configurations in a dynamic testing environment. Track visualization will be delivered through the existing ACS console Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs). The solution will support current operator track management and decision-making and integrate with the AEGIS Test Bed (ATB) to facilitate system evaluation against more advanced threats. The solution will provide an enhanced capability to address targets in all configurations and optimal engagement options to the sailors, which will increase mission capability and effectiveness against the latest threats.

title: Automated Hardening for Cyber Secure Operating Systems
summary: Navy platforms have computing devices that drive their operational capabilities, especially autonomous or unmanned systems. Many platforms such as autonomous vehicles have some version and distribution of Linux as their operating system (OS) as well as an application running on it.
description:
Navy platforms have computing devices that drive their operational capabilities, especially autonomous or unmanned systems. Many platforms such as autonomous vehicles have some version and distribution of Linux as their operating system (OS) as well as an application running on it. Providing cybersecurity to these platforms is not only challenging due to their complexities but also very time consuming from a manpower perspective. This workload includes analyzing all levels of software (to include the OS) and configuring them to make them more secure as well as other cyber hardening operations such as software debloating to remove unnecessary functionality. The Navy has many platforms so each would require its own analysis and hardening. There are various means for improving the cybersecurity posture of the platform, each either manual or with its own tool, which creates undue burden on the developer of the platform for hardening without missing certain security features.

The focus of this SBIR effort is strictly on the OS, in this case Linux. The tool should determine the Linux OS functionality actually required by a specific platform instantiation, remove unnecessary OS components and functionality, and configure the remaining Linux OS to improve cybersecurity posture while preserving required system functionality. The goal is to create an automated tool that analyzes the various specifications, configurations, applications, etc. to harden the cybersecurity posture of the underlying Linux OS. The performer should propose their own platform, preferably either a commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) or open source platform that has a Linux OS and use this for design and experimentation on how to automate the cyber hardening of just the OS. It is preferred that the device be some type of autonomous vehicle. The performer will produce an overall software architecture for the automated OS hardening tool as well as a demonstration of the conceptual capability in Phase I while Phase II will involve development of a prototype in cooperation/guidance with Navy personnel. Metrics to demonstrate the improvements from the automated tool should be provided in the proposal.

title: Low-cost Mid-wave Infrared Focal-Plane Array (FPA) Fabrication through Direct-bond Interconnection
summary: Electro-Optic and Infrared (EO/IR) sensors are used in a wide variety of applications, such as navigation, wide-area surveillance, and targeting.
description:
Electro-Optic and Infrared (EO/IR) sensors are used in a wide variety of applications, such as navigation, wide-area surveillance, and targeting. Operating in the visible and near-IR bands, EO sensors are available with small pixels and in large arrays at low cost, because the Si-detector wafer and Si-ROIC wafer can be 3D-integrated directly through wafer-to-wafer bonding with high yield at high volume based on material and complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS)-process compatibility. By contrast, sensors operating in the MWIR employ III-V detector materials, which are not CMOS-process compatible, while III-V epi-layer detectors cannot be epitaxially grown directly on Si, as required to produce the crystalline order of high-quality detectors [Refs 1-2]. Instead, the III-V detector epi-layer is grown on a lattice-compatible substrate wafer, which is then flip-chip bonded to a Si-ROIC through a dense array of sub-pixel indium bumps placed on each wafer, followed by detector-substrate removal. The technically demanding process of depositing, aligning, and compressing the dense arrays of indium bumps on detector and ROIC die, results in a labor-intensive, inefficient, low-yield process for IR FPA fabrication, which greatly increases cost.

In recent years, 3D-heterogeneous integration has enabled a single integrated chip of greater overall functionality to be realized at reduced cost by assembling multiple smaller chips, each having unique functionality, material, node size, and/or foundry origin. Direct-bond interconnection (DBI) [Refs 3-5] is a 3D-heterogeneous integration technique that can potentially enable low-cost MWIR FPA fabrication. In principle, DBI should enable very large format FPAs with small pixels to be fabricated, as the process is largely independent of wafer and pixel size, in contrast to conventional bump-bonding. Moreover, the DBI process utilizes a temperature range that is compatible with MWIR IR detector materials.

The goal of this SBIR topic is to demonstrate the use of DBI or a similar process for fabrication of high-performance, large format, small-pixel, MWIR FPAs at low cost with the objective of refining the technique sufficiently to potentially replace conventional bump-bonding.

title: “Self-Replicating Evolutionary Agentic AI Swarming Force” with Autonomous Embedded AI Guardrail Enforcers
summary: This SBIR topic seeks hardware-agnostic Agentic AI swarm-teaming technologies capable of self-replication, hybrid-evolution (self-evolution and coevolution), and self-organization into teaming many arrangements. It is important to note that this project does not challenge the importance of physical platforms/machines (i.e., unmanned assets) that have physical presence in operational environments.
description:
This SBIR topic seeks hardware-agnostic Agentic AI swarm-teaming technologies capable of self-replication, hybrid-evolution (self-evolution and coevolution), and self-organization into teaming many arrangements. It is important to note that this project does not challenge the importance of physical platforms/machines (i.e., unmanned assets) that have physical presence in operational environments. The envisioned Agentic AI system is the machine’s intelligent autonomy software that controls the platform’s presence and its interactions with entities in the operational environment. It autonomously configures individual swarms with unique missions and networks of collaborative swarms operating in multiple operational domains with specific teaming assignments.

The envisioned swarm system is agentic as it pursues goals autonomously. It interprets assigned mission objectives and determines how to achieve them. It knows how to process, fuse, and exploit all source intelligence (ASI) and live sensor feeds to determine the course of action (CoA) and keeps adjusting it until the outcome is reached. It decides which payloads to use and when to use them, for example, active and/or passive intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting (ISRT) sensors, point-to-point or omni-broadcast communication, or weapon systems, etc. It adapts when situations or environmental conditions change, or certain aspects of a plan fail. It can recover from various system failures and processing errors. It is designed with embedded AI-Guardrail-Enforcers to manage, validate, and verify every aspect of the Agentic AI system’s performance and associated risks to ensure that the end-to-end system adheres to established policies set forth by the Department of War and the U.S. Navy including operational safety requirements as well as the national security doctrines and mandates. The highest priority for this program is to establish ZERO tolerance for AI-generated rogue populations of unaligned agents rapidly and uncontrollably increase.

The hybrid-evolutionary aspect of the Agentic AI system focuses on attaining new operational proficiency and know-how to execute emerging missions with the highest accuracy, persistence, and endurance. The self-evolving AI system monitors endogenous performance of all subsystems, gets feedback, and improves its own internal design configuration autonomously, for example, altering or generating new internal models. The coevolutionary AI system monitors exogenous performance interactions and coevolves the internal design in response to interactions with the environment and adversaries. It improves autonomous teaming performance interactions and reconfigurations, for example, altering or generating new swarming models, plans, and configurations to maintain operational tempo.

The self-replication aims to create autonomous, self-improving agents capable of independent survival and expansion. This Agentic AI system autonomously improves itself, creates its own successors, and builds specialized sub-agents to solve operational issues.

The self-configuring aspect of the Agentic AI system focuses on a variety of mission-focused collaborative teaming arrangements, including scouting teams for early detection of indications and warning signs to ensure survival, trip-wire teams to detect encroaching threats, ad-hoc networking teams for continuous collaboration and tracking threats, a self-defense team for fault-tolerant operations, and offensive teams to ensure survival. In aggregate, these teams form an Agentic-Force that self-adapts, self-organizes, and self-heals.

The Agentic AI Swarming-Force addresses mission capability gaps that require agile adaptation to novel adversarial TTPs and unanticipated asymmetric countermeasures. The envisioned AI capability requires AI-based evolutionary modelling techniques for learning, reasoning, recognition, and autonomous decision-making to counter emergent and/or unanticipated observable patterns of life activities or events. In other words, agentic discovery of unknown-unknown events/assets posed by the intelligent adversaries. It ensures the timely execution of CoA plans to neutralize emerging threats, including asymmetric attacks, novel deployment of joint civilian and military assets, cloaked military assets, decoys, and deceptive asset deployments. A representative set of agentic impelling operations may be conducted overtly or covertly to influence hostile forces to undertake desired actions, including adopting specific courses of action or modifying their pattern of life to safeguard critical assets through reconfiguration, relocation, or repurposing. These observable responses can then be exploited by the Agentic AI Swarming Force to degrade adversarial autonomy and disrupt, reshape, and ultimately defeat their operational plans and tactical engagements.

A notional framework for developing the required critical technologies is as follows. First, meta-learning and meta-reasoning capabilities—learning how to learn and reason—are foundational. Rather than relying on static training, agents continuously refine their internal learning processes to autonomously adapt to new tasks and conditions. This allows the system to create specialized sub-agents for various operational tasks and teaches them optimal strategies. Second, replication logic creates next-generation agents to improve operational efficiency, reduce false-alarm rates, and field additional task-organized agents to address emergent or previously unanticipated requirements. Third, autonomous resource management mechanisms must dynamically replicate, allocate, sustain, scale, or retire agents to maintain operational efficiency and mission alignment. Finally, secure, low-probability-of-intercept/low-probability-of-detection (LPI/LPD) ad hoc networking and communications are essential to enable mission-focused teaming, decentralized coordination, and Reachback to share operational insights across agent networks beyond local clusters. Critical AI technology components and developments are as follows:

• Self-reflecting Agentic AI system to provide: 1) an introspection feedback loop to enable the Agentic AI system to analyze its own plan, spot errors or weak reasoning logic, and revise them before acting, which would make the system better at goal-seeking and improve its strategy; and 2) a retrospection feedback loop to enable the Agentic AI system to analyze its past plans, decisions, and resulting outcomes. Spot and learn from both the advantages and the shortcomings of those past decision processes to improve future planning and reasoning logic.
• Identification of novel and evolutionary behaviors appearing in a new generation of AI-agent models.
• Methodology to specify how self-replication and coevolutionary processes are initiated and developed, strategic life-cycle planning, resource acquisition for autonomous self-replication, and survival tactics that exploit operational ecosystem.
• Contextual modeling: relational, spatial, logic-based, uncertainty, and hybrid context modeling.
• Meta learning: decision tree and multilayer perception classifiers, collaborative filtering, pattern mining, deep learning.
• Spatiotemporal synchronization methods for multimodal data across decentralized architectures.
• Multimodal contextual signal processing and fusion.
• Cross-domain contextual collaborative learning, inference, and recognition.
• Meta reasoning, contextual reasoning, and risk assessment and reduction.
• Contextual priority-based task management balancing operational objectives such as persistence, endurance, and collections.

The scope of the initial feasibility study and deliverables are as follows: a) define the challenge problem that will likely meet the benchmark performance metrics; b) review a set of candidate Agentic AI methods and data requirements; c) develop a low-cost initial proof-of-concept prototype for the assessment; d) evaluate feasibility against measurable criteria; and e) deliver a proposed Phase II prototype development plan including technical risk reduction criteria and next steps.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. title: Electro-Optical/Infrared Tactical Decision Aid
summary: The United States Navy (USN) requires the capability to rapidly predict the performance of sensors that depend on the propagation of electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) radiation (i.e., wavelengths from 0.4 to 12 micron) in air. Sensor performance is subject to environmental/meteorologic conditions, as well as sensor, platform, background/clutter, and target characteristics.
description:
The United States Navy (USN) requires the capability to rapidly predict the performance of sensors that depend on the propagation of electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) radiation (i.e., wavelengths from 0.4 to 12 micron) in air. Sensor performance is subject to environmental/meteorologic conditions, as well as sensor, platform, background/clutter, and target characteristics. For a given sensor on a platform and a target in background/clutter, a forecaster should be able to determine key performance metrics; for example, maximum detection range based on the forecasted meteorological conditions. In this way, USN commanders can make tactical decisions based on the predicted sensor performance given ambient/forecast weather conditions. Key modeling components within a TDA include the land/maritime surface background, target signature, radiative transfer, and sensor performance models. These models are often interdependent, requiring feedback between them (e.g., radiative transfer between target and background models is needed to compute the contrast of the target in the background, which then feeds into a sensor performance model).

Target Acquisition Weapons Software (TAWS), a successor to Electro-Optic Tactical Decision Aid (EOTDA), was originally developed by the Air Force Research Laboratory (AFRL) and released in 1998. Later a target scene model improvement for selected high-resolution targets was implemented with Multi-Service Electro-optics Signature (MuSES). The USN is looking for an innovative and accurate EO/IR TDA, which would be an alternative/improvement to TAWS. Improvements could include support for three dimensional meteorological inputs. The primary challenge for implementing an EO/IR TDA is the methodical verification and validation (V&V) of the constituent models and submodels being developed. This SBIR topic seeks innovative solutions to the development of an EO/IR TDA with particular focus on the methods proposed to verify and validate developed models. A list of prior V&V efforts on proposed submodels should be made clear in the responses to this solicitation, as well as the proposed means/methods to conduct V&V under a Phase II and/or Phase III.

title: Autonomous Multi-Intelligence Acoustic Reasoning Agent for Anti-Submarine Warfare
summary: The Department of the Navy (DON) seeks development of an autonomous decision-support and reasoning capability for ASW that can reduce dependence on continuous human interpretation of complex acoustic displays and enable future distributed unmanned ASW operations.
description:
The Department of the Navy (DON) seeks development of an autonomous decision-support and reasoning capability for ASW that can reduce dependence on continuous human interpretation of complex acoustic displays and enable future distributed unmanned ASW operations. Current ASW performance is heavily dependent on trained operators who interpret passive narrowband, passive broadband, Demodulation of Noise (DEMON), and other acoustic products while simultaneously incorporating situational knowledge such as geography, bathymetry, Conductivity Temperature and Depth (CTD) data for sound-speed structure, Global Positioning System (GPS), Automatic Identification System (AIS), organic/non-organic tracks, surface traffic, tactical geometry, and expected target behaviors. This human fusion process is effective but difficult to scale across persistent unmanned systems operating at range, under intermittent communications, and in acoustically cluttered environments.

This SBIR topic requests development of an autonomous ASW agent that can ingest heterogeneous acoustic detections and associated confidence measures, correlate them with non-acoustic common operating picture data, reason over environmental acoustic propagation, and maintain multiple explainable track and classification hypotheses over time. The capability should explicitly account for confusers such as merchant shipping, fishing vessels, biologics, own-force and friendly surface ship contributions, reverberation/clutter, and geographically-dependent propagation effects. The resulting system should not be a single-sensor classifier only; it should demonstrate multi-source temporal reasoning that can explain why a contact is assessed as likely submarine, non-submarine, ambiguous, or requiring additional sensing. The approach should be modular and compatible with Navy acoustic processing and performance-prediction workflows, while allowing Navy-provided threat behavior models, environmental data, and acoustic feature streams to be incorporated without redesign. Submissions should include a description of prior sensor fusion development that will serve as a baseline for the proposed ASW fusion architecture.

title: High Sensitivity Tunneling Magnetoresistive Magnetometers
summary: Many Navy systems utilize magnetometer technologies for the remote detection, localization, and classification of ferrous objects. Decades of research into different technologies including optically pumped magnetometers have provided highly sensitive technologies which meet most Navy sensitivity needs.
description:
Many Navy systems utilize magnetometer technologies for the remote detection, localization, and classification of ferrous objects. Decades of research into different technologies including optically pumped magnetometers have provided highly sensitive technologies which meet most Navy sensitivity needs. However, higher sensitivity magnetometers also possess increased SWAP-C, which limits their applicability in many Navy applications.

Therefore, there is a direct need for highly sensitive magnetometers that are also compact, low cost, and low power to support a broader range of Navy mission requirements including one-way attack vehicles, expeditionary warfare, mine warfare, and swarming systems. Over the past 30 years, an adjacent technology known as tunneling magnetoresistance (TMR) has had drastic improvements in system sensitivities, unlocking a potential new regime of magnetometer technologies that exhibit ultra-low SWAP-C while maintaining Navy relevant sensitivities.

Design Requirements:
-Size: less than 10 mm x 10 mm per axis
-Power: less than 100 mW per axis
-Sensitivity: less than 50 pT/rt(Hz) @ 1 Hz
-Frequency Range: DC-500KHz
-Dynamic Range: -100 uT to 100 uT
-Nonlinearity over dynamic range: less than 0.1 %
-Standardized per unit electrical packaging

title: Improved Ionosphere D-region Specification for High Frequency Propagation
summary: HF and VLF skywave propagation depend on knowledge of the altitudinal structure of the ionosphere for reliable system operation. The D-region ionosphere, a region typically between 60-90 km altitude above the Earth’s surface, is particularly challenging to predict with sufficient fidelity for skywave mission planning because the region is difficult to measure with in situ measurements.
description:
HF and VLF skywave propagation depend on knowledge of the altitudinal structure of the ionosphere for reliable system operation. The D-region ionosphere, a region typically between 60-90 km altitude above the Earth’s surface, is particularly challenging to predict with sufficient fidelity for skywave mission planning because the region is difficult to measure with in situ measurements. Remote sensing methods provide a limited dataset from which to develop detailed physical and assimilative models that can reliably produce the regional behavior on a day-to-day basis.

Operational models like the D-Region Absorption Product (D-RAP) produce maps of outage areas as a function of radio frequency (RF) to inform HF system users of anticipated degradation or blackouts due to radiation increases. These predictions primarily address HF absorption due to solar X-ray flares at low and mid-latitudes and do not address the VLF propagation use case. While solar X-ray flares are important effects with Navy relevance, the effects of flares typically only last for a few hours and occur 10-20 times a year. For sufficient use in HF absorption and VLF propagation applications, a D-region ionosphere is required to capture seasonal, solar cycle, and day-to-day variability at all latitudes in addition to solar flare phenomenology.

The intended capability is improved D-region specification and forecast in the 60-70 km and 80-90 km altitude regions for VLF propagation and HF absorption, particularly day-to-day variability and in the high latitude regions at night.

Climatological models like the International Reference Ionosphere (IRI) produce an altitude profile at D-region altitudes. The IRI model is based on about a hundred historical rocket profiles, so it captures some of the basic day/night, latitudinal, and seasonal variations in the D-region ionosphere but the model does not capture day-to-day variations or solar X-ray flare events. The model may be sufficient for some HF propagation applications but has been shown to be severely deficient in the high latitude region and during nighttime. In addition, the observations used to create the model do not accurately capture the shape of the lower D-region, which is required for VLF propagation applications.

The Next-generation Ionospheric Model for Operations (NIMO) is an assimilative geospace model developed to address operational USN space weather needs in the ionosphere. NIMO harnesses contributions from both near real-time data and state-of-the-art implementation of ionospheric theory to provide hindcasts, nowcasts, and forecasts for operational or research purposes. NIMO is currently configured to assimilate various types of electron density measurements through the Ionospheric Data Assimilation Four-Dimensional (IDA-4D) data assimilation schema. The D-region is not included in the data assimilation process but is simply added in post processing to the bottom of the electron density grid. The D-region model includes influence from changes in the solar conditions, but uses a climatological model for the neutral atmosphere, so it does not capture the day-to-day variability that is seen in the ionosphere.

Key performance Metrics/Goals:
Techniques to improve the global specification and forecast of the D-region ionosphere is sought with particular emphasis on the low latitudes (< 30 degrees) and high latitudes (> 60 degrees). Note: Any measurement techniques should provide measurements or any model should ingest measurements of the D-region and demonstrate improvement over existing models in two key altitude regions: 60-70 km altitude and 80-90 km altitude, which are required for VLF propagation and HF absorption, respectively.

Key parameters include
1. Specify electron density in the 60-70km and 80-90km regions within 10% error. Alternatively, an improvement 75% of the time over existing models is sought.
2. Specification at a temporal cadence of 5-15 minutes
3. Specification at a spatial resolution of 5 degrees in latitude and longitude

Technical concepts may include developing prototype concept improvements to measurement techniques and systems, developing improvements to data exploitation and modeling, or a combination of the two.

title: Expeditionary Water Quality Sensors
summary: Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption.
description:
Expeditionary forces need updated water testing capabilities to support operations in austere, contested environments. Without proper water testing, water purified in the field are not certified potable for consumption. This creates an unacceptable logistics burden to transport water, or a health risks when consuming untested water; hindering the self-sufficiency, readiness, and lethality required for operations against a pacing challenge. Current approved state-of-the-art water quality testing kits are accurate but cumbersome, and overly complex, requiring chemical reagents, significant operator training, and for some parameters shipping to a certified lab. Present water quality testing methods are not practical for the small, distributed Stand-in Forces operating in expeditionary conditions.

In the event of detection of certain pathogens and contaminants, confirmation through certified laboratories may be required, necessitating sample transportation to CONUS, host-nation, or ally facilities—a process that can take 4-6 weeks. Delays of this magnitude are operationally unacceptable for forces in contested environments that need immediate assurance of water safety at the point of use. In addition, many critical parameters that impact water safety—including heavy metals, organic chemicals, and other contaminants—are not reliably tested with currently fielded sensors.

Force Design 2030 compels distributed forces to reduce their reliance on centralized logistics convoys; therefore, small units are increasingly required to produce and consume water at the tactical edge and at the point of need. Without a reliable and practical method to verify water quality in the field, these units face an alarming tradeoff between logistics supply certainty and warfighter health.

Therefore, the Navy needs simple, field-ready solutions to certify that expeditionary purified water conforms to TB-MED 577 short term potability military field water standards (STW MFWS) without external laboratory support. This SBIR topic seeks the development of new sensors and/or methodologies that will significantly improve existing water testing field kits. Improvements sought include but are not limited to: size and weight, more rapid testing results, simpler procedures requiring minimal training, elimination of liquid chemical reagents, and cost. Proposals can address one or more targeted improvements and can target one or more of the water parameters listed in the STP MFWS, such as physical properties, chemical properties, microbial contamination, chemical warfare agents, or radiological. Resulting improved sensors or methodologies must be integratable into future modernized water testing kits to allow squad- and platoon-level forces to verify compliance with TB MED 577 water safety standards in the field, reducing risk to personnel and decreasing reliance on vulnerable resupply chains. The expected end state of this effort is a fully developed, ruggedized, integratable sensor or set of sensors that enable rapid, automated testing of water quality in expeditionary environments in under 15 minutes (Threshold) / under 5 minutes (Objective), and/or detect all microbial threats in under 1 hour (Threshold) / under 15 minutes (Objective) without incubation or liquid reagents. Modular systems targeting specific critical parameters are equally encouraged and will be evaluated on technical merit.

title: Rapid Thermoplastic Patching Capability for Legacy Thermoset Airframe Sustainment
summary: Current composite airframe repair methodologies rely on a combination of wet-layups, B-staged epoxy prepregs, and bonded pre-cured thermoset patches. While pre-cured patches are the standard for high-quality depot repairs due to their autoclave-consolidated strength and “inspectability”, they present significant operational and logistical limitations.
description:
Current composite airframe repair methodologies rely on a combination of wet-layups, B-staged epoxy prepregs, and bonded pre-cured thermoset patches. While pre-cured patches are the standard for high-quality depot repairs due to their autoclave-consolidated strength and “inspectability”, they present significant operational and logistical limitations. All these traditional methods require secondary adhesive bonding (using paste or film adhesives) to attach the repair to the airframe. This secondary bond is the inherent weak link of the repair, demanding long thermal cure cycles (often 4 to 24 hours), strict environmental controls, and burdensome cold-storage logistics (freezers) for the B-staged resins and adhesives. Furthermore, these out-of-autoclave epoxy repairs often struggle to meet the high service temperature requirements of advanced tactical aircraft.

This SBIR topic seeks to evolve the current pre-cured repair methodology by transitioning from secondary adhesive bonding to high-speed fusion welding. The objective is to develop the capability to use pre-consolidated, high-temperature thermoplastic patches (e.g., Carbon/PEEK, Carbon/PEKK) on legacy thermoset aircraft (epoxy/Bismaleimide [BMI]). By replacing the lengthy adhesive cure cycle with a rapid welding process, this technology aims to achieve flight-ready repairs in expeditionary and carrier-based environments in a fraction of the time.

Because thermoplastics melt and thermosets do not, achieving a structural weld between these dissimilar materials is the primary barrier to fielding this capability. The Department of War seeks complete thermoplastic patching solutions that incorporate the requisite chemical or mechanical interfacial enablers—such as plasma surface activation, novel chemical tie-layers, or laser-ablated mechanical interlocking. These enablers must allow the thermoplastic patch to successfully fuse with a fully cured, legacy thermoset airframe using portable ultrasonic, resistance- or -induction welding equipment. The outcome must be a deployable repair process that eliminates cold-storage logistics, restores full structural integrity, meets high service temperature demands, and drastically reduces Aircraft on Ground (AOG) time.

title: Navy Shipboard Gas Turbine Rotating Detonation Combustor Operation with Diesel Fuel
summary: As background, the typical arrangement used on U.S. Navy surface combatants consists of four (4) large (20+MW class – GE LM-2500) gas turbines for propulsion and three 3 smaller (3 MW class – Rolls Royce 501-K34) gas turbines for ship service electrical power generation. Presently U.S. gas turbine powered warships use simple cycle machines.
description:
As background, the typical arrangement used on U.S. Navy surface combatants consists of four (4) large (20+MW class – GE LM-2500) gas turbines for propulsion and three 3 smaller (3 MW class – Rolls Royce 501-K34) gas turbines for ship service electrical power generation.

Presently U.S. gas turbine powered warships use simple cycle machines. However, complex cycles with reheat and other cycle enhancements have been considered and analyzed with the potential for increased efficiency. Further examinations have been performed to evaluate improvements in maintainability/reliability, overall generator set power density/stack up length, and alternative configuration installation flexibility for use in overall electric plant designs.

RDCs are advanced power-generation and propulsion devices that operate by propagating one or more supersonic detonation waves continuously around an annular chamber. As fresh fuel and oxidizer are continuously injected into the channel, the rotating shock wave rapidly compresses and ignites the mixture, creating a self-sustaining zone of intense heat and pressure. Thermodynamically, RDCs utilize a detonation-driven pressure-gain cycle, which is most accurately modeled by the Fickett-Jacobs-Salsburg (FJS) cycle and frequently approximated as the constant-volume Humphrey cycle. Unlike conventional gas turbines that rely on the constant-pressure Brayton cycle, the FJS detonation cycle in an RDC generates a substantial net increase in total pressure across the combustor. This inherent pressure gain drastically reduces the workload required by upstream mechanical compressors and significantly boosts the overall thermal efficiency and power output of the gas turbine system. While initial government and industry investigations have centered on the use of RDCs in aerospace applications, future shipboard applications will require a greater understanding of the ability to operate with diesel fuel for long continuous operation as well as a quantification of performance benefits that can be achieved in overall shipboard electric architecture design.

While not required, discussions with Navy shipboard gas turbine Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEM) are recommended.

title: Rapid Imagery Creation for Navy Training
summary: Currently, imagery analysts are excluded from, or extremely limited in, participating in dynamic Navy operational and staff training such as Surface Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (SWATT), Information Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (IWATT), Fleet Synthetic Training General Commander/Joint (FST-GC/J), and Commander Training Unit Exercise (COMPTUEX).This is due to the limited ability to dynamically…
description:
Currently, imagery analysts are excluded from, or extremely limited in, participating in dynamic Navy operational and staff training such as Surface Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (SWATT), Information Warfare Advanced Team Trainer (IWATT), Fleet Synthetic Training General Commander/Joint (FST-GC/J), and Commander Training Unit Exercise (COMPTUEX).This is due to the limited ability to dynamically generate the required products for imagery analysts within a reasonable amount of time at a quality that supports training.

Currently, either summaries are provided to the training audience circumventing the imagery analysts all together or providing GRAPHPLOTS - the equivalence of stick figure drawing - to track the order of battle (OOB) made up of aircraft, ships, vehicles, etc., without any use of actual imagery or geospatial analysis.
A technology to address this shortfall would need to take real-world geo-rectified imagery as a base and then rapidly adjust/modify the image to reflect the desired OOB and in a National Imagery Transition Format (NTIF) to be provided to the training audience for imagery analysts to process.

For example, in real-life Port A, identified by Basic Encyclopedia (BE) number, is of high interest and has a collection requirement against it for satellite imagery to be collected. In reality, Port A has three Kilo-class submarines and one Luhu-class destroyer, but in the scenario things have dynamically changed such that one of those submarines is now underway and an additional Luda I-class Destroyer has arrived, requiring the rapid (less than 10 minutes) production of an NITF image depicting two Kilo-class submarines, one Luhu DD, and one Luda I DDG to provide the training audience for analysis. The same would be required for airfields depicting aircraft movement as well.

title: AI-Enabled “Just-in-time” Knowledge Delivery for Naval Maintainers
summary: This effort is aimed at addressing the critical operational challenge of maintaining increasingly diverse and technologically complex arrays of systems with generalist knowledge. The solution requested in this SBIR topic is a just-in-time knowledge delivery system for Fleet maintainers that tells them what they need to know, when they need to know it.
description:
This effort is aimed at addressing the critical operational challenge of maintaining increasingly diverse and technologically complex arrays of systems with generalist knowledge. The solution requested in this SBIR topic is a just-in-time knowledge delivery system for Fleet maintainers that tells them what they need to know, when they need to know it. It would provide detailed procedures and technical knowledge for diagnostics, repair and maintenance procedures on demand, both ashore and at sea, where there will be limited access to remote data stores. The system will employ generative AI to analyze authoritative technical documentation and historical maintenance records, at both the Fleet and individual asset levels, and generate summarized technical guidance initiated by free-text queries or guided diagnostic dialogues. Post-task, the system will prompt the technician for repair feedback, synthesizing their insights to update the database with both general maintenance guidance and individual asset histories. Problems with current knowledge delivery are particularly acute when new systems and technology are introduced to the Fleet, such as with the introduction of unmanned systems (UxS), and when locally developed knowledge needs to be propagated across the larger maintenance community.

Operational readiness is currently bottlenecked by an inefficient maintenance paradigm: generalist maintenance technicians constantly face unfamiliar equipment without access to historical repair data, while frequent duty rotations continually erase localized (tribal) knowledge. This over-reliance on a transient pool of specialists causes extended system downtime and degrades operational readiness. These problems are particularly acute when new systems and technology are introduced to the Fleet.

While new advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and generative AI present an opportunity to create sophisticated human-machine teaming tools for providing real-time interactive support, state-of-the-art predictive maintenance systems are not attuned to the unique challenges of the Navy’s maintenance environment. Effective solutions will need to integrate diverse approaches and overcome existing hard science problems to arrive at the desired solution. Current approaches in this domain excel at forecasting component failures and recommending procedures; however, they lack the interactive step-by-step guidance required to conduct the procedures or for dynamic on-the-job technical support to the maintainers. Existing maintenance knowledge tools operate as one-way information pipelines that fail to capture critical institutional knowledge and platform-specific maintenance histories, which prevents the continuous, enterprise-wide learning loop necessary for resilient maintenance operations.

Solutions must be able to ingest, synthesize, and appropriately structure a wide variety of data formats (e.g., technical manuals, structured databases, handwritten logs) while also integrating newly produced recurrent maintenance reports. This data should serve as a dynamically updated foundational knowledge base that is contextualized by the physical and operational situation unique to each repair, providing customized guidance to the technician. The solution should adapt its guidance to the user's specific skill level and experience to ensure interpretability across levels of expertise. Lastly, the desired Maintenance Associate solution must be capable of operating on local hardware in low-bandwidth and disconnected environments, operating on local storage and syncing fleetwide as connectivity allows.

This SBIR topic is seeking proposals that would contribute to the development of an AI-Enabled Maintenance Associate. It is expected that the initial capability would be focused on a specific technical domain and a representative set of equipment that would serve as a prototype that can be scaled up to apply to multiple domains and an array of deployed systems. One target domain of immediate interest is the maintenance and repair of unmanned systems. However, any equipment and application domain that is found within Naval systems is of interest.

The envisioned system workflow will ingest and distill technical documentation into interactive, multi-media or hard-copy repair procedures—complete with parts lists, safety warnings, and annotated tribal knowledge—delivered through a user-friendly Human-Machine Interface (HMI). The system will capture post-repair outcomes to continuously update the foundational knowledge base. Proposed solutions may address individual components of the Maintenance Associate system or work to develop a complete system.

Components of the Maintenance Associate System that may be addressed for this SBIR topic should include:
• A database management system for repair service/technical manuals and logs for distillation into maintenance procedures.
• An HMI for technician requesting support that delivers summary procedure, to include tools, parts lists, cautions, and warnings; and provides results that are appropriately annotated localized (tribal) knowledge (best practices, tips, and comments from other users).
• System products to end-users delivered as: multi-media content and/or hard copy outputs for technicians to access when performing procedures.
• An incorporated mechanism to capture results/maintenance outcomes with a data integration mechanism that feeds into the knowledge base for future reference.

Ideally, this transition effort will specifically focus on supporting the complex maintenance, diagnostics, and repair requirements of UxS hardware and platforms (e.g., Unmanned Surface Vessels, Unmanned Underwater Vehicles, Unmanned Ground Systems, and Unmanned Aerial Systems), although use cases for other Naval Applications and alternative transition customers would be acceptable. Unmanned systems and commands are nascent, and subject to wholesale platform change in short order. Operators and maintainers rely on vendor provided maintenance doctrine as they are developing historical context. Grounding for the Associate must include these documents which may be CUI or SECRET, performers must be able to operate at required classification levels. Reported technical evaluations, capability demonstrations, and success metrics will focus on the accuracy/interpretability of maintenance guidance and quality of the human-machine interaction as assessed by real-world end users and the generalizability of the technical approach across platforms and domains.

Offerors are reminded that SBIRs are expected to sufficiently develop one or more capabilities that will receive endorsement from an acquisition/development organization and who will provide matching funds for transition/acquisition during Phase II of the SBIR. Prospective agencies for potential matching funds should be identified in the Phase I proposal along with the description of the baseline capability to be delivered that the proposer believes that acquisition agency would be interested in funding during Phase II.

The proposer will need to:
1) Develop an AI-driven, maintenance task context-aware guidance prototype that functions as an on-demand technical expert and centralized intelligence hub for maintenance technicians, providing interactive support for complex diagnostic and repair tasks.

2) Incorporate a mechanism to ingest, process, and index a wide array of reference materials, including technical manuals, vendor publications, Maintenance Required Cards (MRCs), after-action reports, and historical service logs from various databases.

3) Demonstrate a workflow for capturing new experiential knowledge, observations, and "lessons learned" from maintainers post-task to ensure the system continuously learns and shares updated information across the fleet.

4) Be designed to operate effectively on simple hardware (e.g., tablets, laptops) in environments with limited or no connectivity by using a local knowledge store, with the capability to synchronize with a central cloud database when a connection is available.

5) Provide an adaptive human-machine interface that guides a user through troubleshooting and repair via natural language, tailors instructions to the technician’s skill level, and recognizes the specific system variant in use.

title: Collapsible Fixed-Wing Low-Cost Unmanned Aerial System for Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance Missions
summary: The Navy has a growing need for a low-cost, portable, and rapidly deployable UAS to support ISR missions. Current systems are often expensive and bulky, and require significant logistical support. This SBIR topic seeks an innovative solution for a collapsible fixed-wing UAS that can be easily transported and deployed by a single operator.
description:
The Navy has a growing need for a low-cost, portable, and rapidly deployable UAS to support ISR missions. Current systems are often expensive and bulky, and require significant logistical support. This SBIR topic seeks an innovative solution for a collapsible fixed-wing UAS that can be easily transported and deployed by a single operator. The UAS should be capable of autonomous flight and integration with standard flight control software (e.g., QGroundControl, Pixhawk).

Key requirements include a total cost under $5,000 for the airframe and components, a flight time exceeding one hour, a communication range of up to 10 km, and the ability to fit within a 2' x 2' x 1' case for transport. The system must support a modular nose payload, be initially equipped with an RGB camera, and have the potential to serve as a signal repeater for transmission of data. The primary technical challenge is to achieve the desired endurance and portability within the stringent cost constraints, requiring innovation in airframe design, materials, and component integration.

title: Attritable Turbine for Low-Cost Attack Systems (ATLAS)
summary: The Department of War has an increasing need for affordable, reliable, and rapidly producible propulsion systems to support the proliferation of attritable Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), loitering munitions, and stand-off strike weapons.
description:
The Department of War has an increasing need for affordable, reliable, and rapidly producible propulsion systems to support the proliferation of attritable Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS), loitering munitions, and stand-off strike weapons. Current small turbofan and turbojet engines in the 150-300 pounds of thrust (lbf) class often rely on traditional aerospace material and manufacturing processes, resulting in high unit costs and long supply chain lead times. These factors are prohibitive for systems intended to be employed in mass or as expendable assets.

This SBIR topic seeks innovative engineering and manufacturing approaches to design a turbofan engine that meets the thrust requirements while dramatically lowering cost per unit. Proposers should consider advanced design and manufacturing techniques to produce a low-cost engine that can leverage existing industrial base capacity to reduce risk to procurement supply chains.

Key technologies and design features to consider are:
• Additive Manufacturing: Utilizing Powder Bed Fusion, Directed Energy Deposition and Direct Metal Laser Sintering (DMLS) to consolidate part count and simplify construction.
• Industrial (Non-Aerospace) Production Capacity: Leverage non-traditional aerospace manufacturing firms to reduce cost. Consider leveraging materials, casting and production techniques found in the automotive sector. Demonstrate a manufacturing pathway that enables rapid scaling and reduces supply chain bottlenecks.
• Short Life/Expendable Components: Utilizing non-traditional lubrication systems, bearings and electronic sub-components to limit cost.
• Optimized Materials: Utilize cost-effective materials suited for limited-life/single-use engine operations rather than traditional high-lifecycle aviation materials, where appropriate.

Performance metrics of interest include specific fuel consumption (SFC), thrust-to-weight ratio, and operational reliability for mission durations typical of attritable UAS or cruise munitions.

The engine will be fully operational utilizing Navy relevant fuels and demonstrate resilience to harsh maritime storage and launch conditions without significant performance degradation. The engine is expected to demonstrate functionality when subject to storage life of 6-12 months in Maritime environments and meet minimum required performance after exposure to shore-based and shipborne launch environments.

Notional performance objectives for this SBIR topic are provided in the Tables below:

Parameter Specification

Parameter Specification

title: Zero-Retrofit Robotic Ammunition Handling for the MK 45 Mod 4, 5-Inch Gun Magazine
summary: The tight confines of a DDG 51 5-Inch ammunition magazine present a difficult challenge for automation. Traditional robotic arms require fixed mounting and large clearance envelopes, requiring complete compartment redesigns. To avoid extensive shipyard work, the robotic prototype must adapt to the ship.
description:
The tight confines of a DDG 51 5-Inch ammunition magazine present a difficult challenge for automation. Traditional robotic arms require fixed mounting and large clearance envelopes, requiring complete compartment redesigns. To avoid extensive shipyard work, the robotic prototype must adapt to the ship. The prototype must navigate narrow aisles, step over "knee-knocker" coamings, and load ammunition into the existing hoists and stowage racks alongside or in place of human sailors.

The robotic prototype must execute capture and lift of 70-pound projectiles and their propelling charges, change their orientations while captured (i.e., pivot), move ammunition between stowage racks and hoists, and safely place the projectiles into the stowage racks and hoists in the proper orientation. Furthermore, the prototype must keep kinematic stability in high sea states (up to Sea State 5) while being able to continue to complete its tasking. The prototype must be resilient to electromagnetic interference (EMI)/electromagnetic pulse (EMP), and have a power supply architecture that enables sustained fire missions without the need for recharge or obstructive cables, and ability to rapidly swap power supplies without substantial downtime.

KEY PARAMETERS FOR ZERO-RETORFIT INTEGRATION:
• Payload Capacity: Continuous capability to lift, pivot, and load 70-pound projectiles and associated propelling charges. System must meet a minimum Threshold of 6 rounds per minute, with an Objective of 12 rounds per minute.
• Form Factor: Must fit within standard 24-inch shipboard aisles and maneuver in confined magazine spaces.
• Locomotion: Able to traverse standard deck plating, step over 6-inch coamings, and brace against ship motion.
• Stability: Maintain balance and load control up to and during Sea State 5 conditions (significant pitch/roll/heave).
• Power: Minimum 2-hour continuous operational endurance with rapidly hot-swappable battery packs (changeable in under 60 seconds).
• Hardening: Built to Military Standard (MIL-STD)-461 (EMI/EMP) and MIL-S-901D (Shock) thresholds.
• Safety/Fallback: Zero-retrofit integration (i.e., no structural alteration), ensuring the space stays 100-percent operational by human fallback crews in case of robot failure.
• Explosive Safety: Must adhere to NAVSEA OP 4 protocols for the safe physical handling of ordnance (Note: meeting specific electrical power level compliance is out of scope for this effort).

title: Innovative Shortwave Infrared High Energy Laser Source and Coupled Imager
summary: The Navy desires a short wave infrared high energy laser illuminator and coupled range-gated imaging sensor, including optics, operating in 1.9-2.5 micron wavelength to increase engagement ranges in adverse marine atmospheric conditions that include absorption, Mie and Rayleigh scattering, thermal blooming, etc. and able to operate in continuous wave (CW) or pulsed operation modes – at a…
description:
The Navy desires a short wave infrared high energy laser illuminator and coupled range-gated imaging sensor, including optics, operating in 1.9-2.5 micron wavelength to increase engagement ranges in adverse marine atmospheric conditions that include absorption, Mie and Rayleigh scattering, thermal blooming, etc. and able to operate in continuous wave (CW) or pulsed operation modes – at a variable power level up to kilowatt powers (average). Adjustable wavelength tunability to match to optimal atmospheric penetration and transmission within the band specified is required. If the entire band is not accessible, then rationale must be provided for limitation or selections made. In addition, it requires these to be ruggedized, so they are suitable to be installed on maritime platforms (i.e., ships, USMC ground vehicles, and aircraft) and be in a wavelength regime that is considered “eye-safer” when considering issues of defuse reflection or scatter when nearby observers are present. Gimbal and optics development or advancements in the shortwave infrared regimes may be offered but are not the primary technical objective in consideration for this topic.

Recent advances in laser sources [Ref 1] with high beam quality at the 2 micron wavelength, using Holmium and Thulium doped fiber optic-based power gain amplifiers, have shown a potential pathways for innovation to reach higher average powers (in Continuous Wave operation) in the multi-kilowatt regime, within the 2.0 to 2.4 micron (µm) band and falling within an atmospheric spectral short-wave infrared (SWIR) transmission band due to their low absorption of light by atmospheric water vapor. A pulsed system with a pulse gated optical imaging sensor offers the unique opportunity to not only provide a simple Laser Detection and Ranging (LIDAR) capability but also provide doppler-based discrimination information on the imaged objects – which could exceed systems’ capabilities typical from the 1.0-1.6 micron near infrared (NIR) band. The marine wave boundary layer (MWBL) can have higher scattering properties when comparing NIR to the selected SWIR bands, and is considered less detectable using widely available commercial, uncooled sensors than standard visible to NIR based illumination systems. A system that can operate in either CW or coupled pulse modes with a time resolved, range gated sensor and with high resolution windowing is the primary objective of this topic.

The Navy and Department of War seeks a unified approach with a scalable prototype device for use in evaluation for Electro-magnetic (EM) Spectrum warfare with an objective of gaining military advantages and achieving freedom of action across missions in support of maritime, surface warfare. However, the one system should show an ability to handle two separate capabilities developed through scaling. The first is development of a small, compact, lightweight SWIR (2.0-2.4 wavelength) high energy laser illuminator and coupled range-gated imaging sensor, including necessary optics suitable for short range sensing from small (group I or II) unmanned aerial vehicles or drones. While shorter ranges are acceptable for these missions (tens to hundreds of meters), the need for higher power still exists to conduct object discrimination at longer range (kilometers) and collect as much information (e.g., doppler shifts) from sensors as is technically possible. These smaller devices may diverge because of the requirements of size, weight and power (SWaP) toward a lower power-ganged diode array of microbolometers that has sufficient optical gain sensitivity to achieve doppler data, at the sacrifice of higher resolution spatial data typically obtained from devices that are based on focal plane arrays. Hybrid approaches combining sensor types shall be considered. Imaged target objects are expected to be in centimeter to meter size, and either stationary or have relatively low velocities (meters per second).

At the other end of the scale, a desire exists for a larger, fixed placement optical device on a moving or mobile platform (i.e., ground, air or sea-based vehicle) that can accurately discriminate and range objects at significantly greater distances (hundreds of meters to tens of thousands of meters) and are larger (tens of meters in length) with higher velocities (from tens to hundreds of meters per second). These systems require significantly higher source power, larger optics and higher quality vibration control, longer photonic travel distance, shorter pulse lengths, and higher peak power; have longer latency of time from emission to reception; and include the optical distortions that occur during light travel, reflection, and return. These larger devices may favor a combination of both focal plane arrays with coupled microbolometers using highly resolution time coupled range gating techniques, and significant relaxation of SWaP and include potentials for active cooling. However, the complexities of field conditions where the systems are deployed can vary greatly, with humidity (0-100%), rain, fog, particulates, and temperature variation (-55°C to +125°C) are not negotiable for either class of system. The need for higher laser power may be approached by beam combining smaller sources, but simplicity is preferred with ruggedness to dynamic shocks required under this topic, at least initially.

This effort is driven by both new threats and available and emerging technologies that have the potential to vastly improve the agility and flexibility of the Navy systems by utilizing high-energy lasers for Battle Space Supremacy and Water Space Management as envisioned by the Chief of Naval Operations (CNO). The current technology for High Energy Laser (HEL) at this wavelength for kilowatt class amplifiers is in early development. A major challenge exists for this technology to be viable for development of doped fiber for the 2 µm kW class fiber amplified systems; however, other potential laser source types will be considered. Gaseous and chemical lasers are not considered to be acceptable for this solicitation. The Navy seeks to address the manufacturability, electrical-to-optical (EO) efficiency and conduct technology risk assessments and risk reduction of this class of solid-state laser amplifier design.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

title: Robust and resilient optical modulators for extreme environment applications
summary: This topic solicits new ENZ based optical modulators that can be manufactured by new approaches to improve the techniques explored in the past. If a new material (or approach) is proposed, it would be useful if the proposers discussed why this new material (or approach) is promising.
