description: This topic solicits new ENZ based optical modulators that can be manufactured by new approaches to improve the techniques explored in the past. If a new material (or approach) is proposed, it would be useful if the proposers discussed why this new material (or approach) is promising. Offerors must address the high temperature stability and durability of ENZ materials in air under either high temperature (up to 800C) and demonstrate ENZ-based modulation device structures, such as metal-insulator-metal or waveguide structure, at MWIR regime. Furthermore, the proposers must address optical light modulation by utilizing electrical or optical tuning, and demonstrate ultrafast switching capability with high-speed, power efficient, and compact optical modulator designs. The successful team will design and demonstrate proof-of-concept devices under high temperatures.

title: Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) for Advanced Cryocooled Electro-Optical/Infrared (EO/IR) Sensors
summary: Current Department of the Navy (DON) platforms are generating unprecedented volumes of data via advanced radar, SIGINT, and high-resolution imaging sensors. Processing of this data at the tactical edge requires extreme bandwidth but can consume excessive powers, creating significant thermal and signal integrity bottlenecks [Ref 1].
description:
Current Department of the Navy (DON) platforms are generating unprecedented volumes of data via advanced radar, SIGINT, and high-resolution imaging sensors. Processing of this data at the tactical edge requires extreme bandwidth but can consume excessive powers, creating significant thermal and signal integrity bottlenecks [Ref 1]. Specifically, for advanced EO/IR sensors that operate in cryocooled temperatures (e.g., 70-140K), the excessive power required to electrically read out the data, i.e., transmit from cold space and receive in warm space, presents a challenging limitation on the size, weight, and power (SWaP) of an integrated dewar cooler assembly. Fiber optics and photonic integrated circuits (PICs) are key optical readout technologies that can offer extreme bandwidth, low power consumption, and mature fabrication but require integrated packaging solutions for next generation DON systems [Ref 2].

CPO offers an integrated solution that considers both optical and electrical elements in EO/IR sensor design, optimizing performance, reliability, and manufacturability. CPO brings the optical transceiver components directly into the same package as the readout integrated circuit (ROIC). This minimizes the electrical channel length or completely eliminates it with photonic interconnects, fundamentally lowering power consumption (energy per bit) and enabling massive bandwidth scaling [Refs 1-4]. To date, commercial CPO solutions are primarily designed for room temperature, climate-controlled hyperscale AI data centers.

This STTR topic seeks to adapt and innovate current CPO technologies for the stringent Size, Weight, Power, and Cost (SWaP-C) and packaging (cryogenically cooled) constraints of advanced Navy EO/IR sensing platforms. The focus of the topic is on the design and development of a CPO architecture that integrates with the ROIC layer of a typical EO/IR sensor chip assembly, enables high-bandwidth cold to warm readout, and operates in cryocooled temperatures.

Proposals must address critical challenges, including:
1. ROIC compatibility: PIC interconnect architecture that is compatible with conventional analog and mixed-signal digital ROICs designed in <180 nm node foundries, optimal number of fiber outputs to meet total ROIC bandwidth.
2. Thermal Management: Dissipating heat effectively when dense photonics and ROICs are co-located in a cryocooled integrated dewar assembly. Minimize PIC power consumption to less than 20 mW.
3. Power Efficiency: Choice of electrical-optical conversion scheme and minimizing power consumption (e.g., half-wave voltage for EO modulators, Vpi), PIC waveguide propagation loss, PIC to fiber input/output coupling losses, and stray light scatter.
4. Integration & Packaging: Complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS)-compatible substrate materials, 2.5D/3D integration techniques, and cost-effective scalable manufacturing processes.

title: Field-Friendly Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Systems
summary: Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance.
description:
Current DNN architectures suffer from inherent "Black Box" vulnerabilities, demanding massive computational scaling and offering no clear link between parameter count and performance. The proposed model must address these shortfalls:
- Optimized Resource Utilization: Unlike DNNs that heuristically overparameterize to boost accuracy, the proposed model must quantitatively map parameter count to expected performance and enable users to identify the minimum configuration required for mission success, significantly reducing computational overhead, complexity, and deployment costs.
- Transparency: The model must replace opaque, distributed neural layers with novel methods for interpretability and trust that go beyond the current post-hoc techniques. By making input-output logic similar to standard programming code, the model should ensure decisions are easily explainable, verifiable, and compliant with auditing standards.
- Reliability: The model must recognize whether it can provide a reliable output for a given problem instance, which will address another well-known criticism of DNNs wherein performance is typically measured as an average, e.g., average accuracy, over many instances of a problem and will help build user trust and acceptability of the model vs DNNs, particularly in sensitive areas like person identification in a crowd video and identifying the source of a cyber-security violation.

The model must deliver DNN-level performance with superior speed and a reduced memory footprint, optimized for lean, secure processing on low-cost CPU and embedded edge hardware. By eliminating cloud-dependence, the model will maximize data privacy and operational security while substantially reducing power consumption compared to GPU-reliant models. It must operate flexibly across mixed CPU-GPU environments, allowing operators to dynamically balance throughput against computational cost. Beyond standard convolutional neural networks (CNNs), the model’s architecture must be extensible to transformer-based and multimodal models handling text, image, and video.

The metrics below establish outer-edge targets specifically for CNN-based image classification. While satisfying every metric is not mandatory, the model will be evaluated on the number of targets achieved and the viability of the engineering trade-offs.
1. Comparison with Base Architecture of ResNet-18 and larger
2. Comparison of the Number of Classes 10 and 100 using 3 datasets: MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, having different combinations of numbers of classes and total number of image pixels (number of channels*number of pixels per image)
3. Mean Average Accuracy of Classification: Same as DNNs or higher
4. Number of Parameters (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less
5. Training MFLOPs/Image (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less
6. Training Memory Size (Fraction of Base Architecture): 50% of DNNs or less
7. Inference MFLOPs/Image: 50% of DNNs or less
8. Rate of Growth of Metrics (5), (6), and (7): Sublinear

In Phase II, similar metrics and their extensibility and relevance to transformers and multimodality scenarios (images and videos as well as their combinations with text to form LLMs and VLMs) will need to be provided and their implementation explained.

This STTR topic requires combinations of research and development, and proposers must demonstrate a strong partnership between the small business and a research institution.

The proposed solution should eliminate the dependency on complex computing infrastructure (e.g., GPUs) by delivering comparable performance on standard off-the-shelf hardware (CPUs, edge devices). It should optimize the cost-to-performance ratio, balancing accuracy with reductions in time, storage, and computational cost. Furthermore, the architecture should ensure robust explainability—like conventional software programs—and provide reliable confidence metrics to establish user trust. At a minimum, the method should result in the development of an alternative to existing CNN-based architectures for image classification.

The many problems with the modern AI/ML architectures and models mentioned earlier are well recognized and reported. Many researchers and companies are currently attempting to address these shortcomings, including a number of startups. Most of the better-known ones are doing so by modifying hardware and software of the industry-leading NVidia systems. None seems to be rethinking the basic formulation of the problem which underlies the direction taken in the approach of the Model. If successful, the Model may turn out to have a major impact on the Naval systems and AI/ML industry which is already very large and growing fast. The deeper impact that could result from the lean design of Model could significantly add to the societal reach of AI/ML methods.

title: Growth and Production of As2S3 Waveguides
summary: Multiple academic papers have indicated that the reverse mode of the SBS interaction between acoustic phonons and coherent 1.55 µm photons can cause Stoke’s peak gain on RF sidebands. It is desirable to harvest that effect for application in the burgeoning field of RF photonics.
description:
Multiple academic papers have indicated that the reverse mode of the SBS interaction between acoustic phonons and coherent 1.55 µm photons can cause Stoke’s peak gain on RF sidebands. It is desirable to harvest that effect for application in the burgeoning field of RF photonics. However, for that to happen, it is desirable that methods be developed to optimize the growth and etching of quasi-epitaxial As2S3, the material with the largest known SBS coefficient. In order to achieve low optical loss, achieving extremely low surface roughness of as-deposited films (< 10 nm rms roughness) is required plus ways to preserve that in producing waveguides of around 100 nm thickness and with high confinement bottom and top cladding. While atomic layer deposition (ALD) growth has produced other chalcogenides with very flat, conformal surfaces, it has not been used for As2S3; moreover, that other material was amorphous as deposited and drastically changed optical properties when crystalized. It may be that highly directional growth onto pre-etched substrate mesas produce better performance waveguides in which to produce amplification. Lastly, it is essential to demonstrate a way to achieve extremely low loss signal transfer on and off the die if RF photonics is to outperform conventional electronics in the future.

Phase I proposals for this STTR topic shall name the deposition and etching techniques that will be developed under the base award and estimate the surface smoothness of both the as-deposited material and the finished waveguides. The work plan must allow the validation of these estimates during the Base award so that the preliminary Phase II plan can define with good certainty the properties achievable in Phase II if awarded.

Measurement of the optical properties of completed waveguides during the Base award is highly desirable. First demonstrations of a method of coupling to the waveguide with losses under 2 dB in the Phase I Option is also desirable. A work division where the non-profit develops the fabrication technology and the company develops the many GHz wide band amplifier and coupling technologies is one possible division of the work. A clear discussion of the dependencies and determinants of the ultimate performance as a photonic amplifier should be included in the initial proposal.

It is highly desirable that, by the effort’s end, how feasible it is that by varying the optical carrier power in and the waveguide length, RF signal gains from 5 to 20 dB can be achieved with total noise figures including all coupling losses of <6 (threshold, 3 objective) dB. Paths to wafer scale fabrication yield above 90% should also be defined.

title: Validated Modular Autonomy for Undersea Multi-Vehicle Coordination
summary: Autonomous undersea vehicles performing expeditionary missions require state-of-the-art cooperative sensing and engagement capabilities. The Navy seeks to enhance those capabilities with modular software designed for reliability and operational effectiveness.
description:
Autonomous undersea vehicles performing expeditionary missions require state-of-the-art cooperative sensing and engagement capabilities. The Navy seeks to enhance those capabilities with modular software designed for reliability and operational effectiveness. The advancement sought is development of a modular coordination layer extending existing single vehicle with decentralized multi-vehicle behaviors to enable autonomous decision making under degraded communications, sensing, and PNT conditions.

The software prototype needs to take in mission requirements provided by existing Navy command and control (C2) systems and sensor data provided by multiple platforms and use those inputs to coordinate mission performance with other vehicles. It should be compatible with modular unmanned autonomy architectures already in use by the Navy, such as the Open Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (OpenAUV) architecture and the Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2). Within those architectures, the prototype must interface with existing autonomy designed for single-vehicle operations with minimal changes to already established systems. When the prototype is disabled or unnecessary, vehicle performance and behavior must conform to what would be expected of an unmodified single vehicle.

The multi-mission management functions of the software prototype need to use a decentralized C2 scheme that is robust in low-information environments and that degrades gracefully if communications or sensing are limited. The C2 scheme must demonstrate sufficient scalability to effectively manage many vehicles: tens to hundreds. Real-time C2 is a must.

The prototype should assume the primary sensing mode of each vehicle is acoustic. Realistic sensors include forward-look and side-scan sonar, possibly with a synthetic aperture. Cameras may be available, but if so, their field of view should not be assumed to allow for keeping other vehicles in sight. Realistic communications include acoustic modems with transmission rates of 5000 bps or less, possibly much less. Communications methods with higher transmission rates are unlikely to be available and may only be possible at extremely close range.

The prototype should assume that access to radar and satellite systems is extremely limited or non-existent. In particular, the prototype should not depend on regular access to global positioning system (GPS) data, and it should take into account the possibility that each vehicle is subject to position, navigation, and timing errors that increase in magnitude as each mission progresses.

The software prototype must include as an essential component a method of continuous validation that establishes and quantifies risk and trust for all autonomous decision-making, with an emphasis on repeatability. Deliverables must include the documentation and software necessary to implement this continuous validation method, as well as a report quantifying the efficacy of the method.

The ideal prototype will be mission agnostic, instead focusing on a generalized set of multi-vehicle behaviors and objectives.

The software prototype should minimize potential negative impacts on mission effectiveness, vehicle endurance, vehicle survivability, and operator workload. The prototype can include enabling hardware, provided that such hardware can be installed on existing autonomous undersea vehicles. The complexity of any vehicle modifications should be minimized. The prototype software and any accompanying hardware should also minimize their overall power consumption. Deliverable reports should include analysis identifying and quantifying any such impacts.

title: Self-Sustaining Wave Energy Capture for Persistent Autonomous Ocean-Going Systems
summary: Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD).
description:
Unmanned surface and undersea vehicles need regular recharging, and since they often operate far from human contact, their charging systems require a reliable, self-sustaining power source. The Office of Naval Research (ONR) believes the ideal power source will be a wave energy capture device (WECD). WECDs capture kinetic and potential energy generated by the movement of ocean waves on or near the surface of open water.

The desired WECD must be portable, specifically, designed as a set of components that can each be carried by one or two people who must be able to quickly assemble and disassemble those components. Components designed for one-person carry should weigh no more than 14 kg with largest dimension no greater than 1.9 m, while components designed for two-person carry should weigh no more than 45.4 kg with largest dimension no greater than 2.3 m. The WECD must be able to be relocated to areas of very different depths, including full ocean depth so the WECD’s design cannot require placement or anchoring on the sea floor. And since the WECD may need to deploy near the shore, its design must allow it to function in waters as shallow as 100 meters.

Ocean weather conditions can be challenging. The WECD should function reliably at Sea State 6 or less (very rough seas, with wave heights of 4 to 6 meters), and it should be able to survive conditions up to Sea State 8 (very high seas, with wave heights of 9 to 14 meters).

ONR assumes the WECD will be tethered to some device at or near the surface of the water. That tethered system may be an autonomous vehicle in loiter mode, and since loitering involves continuous vehicle movement, the WECD should operate reliably while in motion, and its design should leverage such motion to increase energy capture.

The WECD should produce a minimum of 20 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per day, but more is highly desirable. ONR believes 100+ kWh per day is achievable. Even in calm seas, the ideal WECD should produce sufficient electricity to charge a 2-kWh battery in 6 hours or less. Vehicle movement may be considered when ensuring this minimum level of power generation.

The desired WECD may be needed in areas where human assembly is impractical. Thus, the deliverables must include a prototype device capable of deploying the assembled WECD from the deck of a medium or large autonomous surface vessel. Like the WECD itself, the deployment device (DD) should function reliably in challenging weather conditions: Sea State 4 or less (moderate seas with wave heights of 1.25 to 2.5 meters).

Once deployed, very little of the WECD itself should be visible at the surface of the water. The WECD should minimize any increase in the visibility of the vehicle it is tethered to. This includes surface and airborne observation, both optically and by radar. Acoustic noise generated by the WECD should either be minimized or disguised to seem environmental or biological.

Cost for the WECD and associated DD should be minimized. ONR expects that under certain environmental conditions or mission requirements, WECDs may not be recoverable. At full-rate production, the ideal price will allow for multiple units per million dollars.

Under normal operating conditions, including Sea States of 6 or less, the expected operational duration of the deployed WECD should be at least one month, with three months or more expected if Sea State 4 or less is maintained.

title: Compact Unmanned Aerial System for Marine Species Monitoring
summary: A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations.
description:
A major remaining hurdle with marine species management is to know if, and when, measurable short-term behavioral and/or physiological responses of marine species to sound exposure results in biologically significant or meaningful effects on individuals and/or their populations. Advances in UAS methods and technology present unprecedented opportunities to improve the capacity to collect this robust data with minimal disturbance to marine species. However, while UAS methods have led to significant advances in our understanding of marine species’ behavior, health, and body condition, thus far many obstacles remain including cost, flight duration, size, and image resolution.

This STTR topic seeks to develop a compact, inexpensive, and NDAA-compliant UAS and payloads designed to collect high-resolution photogrammetry imagery to improve marine mammal monitoring, health measurements, and behavioral sequencing. In particular, the prototype device should contain the following technical parameters: high resolution flat zoom lens camera integrated with a gimbal system; highly maneuverable and flexible payload system; lightweight batteries less than 100 Watt hours; an accurate Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) altimeter and range finder integrated with the camera and capable of measuring distances up to 50m or more; and a monitor that is operational in direct sunlight and with polarized sunglasses;. It should be designed for flight times as much as or greater than 40 minutes; be compact and portable in both size and weight such that the UAS and case can fit airline luggage restrictions; have the ability to be quickly calibrated, launched, and caught by hand during small boat-based operations and to tolerate temperature range of -20 degrees to +40 degrees Celsius; and have a minimum weather resistant rating of IP45 to allow for operations in wet conditions; be capable of dynamic home point positioning; and produces minimal noise.

While there are several existing NDAA-compliant drones available in the marketplace, the desired components and capabilities only exist in piecemeal and further, these UAS are prohibitively expensive for the field. The DON seeks to develop a prototype device to be designed and optimized for marine species monitoring, encompassing all the above technical parameters. Critically, this device must be affordable for the marine research community with the target market price between $10,000 - $15,000.

title: Multi-Modal Luminescent Paint Systems for Underwater Surface Diagnostics
summary: Quantifying coupled boundary layer interactions along hydrodynamic surfaces require non-intrusive, full-field imaging of surface pressure, temperature, and skin friction (shear stress).
description:
Quantifying coupled boundary layer interactions along hydrodynamic surfaces require non-intrusive, full-field imaging of surface pressure, temperature, and skin friction (shear stress). While optical diagnostics have revolutionized aerodynamic testing, adapting luminescent paints to hydrodynamic testing in water introduces fundamental physical and application constraints that current state-of-the-art systems cannot overcome:
• Pressure-Sensitive Paint (PSP): Conventional PSP relies on oxygen-quenching physics. When submerged, oxygen diffusion into the polymer binder is severely inhibited by the liquid boundary layer and low oxygen solubility, rendering standard PSPs insensitive or plagued by extremely slow response times. Furthermore, severe temperature cross-sensitivity corrupts the pressure signal.
• Temperature-Sensitive Paint (TSP): Accurate dynamic temperature measurements are crippled by the standard utilization of Taylor’s frozen-flow hypothesis, which inaccurately assumes turbulent structures remain unchanged as they advect. In water, non-equilibrium flow, high thermal mass and rapid localized diffusion cause this hypothesis to break down, failing to capture true high-frequency temperature fluctuations.
• Mechano-Luminescent Paint (MLP): MLPs offer a direct optical pathway to map shear stress via mechanical deformation. However, current MLP formulations are in their technological infancy, suffering from poor dynamic range, low luminous efficiency, and signal degradation from material fatigue and hydrostatic pressure cross-talk.

In addition to the above challenges, current formulations are difficult to apply uniformly over large areas. Existing techniques fail to maintain a consistent, repeatable coating thickness on complex, curved, or non-flat surfaces. This inconsistency skews calibration and compromises measurement reliability across large-field hydrodynamic models. Innovative material architectures, such as utilizing distinct, multi-color mechano-luminescent particles or multi-core/shell dye structures, may enable simultaneous, uncoupled optical separation of pressure, shear, and temperature in all flow environments, i.e. gas, liquid, and multiphase flows.

This STTR topic seeks an integrated material, application, and optical processing suite. The system must decouple cross-sensitivities and deliver simultaneous, high dynamic range, full-field quantitative maps of the wall pressure, shear, and temperature fluctuations.

title: Membranes for Separation, Purification, Compression, and Storage of Carbon Resources from Alkaline Water
summary: This STTR topic seeks to develop a low-cost, low-energy, low-temperature (not to exceed 50°C), high-throughput nonmetallic membrane process to purify and store carbon dioxide (CO2) (from acidic seawater solutions). Carbon resources harvested from seawater represent a critical renewable feedstock for the localized synthesis of tactical fuels, materials, nutrients, and pharmaceuticals.
description:
This STTR topic seeks to develop a low-cost, low-energy, low-temperature (not to exceed 50°C), high-throughput nonmetallic membrane process to purify and store carbon dioxide (CO2) (from acidic seawater solutions). Carbon resources harvested from seawater represent a critical renewable feedstock for the localized synthesis of tactical fuels, materials, nutrients, and pharmaceuticals. Developing the capability to generate these resources in-theater or at the tactical edge enhances multi-domain operational sustainment. Current technologies used to recover the dissolved CO2 produced from electrochemically processed seawater often result in dilution of the CO2 with air and water vapor that can lead to detrimental sintering and oxidation of catalysts used in thermochemical and biological synthetic approaches. In addition, there are volumetric and compression penalties associated with the dilution of the targeted gas. The proposed membrane process will reduce the complexity, size, and costs associated with supplying pure carbon dioxide resources from alkaline water sources.

The integrated membrane, purification, and compression process will provide equipment, process, design criteria, energy and material balance; and establish operational performance parameters.

title: Domestic Manufacturing of Large Area Raman Laser Materials
summary: The Navy employs laser systems on air- and sea-borne vessels that serve a wide range of applications including laser range finding, target designation, shipboard and airborne LiDAR, and directed energy platforms.
description:
The Navy employs laser systems on air- and sea-borne vessels that serve a wide range of applications including laser range finding, target designation, shipboard and airborne LiDAR, and directed energy platforms. Future naval systems require improvements in spectral agility, optical efficiency, and power, with reductions to size and weight while maintaining operation in harsh maritime environments.

Current laser architectures rely upon a limited set of mature gain and nonlinear optical materials including Nd- and Yb-doped yttrium aluminum garnet (YAG), potassium titanyl phosphate (KTP), lithium triborate (LBO), and barium borate (BBO). While these technologies provide reliable performance, wavelength conversion often requires multiple optical stages that increases system complexity, introduces alignment sensitivity, and can limit scalability to higher optical powers and larger apertures.

Raman active optical materials offer a pathway toward compact and wavelength agile laser architectures capable of generating multiple output wavelengths from a single pump source. Such materials may enable simplified optical systems with reduced alignment complexity, improved robustness to vibration and shock, enhanced spectral diversity, and compact eye-safe laser sources. Many Raman laser crystals have been demonstrated to be grown to large sizes at high quality, but broader adoption of Raman active optical materials in these systems hinges on improving domestic production. Many candidate Raman laser materials are produced in small quantities at limited sizes and lack established domestic manufacturing capability and therefore development of domestic manufacturing technologies compatible with large crystal sizes is of importance for future naval laser systems.

Candidate materials shall be compatible with bulk crystal growth processes capable of producing large aperture, high optical quality single crystals and offer a pathway toward crystal sizes of 50 mm and greater.

This STTR topic seeks to develop a prototype manufacturing technology and process which can produce one or more Raman active materials at large crystal sizes with the potential to scale to high throughput. The prototype should minimize reliance on expensive precious metal crucibles. The prototype shall produce Raman active crystals that are large (> 5mm x 5mm x 25mm), achieve laser damage thresholds exceeding 10 J/cm², support self-Raman operation through rare earth doping, and meet the following optical quality criteria:

Objective Threshold Notes
Refractive Index Homogeneity: Threshold = <10 ppm; Objective = <5 ppm

Transmitted Wavefront Distortion (at 50mm aperture): Threshold = Lamda/6; Objective = <Lambda/8

Surface Quality (Scratch-Dig): Threshold = 20-10; Objective = 10-5 (NOTE: The first number relates to the maximum allowable width of a scratch in micrometers, while the second number relates to the maximum allowable diameter of a dig or pit in hundredths of a millimeter.)

Dislocation Density: Threshold = <10 cm^(-2); Objective = < 1 cm^(-2)

Inclusion/Bulk Defect Density: Threshold = <5 inclusions greater than 1µm per cm^3; Objective = No detectable inclusions greater than 0.5µm per cm^3

Materials of interest include:
Undoped and doped (Nd, Yb, Er, Tm) potassium gadolinium tungstate (KGW) and Potassium yttrium tungstate (KYW) [Refs 1,2,3]
Undoped and doped (Nd, Yb, Er, Tm) Barium molybdate and Barium nitrate [Refs 4,5]
Other Raman active tungstate, molybdate, nitrate, vanadate or related compelling Raman crystal systems

Alternative material systems are encouraged provided performers demonstrate a credible pathway toward large aperture crystal production and significant Raman gain performance.

title: Persistent, Geochemically-Driven Low-Temperature Power Systems for Subsea Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance
summary: The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries.
description:
The Department of the Navy’s expanding operational requirements in the Arctic domain demand persistent subsea situational awareness. Current seabed ISR nodes and Unmanned Underwater Vehicle (UUV) docking stations rely on conventional lithium-chemistry batteries. These legacy power sources present severe logistical and operational limitations: they suffer from rapid capacity degradation in extreme cold, possess highly toxic/hazardous chemistries, and require frequent, resource-intensive physical replacement (battery swapping) in highly contested or ice-covered environments.

To achieve persistent, logistics-free ISR, the Navy has a critical need for an environmentally benign, deploy-and-forget power architecture. This STTR topic seeks the development of Seafloor Electrochemical Power Harvesters to generate continuous electrical current by exploiting the natural oxidation-reduction (redox) potential difference between the anoxic marine sediment (mud) and the oxygenated overlying seawater. The proposed approach must demonstrate a credible path to 5W power and 24-month endurance in sub-zero Arctic conditions through a ruggedized seabed electrochemical power-harvesting architecture that maximizes long-term energy extraction while using only indigenous sediment microbial communities and naturally occurring geochemical gradients. Proposed solutions may use abiotic or biologically mediated mechanisms via electrode design, power management, and optimum emplacement.

Biocatalytic Prioritization & Environmental Strictures:
While purely abiotic electrochemical approaches will be considered, approaches that leverage biologically-mediated processes (e.g., utilizing natural biocatalysis to enhance electron transfer at the anode) will be prioritized due to their potential for higher power density and self-renewing longevity.

However, to prevent any risk of ecological disruption to fragile Arctic ecosystems, solutions must strictly rely on harnessing the naturally occurring, indigenous populations already present in the local sediment. The introduction, deployment, or seeding of any exogenous, synthetic, lab-grown, or non-native biological agents (microbes/bacteria) is strictly prohibited.

By utilizing advanced electrode materials that naturally synergize with the local subsea environment, the system must reduce or avoid reliance on deployable primary batteries for the supported payload while ensuring operational viability in extreme cold and high-pressure conditions.

title: Heterogenous Swarm Control through Artificial Intelligence-embodied Architecture
summary: Current methods of heterogeneous swarming control often involve individual entities with incompatible messaging protocols, ridged data interpretation, and lack of broader situational awareness, generating a protocol/perception problem that results in fragmented decision-making.
description:
Current methods of heterogeneous swarming control often involve individual entities with incompatible messaging protocols, ridged data interpretation, and lack of broader situational awareness, generating a protocol/perception problem that results in fragmented decision-making. Model Context Protocol (MCP), Large Language Models (LLMs), and related Agentic AI architectures, can enable a Universal Serial Bus Type C (USB-C) solution to this fragmentation problem by allowing individual entities to communicate with human operators or other entities through natural language.

The Department of the Navy is seeking development of Agentic AI-enabled COTS small UAVs or small UGVs USB-C capabilities for demonstration of applicability in Naval and Marine Corps tasks. The goal is to deliver a small heterogenous swarm of low-cost uncrewed systems capable of receiving tasks through a natural language interface and performing complex tasks such as inspection of a facility for damage, evaluating road conditions, conducting security operations, and/or intercepting of other platforms. Performers should focus on software development to run on low cost and edge compute devices attached to highly expendable COTS platforms. Submissions will leverage preexisting DoW compliant hardware deployments using either compute resources organic to the UAV/UGV platform or flight-ready modules (e.g., Single Board Computer NVIDIA JETSON NDAA) with favorable Size, Weight, and Power (SWAP). Submissions should identify the unique nature of their Agentic-AI capability in accomplishing the objective.

title: Mission-Specialized Large Language Models for Operational Training and Knowledge Integration
summary: The Department of the Navy faces increasing challenges associated with workforce modernization, technical skill development, personnel turnover, distributed operations, and the growing complexity of mission systems and operational environments.
description:
The Department of the Navy faces increasing challenges associated with workforce modernization, technical skill development, personnel turnover, distributed operations, and the growing complexity of mission systems and operational environments. As experienced personnel retire or transition, critical institutional knowledge and operational expertise are frequently difficult to preserve, transfer, and scale across the workforce.

Simultaneously, Navy training and workforce development communities must support increasingly divergent learning requirements across accession, technical education, and qualification pipelines. Existing training approaches often rely on static instructional materials, fragmented knowledge systems, and limited mechanisms for adaptive or individualized instruction.

Commercial large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong broad-domain reasoning capabilities but are fundamentally limited in their ability to reliably incorporate organization-specific knowledge without hallucination. They are unable to incorporate organization-specific terminology, mission procedures, technical constraints, and authoritative instructional content unique to mission environments. Additionally, these systems frequently generate responses without traceable references, limiting user trust and reducing suitability for technical learning and operational instruction. This gap creates a strong need for a specialized LLM system precisely tuned to an organization's corpus and operational requirements.

The Navy seeks development of a hyper-parameterized, explainable LLM framework designed specifically to support mission-focused training and knowledge transfer. The system should enable personnel to learn new technical and operational topics through an interactive interface. Outputs should be grounded in authoritative manpower, personnel, training, and education (MPTE) documentation while also leveraging the broad contextual understanding available from foundation LLMs. The proposed capability shall support accelerated workforce proficiency development, preservation of institutional knowledge, and adaptive learning across operational, technical, and mission-support communities while providing transparent, auditable, and trustworthy instructional guidance tailored to user roles, experience levels, and training objectives.

Explainability is a critical requirement for organization-specific LLMs operating in mission environments. The proposed solution must provide transparent and auditable reasoning pathways that allow users to understand how conclusions, recommendations, or generated outputs were derived.

The proposed capability should function as an intelligent training and instructional assistant capable of:
• Teaching mission-specific topics using authoritative organizational documents and instructional materials
• Combining proprietary knowledge with broad-domain contextual reasoning from foundational LLMs
• Guiding users through complex technical, operational, engineering, and/or procedural concepts
• Adapting explanations and instructional depth based on user role, expertise, and/or training objectives
• Providing explainable outputs with traceable references to source documentation
• Reducing hallucination through structured retrieval and grounded response generation
• Supporting continuous updates as training materials, policies, and mission guidance evolve

title: Computational Frameworks for the Development and Qualification of Additive Manufacturing-Tailored Wire Feedstock for Naval Directed Energy Deposition
summary: As the Department of the Navy prepares for contested logistics environments, the ability to manufacture large, mission-critical replacement parts at the point of need has become a strategic imperative.
description:
As the Department of the Navy prepares for contested logistics environments, the ability to manufacture large, mission-critical replacement parts at the point of need has become a strategic imperative. Wire-fed DED is uniquely suited to this role: it operates safely with reactive metal alloys, achieves high deposition rates for large structural volumes, and is robust enough for shipboard and expeditionary deployment. Despite this operational advantage, a persistent and quantifiable performance gap prevents wire DED parts from meeting Navy structural qualification standards without extensive post-processing.

The root cause of this gap is a thermal physics and geometric mismatch. Additive manufacturing (AM) processes span approximately five orders of magnitude in solidification cooling rate, which is the master variable governing grain size, phase selection, and precipitate morphology.

Current wire feedstock is manufactured to welding wire specifications, engineered for arc welding thermal histories rather than the specific precision and cooling rates of robotic DED. The consequences are well-documented:
• Microstructural Deficits: Precipitation-strengthened aluminum alloys exhibit a 40-70% yield strength reduction in DED compared to laser powder bed fusion, driven by insufficient cooling rates to nucleate strengthening dispersoids. Titanium alloys (e.g., Ti-6Al-4V) develop continuous grain boundary alpha films that degrade ductility and fatigue life.
• Residual Stress Instability: Residual stresses retained from the wire drawing process cause wire tip instability (cast/helix) in the DED melt zone, producing porosity and build failures.
• Geometric and Surface Topography: Macroscopic inconsistencies in wire diameter dictate volumetric feed-rate errors, causing fluctuating energy-to-mass ratios in the melt pool. Simultaneously, surface roughness (poor smoothness) induces micro-stuttering in the robotic feed conduit and scatters laser impingement, severely destabilizing thermal absorption.

No existing ICME framework addresses these deficiencies upstream of the melt pool—every published AM modelling chain begins at deposition, leaving the wire manufacturing sub-chain entirely unmodelled.

The Navy seeks a comprehensive end-to-end computational framework that closes this gap through alloy-process co-optimization. Proposers should develop a model chain that links the entire wire feedstock lifecycle—from primary alloy synthesis and thermomechanical processing through final drawing and surface conditioning—directly to AM deposition dynamics and deposit properties. This model must account for the coupled effects of advanced state variables (e.g., dislocation density, oxide thickness).

The framework should incorporate Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML) surrogate models that consume upstream feedstock history to predict how a specific wire lot will respond to DED thermal conditions and should employ AI-guided experimental design to identify the minimum number of physical tests required to achieve robust statistical qualification. The ultimate deliverable is a computational materials passport: a traceable digital record linking a wire lot's manufacturing history to its predicted and validated AM performance, supporting the Navy's Digital Engineering Strategy and enabling condition-based qualification for fleet sustainment.

title: Conformal Printed Antennas for Missile and Weapon Composite Airframes
summary: Rockets, missiles, aircraft, and tactical weapons are extremely weight constrained. Antennas for Global Positioning Systems (GPS) (including anti-jam), command and control, telemetry, datalink, and seeker functions must coexist with structural, thermal, environmental constraints on curved airframes.
description:
Rockets, missiles, aircraft, and tactical weapons are extremely weight constrained. Antennas for Global Positioning Systems (GPS) (including anti-jam), command and control, telemetry, datalink, and seeker functions must coexist with structural, thermal, environmental constraints on curved airframes. Conventional fabrication produces these antennas as discrete elements mounted on brackets inside separate radomes, connected to receivers via coaxial cables and connectors. This architecture imposes parasitic mass, parasitic volume, signal loss through cables and connectors, and long-term reliability degradation as connectors corrode and radomes delaminate over shipboard storage life.

Conformal printed antennas integrated directly onto composite airframe surfaces offer substantial advantages: reduced mass, reduced volume, eliminated cable and connector losses, and structural integration with the airframe itself. The technical challenge: printing radiating elements onto curved carbon-fiber substrates couples electromagnetic design with structural design, environmental protection, and the complex electrical interaction between printed conductors and the underlying conducting carbon-fiber substrate.

Multi-material printed electronics, particularly aerosol-jet and inkjet direct-write processes, have matured to where conductors, dielectrics, and substrates can be co-deposited into conformal structures with controlled electromagnetic properties. The unaddressed capability is the integrated design of printed antennas on airframe substrates, with environmental protection co-designed for operational survival.

The antennas shall be designed using direct-write printed electronics methods (aerosol-jet, inkjet, or comparable approaches) capable of multi-material co-deposition on curved composite substrates. Coating or environmental protection schemes shall be integrated into the design from the outset, with explicit treatment of electromagnetic transparency, loss, and detuning effects.

title: Photonic-Crystal Surface Emitting Lasers (PCSELS) in the Near-Infrared (NIR)
summary: The Navy seeks innovations in PCSELs that combine novel in-plane photonic crystal designs with out-of-plane epitaxial and gain structures to overcome the limitations of current approaches and produce the next generation of semiconductor laser technologies.
description:
The Navy seeks innovations in PCSELs that combine novel in-plane photonic crystal designs with out-of-plane epitaxial and gain structures to overcome the limitations of current approaches and produce the next generation of semiconductor laser technologies. Current PCSEL architectures face power-scaling limitations as device aperture increases because the mode margin between the desired fundamental mode and competing higher-order modes decreases, making stable, single-mode, diffraction operations increasingly difficult at higher powers. Capabilities that enable single mode, high power density, combinable lasers in the one-micron regime are the focus for any near-term transition. Concepts that maximize laser device area above previous limits, either by increasing the number of photons generated per unit area or increasing conversion efficiency, are potential options. Other potential approaches include reducing optical, electrical, and other losses – either with single devices, or through multi-device combinations. For example, stacking multiple gain regions vertically and horizontally, a successful technique used in vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers ( VCSELs) arrays, may limit current PCSEL designs because of interactions between n++/p++ tunnel junctions in gain layers introducing unwanted absorption. Means to correct this issue through material modification might offer counteracting but beneficial additional total gain from a single device – especially when combined in the far field. Similarly, adding optical features as part of the photonic crystal to extend single-mode operation, especially those with higher conductivity material might reduce thermal distortions and lead to better performance even at the potential limits of vertical heat conduction. Further, adaptive metasurfacing of an existing PCSEL device (through micro- or nano-etching) might create new surface structures that modify laser output to enable more efficient photon conversion through the development of improved cavity properties.

The potential to demonstrate military utility by showing power scalability greater than single digit watts from an individual PSCEL, while maintaining single mode operation that result in combinable Solid State Lasers (SSLs) sources (through spectral beam combining or coherent beam combining) or other resonant gain media structures - where the result is a single mode - where emissions has already been demonstrated from fiber lasers, but can potentially be replaced by a single PCSEL integrated optical device - opens up the possibility of high energy laser (HEL) single stage output. The Navy desires higher power, higher efficiency laser and optics to increase engagement ranges, even in adverse marine atmospheric conditions.

The Navy seeks an approach with a scalable demonstration device in the evaluation of new combinable PCSEL devices that support Electro-magnetic (EM) Spectrum warfare dominance with an objective of gaining military advantages through increased laser power and efficiency - achieving freedom of action across missions in support of maritime, surface warfare.

Work produced in Phase II may become classified. Note: The prospective contractor(s) must be U.S. owned and operated with no foreign influence as defined by 32 U.S.C. § 2004.20 et seq., National Industrial Security Program Executive Agent and Operating Manual, unless acceptable mitigating procedures can and have been implemented and approved by the Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) formerly Defense Security Service (DSS). The selected contractor and/or subcontractor must be able to acquire and maintain a secret level facility and Personnel Security Clearances. This will allow contractor personnel to perform on advanced phases of this project as set forth by DCSA and ONR in order to gain access to classified information pertaining to the national defense of the United States and its allies; this will be an inherent requirement. The selected company will be required to safeguard classified material during the advanced phases of this contract IAW the National Industrial Security Program Operating Manual (NISPOM), which can be found at Title 32, Part 2004.20 of the Code of Federal Regulations.

title: Wafer-scale low-loss hyperbolic optical material
summary: Conventional optical systems are limited by diffraction, which sets the smallest features they can pattern, image, or confine to roughly the wavelength of the light used. A class of strongly anisotropic, or "hyperbolic," optical materials can confine and route light far below this limit, enabling a family of compact, low size-weight-and-power photonic components of direct interest to OUSW (R&E).
description: Conventional optical systems are limited by diffraction, which sets the smallest features they can pattern, image, or confine to roughly the wavelength of the light used. A class of strongly anisotropic, or "hyperbolic," optical materials can confine and route light far below this limit, enabling a family of compact, low size-weight-and-power photonic components of direct interest to OUSW (R&E). Hyperbolic behavior has historically been realized in artificial metamaterials, which are optically lossy, and difficult to fabricate and scale. Certain naturally occurring crystals exhibit the same behavior with far lower loss, but the available examples operate only in the infrared and have been produced only as small, research-grade crystals by batch methods incompatible with standard microfabrication. There is presently no commercial source of wafer-scale, low-loss hyperbolic material that operates at visible and telecommunication wavelengths in a form compatible with standard semiconductor fabrication, and it is important for the Air Force to establish a domestic supply source for such a material.

title: B-52 Multi-Factor AI Performance Charts
summary: The B-52 Stratofortress has been the backbone of the United States Air Force's long-range strategic bomber capability for more than six decades.
description:
The B-52 Stratofortress has been the backbone of the United States Air Force's long-range strategic bomber capability for more than six decades. Despite multiple upgrades to its avionics and mission systems, aircrews continue to rely on labor-intensive, manually interpreted paper Technical Order performance charts and multi-step worksheets to calculate critical operational calculations such as takeoff and landing distances, brake energy limits, crosswind restrictions, runway condition impacts, directional control limits, and degraded-performance scenarios. These manual processes are time-consuming, increase cognitive workload and introduce opportunities for human error, and require aircrews to make high-stakes decisions under challenging time constraints, often during dynamic operational scenarios. Continued reliance on manual processes reduces operational efficiency, increases crew workload, and can negatively impact decision-making, especially in contested or degraded environments.

The current state of the art within commercial aviation utilizes Electronic Flight Bag (EFB)-based performance planning tools capable of rapidly calculating aircraft performance using approved aircraft data and validated calculation methodologies. While these solutions demonstrate the feasibility of digital performance-planning capabilities, they do not incorporate B-52-specific TO data, military performance procedures, cybersecurity requirements, airworthiness considerations, or Department of the Air Force EFB integration requirements. As a result, a capability gap exists between current B-52 performance-planning processes and modern digital aviation decision-support systems. The proposed effort will begin at approximately TRL 3-4, leveraging prior Phase-I-like work including operational requirements analysis, commercial market research, chart digitization methodologies, deterministic algorithm concepts, and successful demonstrations of related technologies in both government and commercial aviation sectors. Commercial aviation performance applications, technical-order digitization technologies, and deterministic calculation engines have demonstrated feasibility and provide a strong foundation for this effort. The objective of the Phase II effort is to advance the capability to TRL 6 through development, validation, and operational demonstration of a prototype capability suitable for transition into the Air Force EFB ecosystem. The Government is particularly interested in approaches that leverage secure research infrastructure, advanced computing resources, AI-assisted data extraction capabilities, and development of government-owned intellectual property to accelerate chart digitization, data validation, and long-term sustainment. Additionally, the Government seeks to leverage existing federally funded research investments such as those within U.S. National Laboratories or other Federally Funded Research & Development Centers (FFRDCs) to the maximum extent possible. Leveraging existing investments around AI security, vulnerability assessments, red teaming, model assurance, secure deployment of advanced models, and evaluation of AI systems supporting national security missions will help accelerate technology maturation and transition.

To meet this goal, the Phase II D2P2 effort is expected to include the following activities:

1. Integration of the AI-driven solution for chart mining and digitization to extract data; Refinement of deterministic algorithms to calculate performance metrics (e.g., takeoff/landing distances, brake energy limits, crosswind tolerances) based on TO and other authoritative data sources.

2. Development of intuitive user interface and operational workflows that align with aircrew feedback and mission requirements, ensuring a transparent and user-friendly application.

3. Rigorous testing and validation of algorithm accuracy, decision-support reliability, and adherence to airworthiness and compliance standards, incorporating inputs from operational stakeholders and SMEs.

4. Coordination with USG relevant Program Offices and certification authorities to support EFB system accreditation, operational testing, and fielding - this would translate into the existing U.S. Government EFB system with offline capabilities to ensure reliable operation in contested, degraded, or denied environments.

5. Coordination with U.S. National Laboratories or FFRDCs already investing in similar capabilities to enable rapid technology advancement, alignment of development roadmaps towards broader national security priorities, and aid in the transition into operational systems.
This STTR effort stands to vastly improve the DoW's technological state by eliminating the inefficiencies of current manual performance calculations and transitioning the B-52 platform into a new era of data-driven, AI-enhanced operations that rapidly generate transparent and auditable aircraft performance assessments using approved source data. The capability shall not generate unvalidated performance estimates, extrapolated values, or inferred outputs when required data are unavailable or outside approved limits. The resulting solution will enable faster, more reliable decision-making, directly enhancing safety and mission outcomes while reducing aircrew workload. Moreover, the offline functionality ensures the tool's efficacy in a range of operational environments, including denied, degraded, and contested settings. Minimum acceptable deliverables include:
• A prototype closed loop EFB-compatible software capability suitable for operational evaluation.
• Digitized and validated performance datasets derived from approved B-52 source material.
• Verified and validated calculation methodologies demonstrating agreement with approved reference calculations.
• User workflows and interfaces suitable for operational aircrew use.
• Test and validation reports documenting accuracy, reliability, and operational suitability.
• Sustainment and transition documentation supporting future EFB integration, cybersecurity accreditation, airworthiness review, and operational fielding.
Through these efforts, the B-52 will evolve to keep pace with the Air Force’s operational imperatives, including enhanced readiness to deploy and fight (Operational Imperative 7) and modernization priorities such as trusted AI and autonomy. Success in Phase II will position this innovation for further development and transition under Phase III, facilitating its adoption as a fielded capability that aligns with the U.S. Air Force’s modernization goals and long-term sustainment strategy for the B-52 fleet.

title: RF Spectrum Operations Enhanced with Distributed AI-Assisted Sharing of Knowledge Sharing (RF-DASK)
summary: Current ES systems are designed to detect enemy electronic signals by extracting Pulse Descriptor Words (PDWs) from these signals. Modern radar systems used by adversaries increasingly employ Artificial Intelligence (AI) and it is becoming increasingly difficult to identify, characterize, and represent their waveforms using PDWs alone.
description: Current ES systems are designed to detect enemy electronic signals by extracting Pulse Descriptor Words (PDWs) from these signals. Modern radar systems used by adversaries increasingly employ Artificial Intelligence (AI) and it is becoming increasingly difficult to identify, characterize, and represent their waveforms using PDWs alone. To deploy effective Electronic Countermeasures (ECM), there is a need to develop novel methods, including machine learning (ML) [1,2] to enable dynamic and scalable data representation and compression methods that represent complex waveforms, which can be efficiently shared with other nodes in the network. The main goal of this project is to develop advanced techniques for dynamic and scalable signal representation to describe complex waveforms in a compressed format for radio frequency (RF) spectrum knowledge sharing and support network level information dissemination for emitter detection, classification and geolocation representative of activity segmentation [3]. Operational size, weight and power (SWaP) constraints should be determined to implement the proposed algorithms on hardware platforms and the developed techniques should be evaluated and demonstrated with hardware-in-the-loop experiments in relevant spectrum environments.

title: Wideband Antenna for RF Photonics Modules
summary: Given its inherent broadband capabilities, RF photonics is a promising technology for both civilian and military applications. It is employed in several platforms, including autonomous vehicles, UAVs, and mobile devices, to sense and navigate complex environments and detect and track mobile targets, among many other use-case scenarios.
description: Given its inherent broadband capabilities, RF photonics is a promising technology for both civilian and military applications. It is employed in several platforms, including autonomous vehicles, UAVs, and mobile devices, to sense and navigate complex environments and detect and track mobile targets, among many other use-case scenarios. Current studies are establishing and advancing RF photonic technology for several applications. However, these advances, especially in the radio frequencies or lower millimeter-wave regime, are still based on bulky antenna solutions, preventing the realization of compact systems that can be easily accommodated in small platforms. Proposals are sought to provide innovative antenna solutions addressing the need for integration with commonly packaged RF photonic modules without impacting their operation bandwidth. The proposed efforts shall build upon the existing integration-friendly antenna solutions to develop a novel antenna technology amenable to integrating electrically small broadband RF-photonic modules. By the end of Phase I, a broadband antenna module compatible with RF-photonics should be numerically analyzed. Phase II should focus on a proof-of-concept experiment of the integrated broadband antenna module with a selected RF photonics system. Overall, this topic aims to advance RF photonics technology with integrated antennas to meet demanding requirements, such as large bandwidth, reduced size and weight, and low profile. Relevant metrics that the proposers should consider are an antenna solution fully compatible to be integrated with the standard packaging topologies of RF photonic modules, an antenna module with excellent performance in the high RF regime, and with a bandwidth beyond Chu's limit.

title: Biolab Mirror: Artificial Intelligence / Machine Learning (AI/ML) Digital Twin for Intent Characterization and Bio-Containment Integrity
summary: The proliferation of dual-use biological technologies and automated, high-containment laboratories globally presents a profound challenge to arms control verification and biosurveillance [3].
description:
The proliferation of dual-use biological technologies and automated, high-containment laboratories globally presents a profound challenge to arms control verification and biosurveillance [3]. A state-sponsored facility operating under a declared, peaceful mandate (e.g., vaccine development, agricultural research) possesses all the necessary infrastructure, reagents, and personnel to rapidly pivot to unauthorized, non-compliant, or undeclared high-risk biological material production [2]. Current verification methods rely heavily on periodic physical inspections, voluntary declarations, and audits of digital LIMS. However, advanced adversaries can digitally spoof BMS, manipulate LIMS records, and conceal clandestine pathogen scaling through “population ghosting” [4][5]. The Department of War (DoW) requires a “Physics-to-Mesh Zero Trust” architecture [6]. This solicitation seeks proposals for a “Biolab Mirror”—a comprehensive Digital Twin that does not inherently trust digital control logs. Instead, the Mirror must continuously cross-validate digital telemetry against the unalterable laws of physics, chemistry, and biology (Conservation of Mass, Thermodynamics, Metabolic Rates). By establishing a rigorous physical baseline (e.g., correlating total water inflow with Effluent Decontamination System (EDS) out-flow, or matching documented animal feed procurement to autoclave waste mass and vivarium Carbon Dioxide (CO2) exhaust), the AI/ML engine must automatically flag the subtle “Coherence Failures” that betray clandestine pathogen scaling, undeclared animal models, or spoofed containment boundaries.
SUPPLEMENTAL INFORMATION
1. Programmatic Metrics and Data Sourcing
• Data Sourcing Strategy Synthetic Baseline Generation (Performer Sourced): The performer is responsible for generating the Phase II training and validation datasets using established biological and physical engineering standards.
• Phase I Exit Metrics Measure of Performance (MOP) 1 (Architecture Delivery): Deliver a Digital Twin architecture mapping cross-domain signatures including specialized cross-domain digital and physical validation points.
2. Strategic Offshoots & Cyber-Physical Emulation
• Executive Summary: The primary objective of the Biolab Mirror SBIR/STTR is defensive: to establish a high-fidelity “Physics-to-Mesh Zero Trust” baseline to detect clandestine activity and intent. Successful completion yields a secondary strategic asset: a perfect, un-spoofed “Cyber-Terrain” map that can be ported into isolated cyber-ranges to simulate, analyze, and train against multi-domain attacks targeting critical high-containment infrastructure [10].
• The Capability Gap in Current Cyber-Ranges: Current cyber-ranges are optimized for IT network emulation and struggle to accurately emulate OT and the physical realities of a BSL-3/BSL-4 environment.
• The Biolab Mirror as the Emulation Foundation: The Biolab Mirror solves this gap. By mapping the continuous physical signatures directly to the discrete digital telemetry, the performer constructs a fully functional Cyber-Physical Sandbox.
The Attack Simulation: Authorized cybersecurity evaluation teams and system auditors can execute multi-stage simulated attacks against this virtual target (e.g., spear-phishing an academic researcher -> pivoting to the BMS network -> manipulating the Effluent Decontamination System). The Red Team must navigate the actual laws of biology and thermodynamics to succeed.
• Strategic ROI & Follow-On Potential: Authorizing the Biolab Mirror effort provides a “two-for-one” return on investment (ROI), yielding a defensive characterization engine and a foundational architecture for dedicated cybersecurity testing and critical infrastructure protection.

title: AI/ML Verification of Microelectronic Integrity for High-Assurance Systems
summary: The Department of War relies heavily on advanced microelectronics sourced from a globally distributed commercial supply chain.
description:
The Department of War relies heavily on advanced microelectronics sourced from a globally distributed commercial supply chain. Securing this supply chain against malicious insertion is a critical national security imperative, repeatedly highlighted by the Government Accountability Office (GAO) as a high-risk area. [2]
For defense systems operating in contested environments, compromised hardware represents a catastrophic vulnerability. Advanced adversaries are capable of introducing microscopic logic alterations (e.g., dopant-level Trojans, malicious dormant circuitry) during fabrication or transit. [3] A primary use case of concern involves hardware-level Trojans engineered to bypass software encryption, forcing ultra-secure communications gear or deployable sensor packages to execute unauthorized radio frequency (RF) transmissions, thereby exposing sensitive mission telemetry to hostile forces.
Furthermore, there is a critical emerging requirement to address sophisticated vulnerabilities residing between the hardware and firmware boundaries. The DoW seeks capabilities to identify malicious logic that facilitates unauthorized data inspection within the data layer, allowing an adversary to silently monitor, filter, or alter encrypted traffic streams at the silicon level. Additionally, the solution must investigate vectors where the data layer is manipulated to trigger unintended electromagnetic emanations from legitimate components, or the covert activation of dormant RF elements, for out-of-band exfiltration. [4]
The DoW seeks proposals for an automated, AI-driven inspection capability to mitigate these threats. The desired solution should ingest a Level 3 Technical Data Package (TDP) or Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) Digital Twin to establish a definitive baseline of intended logic gate behavior. It must then utilize advanced algorithms to process data from Non-Destructive Evaluation (NDE) techniques to physically and logically interrogate the delivered hardware against that baseline, identifying deviations that could enable data-layer subversion, unauthorized emissions, or system failure. [5]
Digital Provenance Integration: This effort seeks to establish an algorithmic layer of assurance compatible with modern secure supply chain initiatives. Proposals should consider the architectural requirements necessary for the proposed engine to interface with emergent DoW digital provenance frameworks, generating unique, verifiable identifiers for individual components before they are integrated into sensitive operational packages.
Data Sourcing Strategy
• Training Dataset (Performer Sourced): Performers must leverage synthetic data (MBSE/GAN generated) and existing open-source physical benchmarks to train models.
• Validation Dataset (Performer Sourced): The performer is responsible for the independent identification, procurement, and physical acquisition of the ICs and Digital Twins required for validation. This must be accomplished without assumption of reliance on Government Furnished Information (GFI); performers may propose use of appropriate GFI if such a database is known and available. This dataset must include a significant subset of components with specific, verified Hardware Trojans to ensure objective benchmarking.

FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS (FAQs)
FAQ 1.0: Commercial Market Overlap and Capability Gaps
• Q1.1: Several commercial companies utilize AI for quality assurance, and emerging platforms offer Deep Supply Chain Illumination and Firmware Assurance. How does this SBIR/STTR effort differ from these commercial offerings, and what specific gap does it close?
• A1.1: This SBIR/STTR bridges the gap between commercial supply chain illumination/firmware analysis and physics-based national security hardware assurance.
• Market Research Summary: The current commercial market includes advanced providers specializing in Deep Supply Chain Illumination, Hardware/Firmware Assurance, and Anti-Tamper & Forensics. Separately, major Failure Analysis (FA) labs utilize tools like Focused Ion Beam (FIB) and Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM) for physical defect localization. [8]
• The Commercial Blind Spot: While firmware assurance platforms excel at identifying counterfeit parts and firmware-level vulnerabilities, they are generally blind to sub-nanometer, perfectly manufactured malicious logic etched directly into the silicon (Hardware Trojans). Furthermore, commercial AI inspection models are optimized for Yield and Reliability. A Hardware Trojan is not an error; it is a Deterministic Malicious Addition. Commercial models will pass a Trojaned chip because it meets all structural tolerances, blinding the supply chain to intentional sabotage. [9][10]
• Bridging the Gap: This proposal funds the development of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) that fuse these disciplines. It seeks to train detection algorithms to find intentionally hidden, malicious logic that commercial defect scanners miss, anchoring that physical assurance to the secure supply chain.
FAQ 2.0: Programmatic Differentiation and Non-Duplication of Effort
• Q2.1: How does this proposed SBIR/STTR effort differ from the DARPA Automatic Implementation of Secure Silicon (AISS) program?
• A2.1: This proposal does not duplicate DARPA AISS. [7] AISS operates in the Pre-Silicon (Design) Phase, automating the insertion of security features into the IC blueprint. This SBIR/STTR operates in the Post-Silicon (Verification) Phase. It assumes a "Zero Trust" posture, acknowledging that adversaries may bypass AISS obfuscation during physical fabrication.
FAQ 3.0: Transition Strategy and the "Valley of Death"
• Q3.1: How does this Phase I/II proposal ensure a viable Phase III transition plan?
• A3.1: By structuring the output as a verification service capable of certifying COTS hardware, the technology becomes an enabling requirement for other acquisition programs. Primary transition targets include defense certification processes and rapid acquisition authorities.
FAQ 4.0: Data Rights and Intellectual Property (IP) Friction
• Q4.1: How will this initiative overcome the reluctance of commercial vendors to share proprietary Level 3 TDPs?
• A4.1: Performers are encouraged to design their AI/ML ingestion models using secure enclave or "zero-knowledge proof" principles to mathematically compare the physical scan against the Digital Twin without exposing human-readable schematics.

title: Compact High Energy Density Capacitors For Pulsed Field X-Ray Generators
summary: High energy density capacitors and their constituent dielectrics are vital components for multiple DoW capability needs for high voltage power supplies, Marx generators, high-power microwave sources, and other pulsed-power technologies.
description:
High energy density capacitors and their constituent dielectrics are vital components for multiple DoW capability needs for high voltage power supplies, Marx generators, high-power microwave sources, and other pulsed-power technologies. The Missile Defense Agency, ONR, NASA and other government agencies have funded efforts into high energy density capacitors for a variety of applications.1 However, it is still very challenging to fabricate high energy density capacitors that reliably meet ultra-compact size constraints for miniaturized high voltage pulse power applications and in a ruggedized field-use system.
Recent prototype development of compact pulsed X-ray generators for portable radiographic imaging applications has underscored the difficulty of scaling capacitor technologies originally developed for larger directed energy and pulsed power systems down to the ultra-compact sizes needed for man-portable or small unmanned systems. Key challenges include preserving dielectric performance and high-voltage hold-off at reduced dimensions, achieving robust voltage reversal tolerance essential for Marx generator topologies, maintaining long operational lifetimes under pulsed conditions with repetition rates up to 100 Hz, and attaining high manufacturing yields with consistent quality for reliable field deployment. This topic specifically targets the development of reliable fabrication processes and advanced dielectric materials to overcome these miniaturization and ruggedization barriers for X-ray generator pulsed power applications.
DTRA seeks to develop reliable and efficient fabrication and production processes for compact high energy density capacitors.
The solution must meet the following minimum specifications:
• Outer Dimensions: No larger than 2 inches x 1 inch x 0.5 inch
• Voltage Rating: 100kV*
• Capacitance: ≥ 2nF
• Voltage Reversal Tolerance: 80%*
• Operating Environment: Dielectric Liquid or Pressurized Gas (e.g., such as SF6)
• Operating Temperature: Capable of meeting MIL-STD
• Ability to survive commercial requirements for shock and vibration (i.e. rough handling)
• Lifetime: Greater than 100,000 full-charge cycles
• Duty cycle: Up to 100 Hz
• Charge/Discharge time: Charging order of 10s of microseconds, discharge order of few nanoseconds
*Note: Operating voltage and voltage reversal are the highest priority specifications. DTRA may consider small deviations from the other minimum specifications (e.g. size) if the solution is capable of approaching or meeting the objective voltage and voltage reversal specifications below.
Objective specifications:
• Voltage Rating: 250kV
• Capacitance: ≥ 10nF
• Capacitance Tolerance: ±10%
• Voltage Reversal Tolerance: 100%
• Operating Temperature: Capable of meeting MIL-STD
• Vibration: Capable of meeting MIL-STD
• Lifetime greater than full-charge 1,000,000 cycles
This effort shall develop a reliable manufacturing process for high energy density capacitors while maintaining the performance parameters outlined above. The proposed effort will require that developed capacitors be tested and validated in Phase 2.

title: Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO)
summary: Army formations, including XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) and its subordinate formations, operating in Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO) face increasingly capable adversary intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) systems that can exploit electromagnetic emissions to detect, characterize, locate, and target command posts, platforms, and other mission-critical nodes.
description:
Army formations, including XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) and its subordinate formations, operating in Large-Scale Combat Operations (LSCO) face increasingly capable adversary intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) systems that can exploit electromagnetic emissions to detect, characterize, locate, and target command posts, platforms, and other mission-critical nodes. The proliferation of networked sensors and increasingly rapid sensor-to-shooter processes creates a need for affordable and scalable capabilities that reduce the effectiveness of adversary electromagnetic sensing and targeting.

XVIII ABC requires capabilities that can be rapidly employed and distributed across formations to improve electromagnetic signature management and enhance survivability and freedom of maneuver in contested environments. This topic seeks innovative approaches for Command Electromagnetic Management & Command-node Awareness, Management, and Obscuration (CEMA CAMO), a low-cost, modular, distributed, and attritable capability for electromagnetic signature management. The desired solution should enable multiple software-configurable nodes to operate cooperatively across an operational area to sense the local electromagnetic environment and generate controlled electromagnetic activity that increases ambiguity and uncertainty for adversary ISR and targeting processes. Potential approaches may include distributed electromagnetic signature shaping, configurable RF effects representations, coordinated emissions, and adaptive management of distributed nodes.
