Proposed solutions should address the ability to sense and characterize the local electromagnetic environment, coordinate activity across distributed nodes, generate Government-authorized RF effects representations, and dynamically adapt system behavior as the electromagnetic environment changes.

The solution should emphasize low cost, low size, weight, and power (SWaP), modularity, scalability, software configurability, distributed operation, and interoperability with Army command-and-control architectures at Corp and Division. Innovative approaches to autonomous coordination, AI-enabled processing, electromagnetic environment awareness, and dynamic signature management are encouraged. The capability should be scalable from individual nodes to distributed networks and adaptable to different platforms and operational environments. Offerors should characterize key trades including frequency coverage, bandwidth, processing requirements, network latency and synchronization, RF-generation capability, SWaP, node density, and unit cost. Solutions should demonstrate a credible pathway toward a fielded node cost below $50,000, with $30,000 desired where technically feasible.

The desired outcome is a prototype capability that demonstrates how XVIII ABC and Army formations can employ distributed, attritable electromagnetic spectrum technologies to improve survivability and freedom of maneuver by complicating adversary ISR, reducing confidence in electromagnetic-derived targeting information, and degrading adversary decision-making and targeting cycles during LSCO.

Throughout the SBIR|STTR Phase I and Phase II, CEMA CAMO prototype capabilities will be demonstrated in partnership with Joint Innovation Out Post (JIOP) through XVIII Airborne Corps (XVIII ABC) experimentation to assess operational effectiveness, inform capability refinement, and demonstrate integration with Army formations and command-and-control architectures.

title: Battle Damage Indications / Battle Damage Assessment Collection, Aggregation, and Analytics Improvement
summary: To preserve decision advantage during contested-space operations, the United States Space Force (USSF) must rapidly correlate multi-source operational data to streamline Phase 5 (Mission Planning & Force Execution) and Phase 6 (Assessment) of the Space Tasking Cycle (STC) and Joint Targeting Cycle (JTC).

title: OPEN- SBIR Direct-to-Phase-II Call for Innovative Defense-Related Dual-Purpose Technologies/Solutions with a Clear Space Force Stakeholder Need
summary: The Space Force is a large and complex organization consisting of many functions, a vast majority of which have similar counterparts in the commercial sector. It is important that potential solutions have a high probability of keeping pace with technological change. Thus, solutions should be closely tied to commercial technologies and solutions supporting the proposed development.
description:
The Space Force is a large and complex organization consisting of many functions, a vast majority of which have similar counterparts in the commercial sector. It is important that potential solutions have a high probability of keeping pace with technological change. Thus, solutions should be closely tied to commercial technologies and solutions supporting the proposed development. This topic is meant for non-defense commercial solutions to be adapted to meet Space Force stakeholders' needs.

The topic is truly 'open' (agnostic of industry, technology, and problem area), but proposals for this topic should demonstrate a high probability of identifying a product-mission fit between a Space Force stakeholder and the proposed adaptation of the non-defense commercial solution.

This is accomplished most effectively through a proposal with a mature non-defense technical solution and a clear understanding of its adaptation to meet a USSF customer's specific need, supported by documentation from a specific motivated, empowered technical point of contact (TPOC) ready and willing to participate in the proposed prototype solution's trial.

According to the USSF Commercial Space Strategy, there are eight (8) mission areas considered for commercial support: Space Domain Awareness (SDA); Satellite Communications (SATCOM); Space Access, Mobility, and Logistics (SAML); Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance (ISR) – hereafter referred to as Tactical Surveillance, Reconnaissance, and Tracking (TacSRT); Space-based Environmental Monitoring (SBEM); Cyberspace Operations; Command and Control (C2); and Positioning, Navigation, and Timing (PNT). Additionally, the USSF will seek hybrid solutions for Space Mission Enablers, those functions that span multiple missions and are fundamental to conducting space operations. Although the USSF also performs missile warning, combat power projection, electromagnetic warfare, and nuclear detonation (NUDET) detection, the USSF is not currently seeking commercial support for these missions.
Additional information on the USSF Commercial Space Strategy can be found at https://www.spaceforce.mil/Portals/2/Documents/Space%20Policy/USSF_Commercial_Space_Strategy.pdf.

Additionally, it is possible for a solution to provide a capability in a previously unconsidered area. Therefore, if an applicant feels its solution does not fit within one of the listed capabilities, it can reference the “BLUE SKY” category, including an explanation of the solution’s ability to provide increased strategic capability within the context of Air Force, Space Force, national, and global constraints. As applicable, the applicant should address the category(ies) to which the solution aligns in the Technical Volume.
Proposals should identify which of the OUSW (R&E) Critical Technology Areas, Component Technology Areas, USSF Commercial Space Strategy Mission Areas the proposed solution addresses or otherwise reference "BLUE SKY" and include an explanation of the solution's ability to provide increased strategic capability within the context of USSF, national, and global constraints.

title: Next-generation Green Monopropellant Gas Generation
summary: The USSF has a desire to use liquid monopropellants for high thrust propulsion (natively in chemical thrusters) and for low-thrust, very energetic missions (in electric propulsion thrusters) - so called Multimode Propulsion (MMP) capabilities - to support Dynamic Space Operations.
description:
The USSF has a desire to use liquid monopropellants for high thrust propulsion (natively in chemical thrusters) and for low-thrust, very energetic missions (in electric propulsion thrusters) - so called Multimode Propulsion (MMP) capabilities - to support Dynamic Space Operations. Such MMP capabilities have a number of very favorable characteristics including high propellant density, reduced need for high pressure storage systems, continued need for chemical propulsion on DoW assets for high thrust prompt maneuver, and compatibility with future on-orbit liquid propellant refueling capabilities.

One critical capability gap is an energy efficient, precision propellant feed system which efficiently converts next-generation liquid monopropellant into non-reactive vapor phase products which can be fed into the electric propulsion (EP) thruster. Key challenges arise from the fact that next-generation monopropellants have negligible vapor pressure and are extremely difficult to combust at low temperature and pressure.

The desired technology should present a solution for a feed system capable of supporting sub-kW to 100 kW class EP systems:
- Operation at minimum on ASCENT propellant (T) or on ASCENT and other monopropellant formulations (O)
- Realtime telemetry, including mass flow rate, species composition, and temperature as inputs to the EP device
- Maintain consistently characterized molecular composition (T) and extremely stable molecular composition (O) of the output vapor and support both steady-state and pulsed operation at frequencies greater than 5 Hz
- Minimal SWaP with particular focus on low power consumption
- Incorporate fluid/vapor facing materials that can reliably withstand long-term exposure to green monopropellants and their breakdown products over the required lifespan. Potential issues also include condensation or freezing for long-duration propellant storage in ullage and plenums if these or similar components are used
- Demonstrate rapid warmup/gas generation in less than 10 minutes (T) or on-demand (O)
- Ensure lifetime design consideration for future multiple refueling opportunities

This work directly supports the Contested Logistics Technologies (LOG) Critical Technology Area with respect to space mobility operations.
